descriptors.title: People in my family
descriptors.description: the people in their family, where they were born and raised, and how they are related to each other
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal experience of their family through lived experience. No formal prior HASS curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the people in their family, where they were born and raised, and explain how family members are related to each other.

nodes.label: Who is in my family
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the members of their family and use family relationship terms (mother, father, grandparent, sibling, auntie, uncle, cousin) to describe who they are.
criteria: Names at least three people in their family using correct relationship terms
Distinguishes between immediate and extended family members
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot name and relate family members cannot build the concept map or personal narrative required in subsequent nodes — the social organisational vocabulary is the foundation.

width.minimum: Name at least three family members and use at least two relationship terms correctly.
width.typical: Identify a range of family members across two generations (self, parents/caregivers, grandparents/extended family) and use a variety of relationship terms; acknowledge that families have different structures.
wider: Explore kinship terms used in First Nations Australian families, such as cousin-brother and mother-auntie, and discuss how family structure and naming differs across cultures
Compare family structures across the class, noting similarities and differences (nuclear, single-parent, extended, blended, grandparent-led)

modes.reason: Students need to build a working vocabulary of relationship terms before they can use them to describe connections. Use photos, drawings and family member visits to build range.

nodes.label: Where family members were born and raised
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify where key family members were born and raised, and locate these places on a simple map or describe them in relative terms.
criteria: Identifies where at least one family member was born or raised
Uses at least one location term to describe that place relative to where they live now

width.minimum: Identify the birthplace or hometown of at least one parent or grandparent and describe it using basic location language (near/far, same place/different place).
width.typical: Identify and describe where two or more family members were born and raised; represent these places on a pictorial map or drawing; use terms like near, far, same city, different country.
wider: Investigate families with connections to countries outside Australia and locate those countries on a globe or world map
Compare family origin stories and discuss why people move to different places

modes.reason: Birthplace and origin vary enormously across a class — use this diversity to broaden understanding of where families come from and what 'place' means.

nodes.label: How family members are related
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how two or more family members are connected to each other, using relationship terms and a visual representation such as a concept map or family drawing.
criteria: Explains how at least two family members are related to themselves
Produces a visual representation (drawing, concept map, photograph arrangement) showing family connections

width.minimum: Explain how at least two family members are related to them and to each other (e.g. 'My grandma is my mum's mum').
width.typical: Construct a concept map or drawing showing connections between self and multiple family members across two generations; label relationships using appropriate terms.
wider: Explore how First Nations Australian kinship systems describe relationships that extend beyond nuclear family structures
Compare how family relationship terms differ across languages spoken in the class community

modes.reason: This node brings together vocabulary from Node 1 and place knowledge from Node 2 into a coherent personal narrative — the concept map is the integration task.

descriptors.title: Celebrations and commemorations
descriptors.description: the celebrations and commemorations of significant events shared with their families and others
descriptors.knowledge: Students have lived experience of family celebrations. No formal prior HASS curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify celebrations and commemorations that are significant to their families and communities, and explain why they are important.

nodes.label: What celebrations and commemorations are
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a celebration (marking a joyful or important event) and a commemoration (remembering a significant person or event), and name examples of each from their own experience.
criteria: Names at least one celebration and one commemoration from their own experience
Describes at least one feature of each (what happens, who participates)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish celebration from commemoration cannot explain why events are significant — the conceptual distinction underpins the next node's explanatory demand.

width.minimum: Name at least one celebration and one commemoration from their own life and describe what happens during it.
width.typical: Identify a range of celebrations (birthdays, religious festivals, cultural events) and commemorations (Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week) from a provided calendar; describe key features of each type.
wider: Compare how different cultural and religious groups celebrate similar occasions in different ways; for example, how New Year is celebrated in different cultures
Explore the role of First Nations Australian celebrations and commemorations, such as NAIDOC Week and Coming of the Light, in maintaining cultural identity

modes.reason: The celebration/commemoration distinction is conceptually subtle at Foundation level. Use concrete examples and visual anchors — what does each look like, how do people feel, what are they marking?

nodes.label: Why celebrations and commemorations are important
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why at least one celebration or commemoration is important to their family or community, using language about significance, memory, and belonging.
criteria: Explains why at least one celebration or commemoration is important to them or their family
Uses at least one term relating to significance, memory or belonging

width.minimum: Explain in their own words why one celebration or commemoration matters to them or their family.
width.typical: Discuss why multiple celebrations and commemorations are important to different people and groups; connect significance to ideas of memory, identity, tradition and shared belonging.
wider: Explore how generations hand on traditions through celebrations and what would be lost if they stopped
Investigate how First Nations Australian ceremonies and storytelling transmit cultural knowledge from one generation to the next

modes.reason: Significance is most accessible when students discuss their own celebrations first, then encounter others'. Use sharing circles and a class calendar to build range.

descriptors.title: Features of familiar places
descriptors.description: the features of familiar places they belong to, why some places are special and how places can be looked after
descriptors.knowledge: Students have lived experience of places they inhabit. No formal prior HASS curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify features of familiar places, explain why some places are special to them, and describe ways places can be looked after.

nodes.label: Features of familiar places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe features of familiar places using observation and simple place vocabulary.
criteria: Identifies at least three features of a familiar place
Uses at least two place vocabulary terms (e.g. natural, built, near, far)
nodes.hinge_reason: Without feature vocabulary for places, students cannot explain what makes a place special or how to care for it — nodes 2 and 3 both require this observational foundation.

width.minimum: Identify at least three features of one familiar place (e.g. the school) using provided vocabulary (natural, built, people, activities).
width.typical: Explore and describe features of multiple familiar places (home, school, neighbourhood, local park); use senses-based observation to identify natural and constructed features.
wider: Compare features of familiar places with places students have visited or seen in stories or on television
Identify features of places in First Nations Australian stories and Dreaming stories, discussing what is special about those places

modes.reason: Build a working vocabulary of place features through observation walks, photographs and drawings before asking students to describe or evaluate places.

nodes.label: Why some places are special
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why a particular place is special to them or others, connecting significance to personal experience, memory or cultural meaning.
criteria: Names at least one place that is special to them
Gives at least one reason why that place is special

width.minimum: Identify one place that is special to them and give at least one reason why.
width.typical: Explain why several different places are special to different people; connect significance to ideas such as belonging, memory, basic needs, recreation and cultural or spiritual meaning.
wider: Explore why Country/Place is special and significant to First Nations Australians and how that significance differs from everyday familiarity
Share stories about special places from different cultural backgrounds represented in the class

modes.reason: Significance varies by person and culture — using class sharing and diverse stories reveals that 'special' is not one thing.

nodes.label: How places can be looked after
nodes.checkpoint: Students can suggest ways to care for a familiar place and describe what would happen if that care was not taken.
criteria: Identifies at least one way to care for a familiar place
Connects the care action to the reason the place is valuable

width.minimum: Suggest at least one action to care for a familiar place (e.g. classroom, playground) and explain why that action matters.
width.typical: Identify multiple ways different places can be cared for; connect care actions to what makes those places important; discuss shared responsibility for looking after places.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australian practices of caring for Country/Place and discuss what these practices involve
Compare how care for a local natural place (e.g. a park or creek) differs from care for a constructed place (e.g. a playground)

modes.reason: This node integrates feature knowledge (what is in the place) and significance understanding (why it matters) into action — caring for places because we value them.

descriptors.title: Country/Place and First Nations Australians
descriptors.description: the importance of Country/Place to First Nations Australians and the Country/Place on which the school is located
descriptors.knowledge: Students have general experience of place from AC9HSFK03. No formal prior knowledge of First Nations Australian concepts of Country/Place.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the importance of Country/Place to First Nations Australians, name the local First Nations Australian language group, and identify the Country/Place on which their school is located.

nodes.label: What Country/Place means to First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why the term Country/Place (capitalised) is used by First Nations Australians and how its meaning differs from everyday uses of 'country' or 'place'.
criteria: Explains that Country/Place means more to First Nations Australians than just a physical location
Gives at least one example of a connection First Nations Australians have to Country/Place
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding the distinct meaning of Country/Place, students cannot identify the local language group or discuss local significance in Node 2 — the conceptual distinction is necessary before applying it locally.

width.minimum: Explain in simple terms that Country/Place is used by First Nations Australians to describe a deep, living connection to land, sea, waterways, sky and animals — not just a physical location.
width.typical: Explore the meaning of Country/Place through stories, invited community members, and visual sources; describe what connections First Nations Australians have to Country/Place (land, sea, sky, living things, spiritual connections).
wider: Listen to and respond to Dreaming and Creation stories that describe the relationship between First Nations Australians and specific Country/Place features
Compare the concept of Country/Place with students' own experiences of places that feel special or belonging to them

modes.reason: The concept of Country/Place as a living relationship (not just a physical location) requires explicit scaffolding. Use concrete anchors — stories, images, community voices — before asking students to explain the concept.

nodes.label: Our local Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and use the name of the local First Nations Australian language group and name the Country/Place on which their school is located.
criteria: Names the local First Nations Australian language group
States the Country/Place on which their school is located

width.minimum: Identify the name of the local First Nations Australian language group and state the Country/Place of the school.
width.typical: Use the name of the local First Nations Australian language group correctly in context; identify local places of cultural significance to that group; listen and respond to community members talking about Country/Place.
wider: Identify multiple local places of significance to First Nations Australians in the local area
Explore how Welcome to Country and Acknowledgement of Country ceremonies are used to recognise Traditional Owners and Custodians

modes.reason: Local community engagement — where possible, invited Traditional Owners or community members — provides the most authentic and respectful context for this node.

descriptors.title: Pose questions
descriptors.description: pose questions about familiar objects, people, places and events
descriptors.knowledge: Students have natural question-asking capacity from lived experience. No formal prior HASS inquiry skills curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students pose questions about familiar objects, people, places and events to guide their own inquiry.

nodes.label: Noticing and wondering
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify something they notice or are curious about when exploring a source (object, photograph, place, story) and express it as a question.
criteria: Generates at least one question about a provided source using a question stem
Question relates to something observable or inferable from the source
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot generate their own questions from observation, all subsequent inquiry work is teacher-driven rather than student-initiated — the questioning habit is the foundation of the entire inquiry skills strand.

width.minimum: Generate at least one question about a provided source using a prompted stem (What is...? Where is...? Why does...?).
width.typical: Generate multiple questions about familiar objects, people, places and events after being prompted to observe carefully; use a range of question stems (What, Where, Who, Why, How).
wider: Generate questions before and after an excursion or visiting community member, comparing what they wanted to know with what they found out
Sort questions by type (What/Where/Who questions vs Why/How questions) and discuss which are easier to answer and why

modes.reason: At Foundation, question generation is a new habit. Build a class repertoire of question stems displayed visually, and practise generating questions from multiple different sources before expecting independence.

nodes.label: Posing inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose questions that would guide an investigation about a familiar object, person, place or event, distinguishing between questions they can answer from memory and those that need investigation.
criteria: Poses at least one question that would require finding information from a source
Can identify whether a question can be answered from memory or needs investigation

width.minimum: Pose at least one question about a familiar topic that requires seeking information beyond personal memory.
width.typical: Pose questions about family and places that would guide an inquiry; identify which questions can be answered from personal experience and which require investigation from sources.
wider: Develop questions about what makes events and places special, generating both factual and personal-response questions
Pose questions for a family member or familiar adult and explain why that person would be a good source

modes.reason: This node integrates noticing from Node 1 with directing inquiry — questions now have an investigative purpose, not just curiosity expression.

descriptors.title: Sort and record information
descriptors.description: sort and record information including pictorial timelines and locations on pictorial maps or models
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal sorting experience from everyday life. No formal prior HASS inquiry skills curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students sort and record information using pictorial timelines and pictorial maps or models.

nodes.label: Sorting information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sort provided sources (photographs, objects, drawings) into categories relevant to an inquiry question.
criteria: Sorts at least four items into two categories using a provided rule
Can explain why an item belongs in a particular category
nodes.hinge_reason: Sorting is the prerequisite for recording — students who cannot sort into categories cannot build a meaningful pictorial timeline or map in the following node.

width.minimum: Sort at least four items into two categories using a provided sorting rule (e.g. old/new, near/far, same/different).
width.typical: Sort a range of sources (photographs, drawings, objects, mementoes) into relevant categories for a HASS inquiry; explain the reason for sorting decisions.
wider: Create their own sorting categories for a set of sources and explain the reasoning behind their categories
Sort sources chronologically and explain what the ordering reveals about change over time

modes.reason: Sorting requires practice with physical materials before moving to recording. Use hands-on manipulation of photographs, cards and objects before expecting students to translate sorting into a recorded format.

nodes.label: Pictorial timelines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can add photographs or drawings to a pictorial timeline in the correct sequence, representing events from their own life or a familiar story.
criteria: Places at least three items on a timeline in correct sequence
Can explain why one item comes before or after another

width.minimum: Sequence at least three photographs or drawings on a provided timeline, placing them in correct time order.
width.typical: Add photographs or drawn representations of significant events to a pictorial timeline; create a timeline of events over the year or key family events; explain the sequence.
wider: Compare two timelines (e.g. their own timeline vs a family member's) and identify events that appear in both
Create a class timeline of significant shared events, discussing how to decide what goes on it

modes.reason: Sequencing is a new cognitive demand at Foundation — practise with clearly ordered physical events before adding less familiar or ambiguous items.

nodes.label: Locations on pictorial maps or models
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify features on a provided pictorial map or model of a familiar place and link drawn representations to their real-world locations.
criteria: Identifies at least two features on a provided pictorial map
Links at least one map feature to a drawing or photograph of that feature

width.minimum: Identify at least two features on a provided pictorial map of a familiar place (e.g. school map) and match them to pictures or drawings of those features.
width.typical: Use a provided pictorial map or oblique aerial photograph to find and link multiple features to pictures; describe the location of features using simple spatial terms (near, beside, opposite).
wider: Add a new feature to a pictorial map using a symbol or drawing and explain its location relative to existing features
Compare a pictorial map with a photograph of the same place and identify similarities and differences

modes.reason: Maps integrate sorting (what features are there) and location vocabulary into a spatial record — this is the node where both come together in a representational format.

descriptors.title: Share a perspective
descriptors.description: share a perspective on information, such as stories about significant events and special places
descriptors.knowledge: Students have opinions and preferences from lived experience. No formal prior HASS inquiry skills curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share their own perspective on information about significant events and special places, using sources to support their view.

nodes.label: Recognising that perspectives differ
nodes.checkpoint: Students can recognise that different people can have different views about the same event or place, and that both can be valid.
criteria: Identifies that at least two people have different views about the same event or place
Describes what each person thinks without judging one as wrong
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot recognise that perspectives differ will present their own view as universal fact, making it impossible for them to genuinely share a perspective (as distinct from stating a fact) in Node 2.

width.minimum: Identify that two people in a story or class discussion have different views about the same thing and describe what each person thinks.
width.typical: Explore provided stories or class discussions where perspectives differ; identify what shapes each perspective (personal experience, cultural background, what someone values).
wider: Compare how the same celebration or place is viewed differently by different family members or cultural groups
Explore First Nations Australian perspectives on places that are also significant to other community members

modes.reason: Perspective-taking is conceptually demanding at Foundation — use concrete scenarios where the divergence is clear and meaningful before asking students to apply the concept to their own views.

nodes.label: Sharing my own perspective
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share their own perspective on a significant event or special place, explaining why they feel that way and using a source to support their view.
criteria: Shares a personal view about a significant event or special place
Gives at least one reason for that view

width.minimum: Share a personal view about a special place or significant event and give one reason for that view.
width.typical: Share perspectives on stories about significant events and special places using provided sources; explain why the place or event is important from their own point of view; connect their perspective to personal experience.
wider: Share perspectives about a place that is important to past generations of their family, explaining why those events and places are special
Listen to a First Nations Australian story about a special place and share a response, comparing it with their own experience of special places

modes.reason: A range of significant events and places gives students more contexts to form and share views — class diversity is the primary resource here.

descriptors.title: Draw conclusions
descriptors.description: draw conclusions in response to questions
descriptors.knowledge: Students have answered questions from personal experience. No formal prior HASS inquiry skills curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions in response to inquiry questions about their family, celebrations, places and ways of caring for places.

nodes.label: Using evidence to answer questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use information from a source (story, photograph, observation) to answer an inquiry question, rather than relying on personal memory alone.
criteria: Answers an inquiry question using at least one piece of evidence from a source
Can identify where the answer came from ('I know this because...')
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat all answers as opinions rather than evidence-based conclusions cannot draw conclusions in the next node — evidence-based reasoning is the prerequisite for conclusion-drawing.

width.minimum: Answer one inquiry question using at least one piece of evidence from a provided source.
width.typical: Use information from multiple sources (photographs, observations, stories) to answer inquiry questions about family, places and celebrations; explain where the answer came from.
wider: Compare answers to the same question from different sources and discuss which source they find more useful and why
Identify when a source answers the question fully and when they need more information

modes.reason: Make the evidence-to-conclusion chain explicit: 'I know this because I saw/heard/read...' Use sentence stems and model the reasoning aloud before expecting students to do it independently.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw a conclusion in response to an inquiry question about family, celebrations, places or caring for places, supported by evidence from sources.
criteria: Draws at least one conclusion in response to an inquiry question
Supports the conclusion with at least one piece of evidence

width.minimum: Draw one conclusion in response to a provided inquiry question, supported by at least one piece of evidence.
width.typical: Draw conclusions about main people in family, important celebrations, features of special places, and ways of caring for places; support each conclusion with evidence from sources or observations.
wider: Draw conclusions about a place and suggest what would change if it were not cared for
Draw conclusions about why a celebration is important by comparing it across two different families or cultural groups

modes.reason: Conclusion-drawing integrates questioning, sourcing and evidence-use — model the full inquiry cycle explicitly before expecting students to execute it independently.

descriptors.title: Share narratives and observations
descriptors.description: share narratives and observations, using sources and terms about the past and places
descriptors.knowledge: Students can tell stories about their own experience. No formal prior HASS inquiry skills curriculum.
descriptors.endpoint: Students share narratives and observations about the past and places, using sources and subject-specific terms for time and location.

nodes.label: Using time and place vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use basic time terms (then, now, yesterday, today, tomorrow) and location terms (near, far, above, below, beside, opposite) correctly in spoken communication.
criteria: Uses at least two time terms correctly in context
Uses at least two location terms correctly in context
nodes.hinge_reason: Without subject-specific vocabulary for time and place, students cannot share narratives or observations in HASS-specific terms — the vocabulary is the communicative tool for the next node.

width.minimum: Use at least two time terms and two location terms correctly in describing a familiar event or place.
width.typical: Use a range of time and place terms appropriately when talking about their own experiences, family events and familiar places; demonstrate understanding of the terms through actions, drawings and talk.
wider: Collect and compare time terms used by different family members or cultural groups (e.g. 'the old days', 'back then', 'once upon a time')
Use location terms to describe directions during a walk or observation of the school grounds

modes.reason: Vocabulary consolidation through frequent, contextualised use — in transition, observation, discussion and labelling — before expecting students to deploy it in narratives.

nodes.label: Sharing narratives and observations using sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share a narrative about a special place or family event using photographs, artefacts or drawings as sources, and use subject-specific terms for time and place.
criteria: Shares a narrative about a special place or family event using at least one source
Uses at least one time term and one location term correctly in the narrative

width.minimum: Share a spoken narrative about a special place or family event using at least one source (photograph, drawing, artefact) and at least one time or place term.
width.typical: Create a display or oral presentation about a special place or family event using multiple sources; use time and place terms accurately throughout; explain the significance of the event or place.
wider: Share a narrative that connects a present event or place to the past using terms like 'then' and 'now'
Use a pictorial map or timeline as a source when sharing an observation about a place or event

modes.reason: This node brings together source use, vocabulary and personal narrative — the communicative endpoint of Foundation HASS inquiry.

descriptors.title: Family structures and roles over time
descriptors.description: differences in family structures and roles today, and how these have changed or remained the same over time
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK01): Students identified people in their family, where they were born and raised, and how family members are related. They used relationship vocabulary and created concept maps of family.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain differences in family structures and roles today, and describe how these have changed or remained the same over time.

nodes.label: Variety of family structures today
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a range of family structures in contemporary Australia and describe how they differ from each other.
criteria: Identifies at least three different family structures by name
Describes one similarity and one difference between two family structures
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding the range of current family structures, students cannot compare them with past structures — the baseline comparison requires knowing what the current variety looks like.

width.minimum: Identify at least three different family structures (e.g. nuclear, single-parent, extended, blended) and describe one way they differ.
width.typical: Explore the full range of family structures including nuclear, one-child, large, single-parent, extended, blended/step, adoptive, foster, grandparent-led and kinship group families; describe similarities and differences between them.
wider: Investigate kinship group structures in First Nations Australian communities and compare with Western family structure categories
Explore how families in different countries are structured differently and what shapes those structures

modes.reason: Students need exposure to a genuinely wide range of family structures before comparison — use books, photographs and class sharing to build the range before moving to comparison.

nodes.label: Roles of family members
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe roles played by different family members (parents, children, extended family) and note that these roles can vary across families.
criteria: Names at least two roles played by family members
Notes that the same role can be filled by different people in different families

width.minimum: Describe at least two different roles played by family members (e.g. caregiver, breadwinner, elder) and give an example of each.
width.typical: Examine roles of parents, children and extended family members across a range of family structures; note how roles can vary by culture, age and circumstance.
wider: Investigate how roles of elders and extended family members differ in First Nations Australian families compared with other family types
Explore how gender roles within families have changed across generations

modes.reason: Family roles are most effectively explored through comparison — use parent/grandparent interviews alongside class sharing to reveal the range.

nodes.label: Change and continuity over time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare family structures and roles from the past (parents' and grandparents' generations) with the present, identifying what has changed and what has remained the same.
criteria: Identifies at least one change in family structures or roles across generations
Identifies at least one aspect of family life that has remained the same over time

width.minimum: Compare at least one family structure or role from a grandparent's time with today, identifying one change and one continuity.
width.typical: Compare family structures and roles across at least two generations using photographs, oral histories and discussions with family elders; identify patterns of change and continuity in family size, roles and composition.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian family and kinship structures have shown continuity despite the pressures of colonisation
Explore how immigration and migration patterns have changed family structures across generations in Australia

modes.reason: This node integrates knowledge of current structures (Node 1) and roles (Node 2) with historical comparison — the change/continuity analysis is the full descriptor demand.

descriptors.title: Daily life continuity and change
descriptors.description: continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK02): Students explored celebrations and commemorations and their significance. From AC9HS1K01: Students compared family structures and roles across generations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify continuity and change between aspects of their daily lives and their parents' and grandparents' childhoods.

nodes.label: Aspects of daily life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify key aspects of daily life (home, family traditions, leisure, school, shopping) and describe what these look like today.
criteria: Identifies at least three aspects of daily life from their own experience
Describes what each aspect looks like today with a concrete example
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need a clear contemporary baseline for each aspect of daily life before they can meaningfully compare with the past — comparison requires knowing what 'now' looks like.

width.minimum: Identify at least three aspects of daily life (e.g. toys, school, home) and describe what they look like today.
width.typical: Explore a range of aspects of daily life including homes, family traditions, religious and cultural practices, leisure, school life, rules and consumer habits; describe each aspect using concrete examples from their own experience.
wider: Examine traditional toys and games used by First Nations Australian children, such as Arrernte string games, and discuss their purpose in cultural learning
Explore daily life aspects for children in another country today and compare with Australian daily life

modes.reason: Build a class inventory of contemporary daily life aspects using personal experience, photographs and objects before introducing historical sources for comparison.

nodes.label: Comparing past and present daily life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare aspects of their daily life with the same aspects in their parents' or grandparents' childhoods, identifying similarities and differences using sources.
criteria: Compares at least two aspects of daily life across generations
Identifies at least one change and one continuity between past and present daily life

width.minimum: Compare at least two aspects of daily life between their childhood and a grandparent's or parent's childhood, identifying one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Compare and comment on photographs and oral histories to find out how daily lives have changed and remained the same across generations; compare homes, toys, school, leisure and cultural practices.
wider: Compare daily life across three generations (grandparents, parents, self) and track a pattern of change over time
Use artefacts and photographs to compare daily life in two different cultural contexts from the same time period

modes.reason: Oral histories and photographs from family members are the richest source — the range of comparison cases in the class creates natural breadth.

nodes.label: Using comparative language for change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use comparative language to describe change and continuity across generations, applying terms from provided vocabulary.
criteria: Uses at least three comparative terms accurately when describing change over time
Comparative language is applied to specific evidence, not used generically

width.minimum: Use at least three comparative terms (e.g. 'bigger than', 'more rainy', 'fewer') accurately when comparing past and present aspects of daily life.
width.typical: Apply comparative language when describing family life over time: 'smaller/bigger', 'closer/further', 'hotter/colder', 'fewer/less', 'younger/older'; use these terms accurately in written and spoken responses.
wider: Create a comparison chart or Venn diagram showing daily life changes and continuities, labelling with comparative language
Identify which changes were the most significant and give a reason for their choice

modes.reason: Comparative language requires accurate usage — practise through categorisation tasks, sentence frames and labelling before expecting fluency in extended writing or discussion.

descriptors.title: Features of local places
descriptors.description: the natural, managed and constructed features of local places, and their location
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK03): Students identified features of familiar places and why some places are special. They used basic place vocabulary (near, far, natural, built).
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify the natural, managed and constructed features of local places and describe their location.

nodes.label: Natural, managed and constructed features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can classify features of local places as natural (hills, rivers, vegetation, weather), managed (farms, parks, gardens) or constructed (roads, buildings), and give examples of each.
criteria: Classifies at least two features as natural, two as managed and two as constructed
Gives a reason for each classification
nodes.hinge_reason: The three-category classification is the analytical framework for this standard — without it, students cannot locate or discuss features coherently in subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Classify at least six features across all three categories (natural, managed, constructed) with at least one example in each.
width.typical: Identify and classify a full range of natural, managed and constructed features in the local area; locate them on a provided map; explore Dreaming and Creation stories that identify natural features of place.
wider: Listen to and view First Nations Australian Dreaming and Creation stories that identify and explain the origin of natural features, discussing what these reveal about connections between people and place
Classify features of a contrasting place (e.g. a beach, a farm, a mountain) and compare with the local area

modes.reason: The natural/managed/constructed distinction is conceptually new at Year 1. Managed features are often confused with constructed ones — use sorting activities and decision trees to make the categories explicit.

nodes.label: Daily and seasonal weather
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the daily and seasonal weather of their local place using simple descriptive terms and compare it with weather in other places.
criteria: Uses at least four weather terms accurately
Identifies one difference between weather in the local place and another place

width.minimum: Describe the local weather using at least four terms (rainy, hot, cold, windy, cloudy) and note one difference between local weather and weather somewhere else.
width.typical: Describe daily and seasonal weather patterns using a range of terms; compare weather across seasons; compare with weather of other known or familiar places.
wider: Record weather observations over a week or season and identify patterns
Compare weather of the local place with weather in a neighbouring region or a place connected to a family member's origin

modes.reason: Weather vocabulary requires repeated practice in context — daily weather recording builds fluency with the terms before comparative use.

nodes.label: Locating and describing features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain where features and places are located using direction and location terms, and locate them on a map.
criteria: Locates at least two features on a provided map
Uses at least two location terms accurately to describe feature positions

width.minimum: Locate at least two features on a provided map and describe their position using at least two location terms (beside, near, forward, close to).
width.typical: Locate natural, managed and constructed features on a map of the local area; describe their position using a range of spatial terms (beside, forward, up, down, near, further, close to, before, after); explain directions to classmates.
wider: Create a simple map of the local area that shows the location and classification of natural, managed and constructed features
Describe a route between two features in the local area using direction terms in sequence

modes.reason: Locating features on a map integrates the three-category classification (what type of feature) with spatial reasoning (where it is) — the map is the integration task.

descriptors.title: Changing and caring for places
descriptors.description: how places change and how they can be cared for by different groups including First Nations Australians
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK03): Students identified features of places and how places can be looked after. From AC9HS1K03: Students classified local place features as natural, managed or constructed.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how places change and how they can be cared for by different groups including First Nations Australians.

nodes.label: How places change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe examples of how local places change, including changes caused by weather, seasons, erosion and human activity.
criteria: Identifies at least two ways a local place has changed
Distinguishes at least one natural change from one human-caused change
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how places change is prerequisite to understanding why they need care — students who cannot identify change mechanisms cannot explain the need for care actions in Node 2.

width.minimum: Describe at least two ways a local place has changed or could change (e.g. erosion, new buildings, revegetation).
width.typical: Observe and describe changes to natural, managed and constructed features in local places; distinguish changes caused by natural processes (seasons, erosion) from those caused by human activity (construction, clearing); compare current observations with past photographs.
wider: Track change in a specific local place over time using photographs, drawings and observations across seasons
Investigate how a significant environmental change (e.g. clearing, flooding) affected a local place and what happened as a result

modes.reason: Change is most visible through direct observation and photograph comparison — multiple change examples across natural and human-caused change gives students the range needed.

nodes.label: Caring for places — why and how
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how and why local places are cared for, and identify who is responsible for different types of care.
criteria: Describes at least two care actions for a local place
Explains why each care action is needed, connecting it to a change risk

width.minimum: Describe at least two ways a local place can be cared for and explain why that care is needed.
width.typical: Describe how local features and places are cared for; connect care actions to specific change risks (e.g. not walking in muddy areas, watering plants in dry weather); identify who provides care and why.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australian practices of managing and caring for Country/Place and explain how these practices work
Compare how different groups (council, community, Traditional Owners) care for the same place and discuss similarities and differences

modes.reason: First Nations Australian caring practices offer a qualitatively distinct model of care — integrate this alongside local council and community examples for genuine breadth.

nodes.label: Reduce, reuse, recycle — local systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what local resources can be recycled, reduced or reused, and describe the local systems (rules, signs, collection) that support these activities.
criteria: Identifies resources that can be recycled, reduced or reused with examples
Names at least one local system that supports sustainable resource management

width.minimum: Identify at least three resources that can be recycled, reduced or reused and name one local system that supports these activities.
width.typical: Distinguish between recyclable, reducible and reusable resources; identify local spaces and systems (waste collection routes, signs, rules) that support sustainable use; connect resource management to caring for places.
wider: Investigate how local government waste management systems work and who is responsible for each part
Compare resource management practices at home, at school and in the wider community

modes.reason: This node connects caring-for-places principles to concrete local civic systems — an integration of geographic stewardship with civic knowledge.

descriptors.title: Develop questions about past and present
descriptors.description: develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS01): Students posed questions about familiar objects, people, places and events using basic stems (What, Where, Who, Why, How).
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present to guide inquiry.

nodes.label: Questions about the past and present
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generate questions about objects, people, places and events in both the past and present, using 'where', 'what', 'how' and 'why' stems.
criteria: Generates at least one question about the past and one about the present
Uses at least two different question stems (Where, What, How, Why)
nodes.hinge_reason: Year 1 inquiry requires students to direct questions to the past as well as the present — students who only ask about now cannot drive the historical comparison tasks that HASS Year 1 requires.

width.minimum: Generate at least two questions about a provided source — one about the present and one about the past — using at least two different question stems.
width.typical: Pose questions using Where, What, How and Why stems about families and places when provided with everyday objects, photos, maps and observation sketches; ask questions before, during and after listening to stories about people and places.
wider: Prepare a set of questions for parents or grandparents about how and where they lived in the past and the places they value
Sort questions about the past and present and discuss what type of source would best answer each question

modes.reason: Past-directed questions require students to imagine a time they cannot directly observe — model the cognitive move explicitly: 'To find out about the past, we ask questions like...'

nodes.label: Questions that guide inquiry
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop inquiry questions that would guide an investigation about families and places, and identify appropriate sources that would help answer them.
criteria: Develops at least two questions that would genuinely guide an inquiry
Identifies a source that could help answer each question

width.minimum: Develop at least two inquiry questions about families or places and identify one source that could help answer each question.
width.typical: Prepare questions for parents and grandparents about how and where they lived; develop questions before, during and after listening to stories about people and places; identify which sources (objects, photos, maps, oral histories) best answer which questions.
wider: Develop questions specifically designed to reveal perspectives of people from different generations or backgrounds
Evaluate whether provided questions are answerable from available sources, and revise unanswerable questions

modes.reason: Question development for inquiry integrates source awareness with historical curiosity — the inquiry interview is the integration task.

descriptors.title: Collect and record information
descriptors.description: collect, sort and record information and data from observations and from provided sources, including unscaled timelines and labelled maps or models
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS02): Students sorted and recorded information using pictorial timelines and located features on pictorial maps or models.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collect, sort and record information from observations and provided sources, including unscaled timelines and labelled maps.

nodes.label: Collecting from a range of sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect relevant information from a range of provided sources (stories, photographs, maps, observations) for a HASS inquiry.
criteria: Collects information from at least two different source types
Identifies at least one piece of relevant information from each source
nodes.hinge_reason: Recording on timelines and maps (Nodes 2–3) requires students to have collected information first — collecting is the prerequisite; without it, there is nothing to record.

width.minimum: Collect information from at least two different types of sources (e.g. a photograph and an observation) and identify what each source tells them.
width.typical: Explore stories from the past and present about people, families and places (fiction, letters, diaries, songs, Dreaming stories, films); gather evidence from local observations, aerial photographs and sketches; identify relevant information from each source type.
wider: Compare what different source types (photograph vs oral history vs observation) reveal about the same topic and discuss why sources differ
Identify which sources are primary (from the time) and which are secondary (created later) and discuss why this matters

modes.reason: Year 1 students need to encounter multiple source types before they can select and use them — build a class repertoire through whole-class exploration of each source type.

nodes.label: Recording on unscaled timelines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sequence events or objects from different generations onto an unscaled timeline in the correct order.
criteria: Places at least three items on a timeline in correct chronological order
Labels each item with a name or drawn representation

width.minimum: Place at least three labelled items on an unscaled timeline in correct chronological sequence.
width.typical: Create a peg timeline or pictorial timeline in which labelled drawn or photographic representations of events or objects from different generations are placed in correct sequence; explain the ordering.
wider: Create a timeline spanning three generations and identify the biggest changes between each generation
Compare two different timelines of the same topic (e.g. toys then and now) and note similarities and differences in what each shows

modes.reason: Sequencing on unscaled timelines requires spatial reasoning about time — use physical peg timelines and sorting before moving to drawn timelines.

nodes.label: Recording on labelled maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can record data about locations and features by labelling them on a map of the local area.
criteria: Labels at least two features or locations on a provided map
Labels are accurate to the feature's location on the map

width.minimum: Label at least two features or locations on a provided map (e.g. their home, a local park).
width.typical: Record data about locations of places and features on maps and plans; label activity spaces on classroom plans; label home location on a map of the local area; record observations of weather and seasons in pictorial form.
wider: Add a layer of classification to a labelled map (e.g. colour-coding natural, managed and constructed features)
Compare a labelled map with an aerial photograph of the same area and identify what each representation shows differently

modes.reason: Labelled mapping integrates observation, feature classification and spatial representation — the labelled map is the capstone recording format for Year 1.

descriptors.title: Interpret observations and comparisons
descriptors.description: interpret information and data from observations and provided sources, including the comparison of objects from the past and present
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS02, AC9HSFS03): Students sorted information from sources and shared perspectives. From AC9HS1S02: Students collected and recorded information from observations and sources.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret information from observations and provided sources, including comparing objects from the past and present.

nodes.label: Using sources to answer questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use information from sources (stories, photographs, satellite images, rock art, fieldwork observations) to answer 'when', 'where', 'what', 'how' and 'why' questions.
criteria: Uses at least one source to answer at least two types of questions
Explains what the source tells them rather than inferring unsupported information
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot extract targeted answers from sources, they cannot compare past and present objects — the comparison in Node 2 requires first being able to read what sources actually say.

width.minimum: Use at least one source to answer at least two different types of questions (e.g. a 'what' and a 'where' question).
width.typical: Use a range of sources to answer When, Where, What, How and Why questions; identify what each source tells them and what it does not tell them; explore First Nations Australian stories about places and the past.
wider: Compare what traditional and contemporary First Nations Australian stories reveal about how places have changed
Use multiple sources on the same topic and identify where they agree and where they provide different information

modes.reason: Model source-reading explicitly: 'What does this photograph tell me? What question does it answer?' Use think-alouds before expecting students to do this independently.

nodes.label: Comparing past and present objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare objects or artefacts from the past with those used today, identifying similarities and differences using comparative language.
criteria: Compares at least two objects from different time periods
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference using comparative language

width.minimum: Compare at least two objects from the past and present (e.g. old and new toys, phones, cooking tools) identifying one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Compare a range of objects from the past with current equivalents (toys, games, clothes, phones, cooking utensils, tools, homework books); categorise similarities and differences; use comparative language accurately.
wider: Arrange a sequence of three or more versions of the same object over time and describe the trajectory of change
Categorise observed changes by type (material, purpose, size, technology) and discuss which types of change are most common

modes.reason: More objects compared means more robust understanding of change patterns — build range of comparison objects across multiple categories.

nodes.label: Categorising features of places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can categorise objects, drawings or images by their features and explain the reason for their categorisation, applying this to place features (natural, constructed, managed).
criteria: Categorises features of a local place into natural, constructed and managed types
Explains the reason for at least one categorisation decision

width.minimum: Categorise at least six items into natural, constructed and managed categories and explain one reason for each category assignment.
width.typical: Categorise features of local places into natural, constructed and managed types; explain reasons for categorisation; compare categorisations with peers and resolve disagreements.
wider: Categorise the same feature differently from multiple perspectives and discuss how viewpoint affects categorisation
Apply the three categories to a place that has changed over time and identify whether the change shifted its category

modes.reason: Categorisation with reasoning integrates source interpretation and place classification — the explanatory demand ('explain the reason') is the integration test.

descriptors.title: Discuss perspectives
descriptors.description: discuss perspectives related to objects, people, places and events
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS03): Students shared a perspective on information, recognised that perspectives differ, and explained reasons for their own views.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss perspectives related to objects, people, places and events, comparing their own views with those of others.

nodes.label: Comparing perspectives across time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare their own daily lives with those of their parents, grandparents or familiar elders, and identify aspects of the past they would or would not want to experience.
criteria: Compares their own life with at least one aspect of a parent's or grandparent's life
States a preference and gives at least one reason for it

width.minimum: Compare their own daily life with one aspect of a grandparent's or elder's daily life and state whether they would have preferred to live then or now, with a reason.
width.typical: Compare daily lives with parents, grandparents, elders or familiar older people; identify which aspects of the past they would or would not want to experience; explain reasons for preferences.
wider: Interview a family member or elder about what they valued most about their childhood and compare perspectives across generations
Explore how perspectives on the same aspect of daily life (e.g. schooling, play, food) differ between generations

modes.reason: Real intergenerational comparison — through interview or family discussion — provides far richer perspective material than textbook examples.

nodes.label: Personal preferences about places and events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can share personal preferences about their world (favourite weather, activities, places, celebrations) and explain why they are favoured.
criteria: Shares a preference about at least one topic with a reason
Listens to and acknowledges a different preference from a peer

width.minimum: Share a preference about at least one aspect of their world (weather, place, celebration) and explain at least one reason for that preference.
width.typical: Share personal preferences about weather, activities, places, celebrations and objects from the past; explain reasons for preferences; listen to and respect differing preferences from peers.
wider: Compare preferences across the class and look for patterns — do preferences relate to cultural background, family experience or personal interests?
Discuss whether personal preferences should influence decisions about places (e.g. what should be in a park) and why

modes.reason: Explaining preferences about places and events is the culminating perspective task — it integrates personal experience with HASS content knowledge.

descriptors.title: Draw conclusions and make proposals
descriptors.description: draw conclusions and make proposals
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS04): Students drew conclusions in response to inquiry questions supported by evidence. From AC9HS1S03: Students interpreted information and compared objects from past and present.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions about continuity and change, how places change, and make proposals for action.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions about change and place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use collected information to make conclusions about continuity and change over time and about how places change.
criteria: States at least one conclusion about continuity or change
Supports the conclusion with at least one piece of collected information
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot draw evidence-based conclusions about change, they cannot make meaningful proposals for action — proposals require a conclusion about what is happening or has happened.

width.minimum: Draw at least one conclusion about change over time or how a place changes, supported by at least one piece of collected information.
width.typical: Use collected information from stories, interviews, geographic pictures and comparisons to draw conclusions about: how family roles, occupations or technologies have changed or remained the same; how places change because of seasons or human activity.
wider: Draw conclusions about change in two different contexts (e.g. family roles AND place features) and compare the types of change
Evaluate whether change was positive, negative or mixed, with a reason

modes.reason: Model the move from evidence to conclusion explicitly: 'The information shows... so I can conclude that...' Use sentence frames and guided note-taking before expecting independent conclusions.

nodes.label: Making proposals for action
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe features of a place that is important to them and propose action to care for it or influence a positive future for it.
criteria: Describes at least one feature of a personally important place
Proposes at least one specific action to care for or improve that place

width.minimum: Describe one feature of a place that matters to them and propose one specific action to care for it.
width.typical: Describe features of a personally significant space (classroom, play area, bedroom, beach) and explain what could be done to care for it; imagine how a local feature or place might change in the future and propose action to improve or maintain it.
wider: Develop a plan of action for caring for a specific place, identifying steps and who could help
Imagine two futures for a local place (with and without care) and explain which is preferred and why

modes.reason: Proposals integrate place knowledge, significance understanding and evidence-based reasoning into action — the proposal is the integrating output of Year 1 HASS inquiry.

descriptors.title: Develop narratives and observations
descriptors.description: develop narratives and share observations, using sources, and subject-specific terms
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFS05): Students shared narratives using sources and basic time/place terms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop narratives and share observations about the past and places, using sources and subject-specific terms for time sequence.

nodes.label: Time sequence vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use time sequence terms (then, now, yesterday, today, past, present, later on, before I was born, in the future, generations) correctly in spoken and written communication.
criteria: Uses at least four time sequence terms correctly in context
Terms are used to express temporal relationships, not randomly inserted
nodes.hinge_reason: Developing a historical narrative requires the vocabulary of time sequence — without these terms, students cannot express the relationship between past and present that HASS Year 1 demands.

width.minimum: Use at least four time sequence terms accurately in a spoken or written description of a change over time.
width.typical: Use a full range of time sequence terms in speech and writing when describing family life over time and changes to places; use terms to order events and connect past to present.
wider: Explore how time sequence terms translate across languages represented in the class and discuss how different cultures describe the passage of time
Create a glossary of time sequence terms with student-generated definitions and examples

modes.reason: Time sequence vocabulary requires deliberate, frequent practice across multiple contexts — use routines (morning meeting time talk, sequencing activities) to build fluency before expecting narrative use.

nodes.label: Retelling historical narratives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can retell stories about life in the past through spoken narratives using pictures, role-plays or photographs, drawing on sources and using time sequence vocabulary.
criteria: Retells a narrative about life in the past using at least one source
Uses at least two time sequence terms accurately within the narrative

width.minimum: Retell at least one story about life in the past using a source (photograph, drawing, role-play prop) and at least two time sequence terms.
width.typical: Retell stories about life in the past through spoken narratives and the use of pictures, role-plays or photographs; use time sequence terms naturally; draw on collected information from oral histories, objects and photographs.
wider: Develop an extended narrative that traces change from past to present using multiple sources
Create a multimodal narrative (images + text + speech) about how a local place or aspect of family life has changed

modes.reason: Historical narrative integrates collected information, time vocabulary and personal/family perspective into a communicative whole — the narrative is the Year 1 HASS communicating endpoint.

descriptors.title: Local significance
descriptors.description: a local individual, group, place or building and the reasons for their importance, including social, cultural or spiritual significance
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1K01-K02): Students compared family structures and daily life across generations. They understand continuity and change and comparative language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the importance of a local individual, group, place or building, including its social, cultural or spiritual significance.

nodes.label: Types of local significance
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different types of significance (social, cultural, spiritual, historical) and give examples of each from their local area.
criteria: Identifies at least two types of significance by name
Gives at least one local example of each type
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a conceptual vocabulary for types of significance, students cannot explain why a specific local place matters — the explanatory task in Node 2 requires these categories.

width.minimum: Identify at least two types of significance and give one local example of each.
width.typical: Explore a range of local individuals, groups, places and buildings; classify each by type of significance; discuss why particular sites have heritage significance or cultural value for present generations.
wider: Identify local sites of significance to First Nations Australians (engraving sites, rock paintings, natural features) and explain their significance from a First Nations perspective
Compare why the same local site might have different significance to different community groups

modes.reason: Social, cultural and spiritual significance are abstract at Year 2 — anchor each type to a concrete local example before asking students to classify independently.

nodes.label: Investigating a local place or person
nodes.checkpoint: Students can investigate the history of a chosen local individual, group, place or building using provided sources and construct an account of what makes it important.
criteria: Uses at least two sources in the investigation
Explains why the chosen place or person is important using at least one type of significance

width.minimum: Use at least two provided sources to describe why a local place, person or building is important.
width.typical: Investigate the history of a chosen person, building, site or place using the internet, books, newspapers, community guides, photographs and audio-visual material; relate the story these sources reveal about the past; explain reasons for importance.
wider: Design a local historical tour of a building or site and develop explanatory notes for each stop
Compare two different local significant sites from different cultural groups and explain what each reveals about the community's identity

modes.reason: The investigation integrates source use, significance vocabulary and local knowledge into an explanatory account — it is the integration task for this standard.

descriptors.title: Technological change in everyday life
descriptors.description: how technological developments changed people's lives at home, and in the ways they worked, travelled and communicated
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1K02): Students compared daily life across generations identifying change and continuity. They used comparative language for change.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how technological developments changed people's lives at home, and in the ways they worked, travelled and communicated.

nodes.label: Technologies past and present
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify technologies from the past and their modern equivalents across multiple categories (transport, communication, home, work) and describe how each has changed.
criteria: Identifies at least two technologies across different categories that have changed
Describes how each technology changed from past to present
nodes.hinge_reason: Students must understand what technologies changed before they can explain how those changes affected people's lives — the effect analysis in Node 2 requires the change baseline.

width.minimum: Identify at least two technologies from different categories (e.g. transport and communication) that have changed and describe how each changed.
width.typical: Examine changes in technologies over several generations by comparing past and present objects and photographs across: land, air and sea transport; transistors to digital streaming; communication over long distances; daily home technologies.
wider: Identify technologies used by local First Nations Australians for daily life (food, shelter, transport) and compare these with European technologies used in the same period
Interview a grandparent or familiar elder about the technologies used in their childhood and record the account

modes.reason: Build a range of technology examples across multiple categories using objects, photographs and elder interviews before moving to effect analysis.

nodes.label: How technology changed daily life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific technological developments changed people's lives at home, at work, in travel and in communication.
criteria: Explains how at least one technology changed at least one aspect of daily life
Uses cause-effect language to describe the relationship between the technology and the change

width.minimum: Explain how at least one technological development changed at least two aspects of daily life (e.g. how TV changed both home life and communication).
width.typical: Discuss how changes to transport, communication and work technologies shaped daily life patterns; suggest what patterns of movement and communication would have been like one or two generations ago; compare with today.
wider: Investigate how current communication and transport technologies connect places internationally and compare with connections possible one generation ago
Explore how accessibility to places changed for different groups (e.g. people with disability, people in remote areas) as transport technologies evolved

modes.reason: Multiple technology categories (transport, communication, home, work) provide richer causal explanation than focusing on one category alone.

descriptors.title: Spatial representation and scale
descriptors.description: how places can be spatially represented in geographical divisions from local to regional to state/territory, and how people and places are interconnected across those scales
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1K03): Students located natural, managed and constructed features on local maps using direction and location terms.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how places can be spatially represented from local to state/territory scale and how people and places are interconnected across those scales.

nodes.label: Geographical divisions and scales
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the geographical divisions from local to regional to state/territory and locate where they live within this hierarchy using maps and a globe.
criteria: Locates home in relation to nearest capital city and state/territory on a map
Names the state/territory they live in and at least one neighbouring state
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the local-to-state/territory scale hierarchy is prerequisite to understanding interconnections across scales — you cannot explain a connection between scales you cannot name or locate.

width.minimum: Locate their home in relation to their nearest capital city and state/territory on a map.
width.typical: Identify where they live in Australia in relation to nearest capital city, region and state/territory on maps and a globe; use geographical tools to explore scale from local to national.
wider: Locate Australia's position relative to neighbouring regions and countries on a globe
Compare the size and population of different states and territories and discuss why they differ

modes.reason: Scale is a new concept at Year 2 — repeated practice with maps, globes and digital tools at different scales builds the spatial vocabulary needed for interconnection discussions.

nodes.label: Interconnections across scales
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how they and their community are connected to people and places at regional and state/territory scale, including through movement, shopping, communication and transport.
criteria: Identifies at least two connections to places outside their local area
Explains how at least one connection is maintained (transport, communication, visits)

width.minimum: Identify at least two ways they are connected to a place outside their local area (e.g. visiting relatives, where food comes from, holidays).
width.typical: Investigate places locally and at broader scale that they and their families visit for shopping, health, recreation, religious or ceremonial activities; identify links with places at regional and state/territory scale; describe how communication and transport technologies connect places.
wider: Map the connections their family has to places at regional and state/territory scale and discuss why those connections exist
Explore how First Nations Australians' songlines connect places across Country and compare with contemporary travel routes

modes.reason: Each student's family connections are different — class sharing creates genuine breadth of interconnection examples.

descriptors.title: Local First Nations interconnections
descriptors.description: the interconnections of First Nations Australians to a local Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK04): Students identified the importance of Country/Place to First Nations Australians and named the local language group. From Y1 (AC9HS1K03): Students explored place features including through Dreaming and Creation stories.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the interconnections of First Nations Australians to a local Country/Place.

nodes.label: Language, Country/Place and spirituality
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the relationship between language, Country/Place and spiritual identity for the local First Nations Australian language group.
criteria: Describes at least one connection the local First Nations language group has to Country/Place
Uses the name of the local First Nations language group correctly
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding the language-Country/Place-spirituality nexus is needed before students can explain interconnections meaningfully — without this, acknowledgement practices become procedural rather than understood.

width.minimum: Describe at least one connection between the local First Nations Australian language group and Country/Place using a provided source.
width.typical: Liaise with community to identify the local language group; explore the relationship between language, Country/Place and spirituality for that group; listen to stories connecting local First Nations Australians with land, sea, waterways, sky and animals.
wider: Investigate why language is central to Country/Place connection and what is lost when language is not maintained
Compare the local language group's connections to Country/Place with those of another First Nations group from a different region

modes.reason: The three-way relationship between language, Country and spirituality is conceptually dense for Year 2 — use community voices and concrete local examples to anchor the concept.

nodes.label: Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain when Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country are used and why they respectfully recognise Country/Place, Traditional Owners and Custodians.
criteria: Explains the purpose of Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country
Correctly states when each is used (Acknowledgement by anyone; Welcome by Traditional Owner)

width.minimum: Explain the purpose of Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country and when each is used.
width.typical: Discuss when to use Acknowledgement of Country and Welcome to Country at ceremonies and events; explain how these practices respectfully recognise the Country/Place and Traditional Owners and Custodians of the land, sea, waterways and sky.
wider: Write or participate in an Acknowledgement of Country for the school that reflects genuine understanding of the local Country/Place and language group
Explore how protocols around Acknowledgement of Country differ between communities and discuss why those differences exist

modes.reason: Acknowledgement and Welcome to Country practices integrate language, Country/Place and interconnection knowledge into a civic act — the integration of understanding into practice.

descriptors.title: Develop inquiry questions
descriptors.description: develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1S01): Students developed questions about objects, people, places and events in past and present using Where/What/How/Why stems, and identified appropriate sources.
