descriptors.endpoint: Students develop questions about objects, people, places and events in the past and present to guide inquiry.

nodes.label: Historical and geographical inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop inquiry questions about historical sites and places using a range of question stems, including perspective-seeking stems.
criteria: Develops at least two inquiry questions about a historical site or place
Uses at least one perspective-seeking stem alongside factual stems

width.minimum: Develop at least three inquiry questions about a historical site or place using at least two different question types.
width.typical: Develop inquiry questions about historical sites (condition, purpose, use, importance, users) and places (features, distance, accessibility, connections); use stems including 'How do I feel about...?', 'What would it be like to...?' and 'What effect...?'
wider: Develop questions that specifically seek First Nations Australian perspectives on a local site or place
Evaluate a set of inquiry questions and revise those that cannot be answered from available sources

modes.reason: Year 2 introduces perspective-seeking question stems — practise across both historical and geographical contexts to build transferable questioning skill.

descriptors.title: Collect and organise observations
descriptors.description: collect, sort and record information and data from observations and from provided sources, including unscaled timelines and labelled maps or models
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1S02): Students collected information from a range of sources and recorded on unscaled timelines and labelled maps.
descriptors.endpoint: Students collect, sort and record information from observations and provided sources using unscaled timelines and labelled maps.

nodes.label: Collecting from historical and geographical sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect relevant information from a range of sources appropriate to both historical and geographical inquiry, identifying relevant information for their purpose.
criteria: Collects information from at least two source types
Identifies which information from each source is relevant to the inquiry question
nodes.hinge_reason: Recording on timelines and maps requires prior collection of information — without collected material there is nothing to record.

width.minimum: Collect information from at least two different source types relevant to a Y2 inquiry (e.g. photographs and maps, or survey data and satellite images).
width.typical: Collect from: photographs, interviews, newspapers, stories, place/street names (historical); surveying peers, satellite images, field photographs, observations of monuments (geographical); identify relevant information from each source.
wider: Compare sources created at different times (e.g. a historical map and a current satellite image) and discuss what each reveals
Evaluate the reliability of different source types for a specific inquiry question

modes.reason: Year 2 introduces geographical data sources (satellite images, field photographs, surveys) alongside historical ones — build familiarity with each source type through whole-class exploration.

nodes.label: Pictorial maps, timelines and location recording
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create pictorial maps with annotations, locate connected places on maps, and order events on unscaled timelines.
criteria: Produces at least one annotated map or ordered timeline from collected information
Annotations accurately represent information from sources

width.minimum: Complete at least one of: annotated pictorial map, location map of connected places, or ordered timeline of local community history.
width.typical: Create pictorial maps with annotations showing historical sites or connected places; locate places they are connected to on maps; order key events in local community history on unscaled timelines; use slideshows or story formats.
wider: Create a layered map that shows both historical sites and current interconnections for the same area
Compare an annotated historical timeline with a modern map of the same area and identify changes

modes.reason: Pictorial mapping and timeline creation integrate collected information, spatial understanding and time sequencing — both formats are the recording integration tasks.

descriptors.title: Interpret information from sources
descriptors.description: interpret information and data from observations and provided sources, including the comparison of objects from the past and present
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1S03): Students used sources to answer questions and compared objects from past and present using comparative language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret information and data from observations and provided sources, including comparing objects from the past and present.

nodes.label: Interpreting distance and location on maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret distance on maps using terms like distant, close, local, many hours, walking distance, and describe the accessibility of different features and places.
criteria: Uses at least two distance terms accurately when describing map locations
Interprets at least one map symbol or legend element correctly

width.minimum: Interpret distance between at least two places on a map using at least two distance terms.
width.typical: Interpret geographic maps, concept maps and digital displays to explore system connections; use distance terms to decide on accessibility; interpret map symbols and legends; describe how places are connected.
wider: Interpret how First Nations Australians' songlines connect places across Country using spatial reasoning
Compare accessibility of a place by different transport modes and discuss the implications

modes.reason: Map distance terms require practice across different map scales and contexts before they are used fluently.

nodes.label: Comparing objects and activities across places and time
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how objects and activities are similar or different depending on conditions in local and distant places, and across time periods.
criteria: Compares at least two items across time or place
Identifies at least one similarity and one difference with a contextual reason

width.minimum: Compare at least two objects or activities across either time (past/present) or place (local/distant) and identify one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Identify similarities and differences between clothes, transport and technology depending on conditions in local and distant places; compare past and present objects; use comparative and contextual reasoning.
wider: Compare objects and activities across all three dimensions simultaneously: place, time and cultural context
Investigate why similar needs (shelter, food, communication) have been met differently in different places and times

modes.reason: Comparing across both time and place is a significant cognitive step — build range through multiple comparison examples before asking students to do multi-dimensional comparisons.

descriptors.title: Discuss perspectives on places and events
descriptors.description: discuss perspectives related to objects, people, places and events
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1S04): Students compared perspectives across generations and shared personal preferences about places and events with reasons.
descriptors.endpoint: Students discuss perspectives related to objects, people, places and events, including perspectives of different community groups.

nodes.label: Why places are significant to different groups
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss why some places are considered special or significant by different groups (parents, First Nations Australians, grandparents, friends, returned soldiers) and explain why significance differs.
criteria: Explains why at least two different groups find the same place significant
Describes at least one reason why significance differs between groups

width.minimum: Explain why the same place is significant to at least two different people or groups, identifying what makes it significant for each.
width.typical: Discuss why some places are special to parents, First Nations Australians, grandparents, elders, friends and returned soldiers; explore how the same place has significance to different groups for different reasons.
wider: Investigate traditional meeting places for First Nations Australians within an urban area and compare their significance with that of nearby buildings or monuments important to other cultural groups
Interview two different people about the same local place and compare their perspectives on why it matters

modes.reason: Multiple perspectives on the same place are more powerful than multiple perspectives on different places — use a single local site to anchor diverse perspective comparison.

nodes.label: Older generations' perspectives on change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine points of view of older generations about changes over time to the natural or built environment or to daily living.
criteria: Describes at least one point of view an older person holds about change
Compares that view with their own perspective on the same change

width.minimum: Describe one point of view an older person holds about a change they have witnessed in their lifetime.
width.typical: Examine perspectives of older generations on changes to the natural or built environment and daily living; compare with students' own perspectives on the same changes; discuss how experience shapes perspective.
wider: Compare perspectives on the same change from two people of different generations and explain what shaped each view
Discuss how perspectives on a change can be positive for one group and negative for another

modes.reason: Perspectives on change integrate historical knowledge of what changed with empathetic understanding of how people experienced that change — the integration of history and perspective-taking.

descriptors.title: Draw conclusions and make proposals
descriptors.description: draw conclusions and make proposals
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1S05): Students drew evidence-based conclusions about change and made proposals for caring for places.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions about local significance, technology change and place connections, and make proposals for positive futures.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions about significance and change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions about local significance, how technology impacted people's lives, and how people are connected to local and distant places.
criteria: States at least one conclusion supported by evidence
Conclusion addresses significance, change or connections as targeted by the inquiry
nodes.hinge_reason: Conclusions are the prerequisite for proposals — students cannot propose meaningful futures without first concluding what matters and why.

width.minimum: Draw at least one conclusion about either local significance, technology change or place connections, supported by evidence.
width.typical: List what makes a local person, place or building significant and conclude how people are connected to it; use Venn diagrams or tables to show continuity/change in technology over time; discuss how a technology change impacted work, travel or communication.
wider: Draw conclusions from a Venn diagram comparing two technologies across time and explain the pattern of change
Conclude how knowledge of special places and natural systems contributes to caring behaviour and conservation

modes.reason: Making the conclusion explicit (as a statement, not just implied) is the skill being developed — use sentence frames to make conclusions visible before asking for proposals.

nodes.label: Proposing positive futures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use knowledge of a familiar place or site to imagine how it might change in the future and propose how they could influence a positive future for it.
criteria: Describes at least one possible future for a familiar place
Proposes at least one action to achieve a positive future

width.minimum: Identify one way a familiar place might change and propose one action that could lead to a positive future for it.
width.typical: Use knowledge about a familiar place or site to imagine two possible futures; propose actions that could lead to positive outcomes; consider who needs to be involved and what resources would be needed.
wider: Develop a proposal for a local place that considers perspectives of at least two different community groups
Forecast a probable future and a preferred future for a local place and explain the difference

modes.reason: Future proposals integrate place knowledge, significance understanding, perspective awareness and evidence-based conclusions — it is the Year 2 evaluating endpoint.

descriptors.title: Develop narratives and share observations
descriptors.description: develop narratives and share observations, using sources, and subject-specific terms
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1S06): Students developed historical narratives using sources and time sequence vocabulary.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop narratives and share observations, using sources and subject-specific terms for time and place.

nodes.label: Subject-specific vocabulary for time and place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use time terms (in the past, years ago, the olden days, in the future) and direction/location terms (north, south, opposite, near, far) accurately in HASS communication.
criteria: Uses at least two time terms correctly in HASS context
Uses at least one cardinal direction term correctly in a location description
nodes.hinge_reason: Without accurate time and place vocabulary, narratives and observations lack the specificity the HASS descriptor demands — vocabulary is the communicative tool.

width.minimum: Use at least two time terms and two direction/location terms correctly in a spoken or written description.
width.typical: Use time terms (in the past, years ago, olden days, in the future) and location terms (north, south, opposite, near, far) when sharing observations about how access to and use of a place has changed; use vocabulary in speech and writing.
wider: Compare how time and direction terms from different languages map onto HASS vocabulary
Create a subject-specific vocabulary reference resource for Year 2 HASS that includes definitions and examples

modes.reason: Direction terms (north, south) are new at Year 2 — build fluency through maps, orientation activities and labelling before deploying in narratives.

nodes.label: Developing narratives from sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop narratives drawing on ideas from sources and share observations about how access to and use of a place has changed over time.
criteria: Develops a narrative or observation report that draws on at least one source
Uses at least two subject-specific terms accurately

width.minimum: Develop a narrative or observation report drawing on at least one source and using at least two subject-specific terms.
width.typical: Develop narratives drawing on comparisons of past and present daily life; share observations using sources about how a place's use has changed; share knowledge about the past using time and place terms in speech and writing.
wider: Develop a narrative that draws on perspectives of at least two different groups represented in the sources
Create a multimodal observation report about a local place that includes maps, photographs and written explanation

modes.reason: Narrative development integrates source use, vocabulary, perspective awareness and factual knowledge into a communicated whole — it is the communicating endpoint for Year 2.

descriptors.title: Local community change and diversity
descriptors.description: causes and effects of changes to the local community, and how people who may be from diverse backgrounds have contributed to these changes
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2K01-K02): Students explained local significance and how technological developments changed daily life. They understand continuity and change and source-based investigation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain causes and effects of changes to the local community and describe how people from diverse backgrounds have contributed to those changes.

nodes.label: Identifying community changes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify changes to the local community over time by examining sources such as photographs, newspapers and oral histories.
criteria: Identifies at least two changes to the local community
Uses at least two source types as evidence
nodes.hinge_reason: Students must be able to identify specific changes before analysing their causes and effects — naming the change is prerequisite to explaining it.

width.minimum: Identify at least two changes to the local community using at least two different source types.
width.typical: Explore photographs, newspapers, oral histories, diaries and letters to investigate how aspects of the local community (transport, environment, technology) have changed; compare photographs from past and present of specific locations to identify change and continuity.
wider: Investigate how an aspect of local community life changed from the time of European settlement to the present day
Compare change rates across different aspects of the community (natural environment vs built environment vs social life)

modes.reason: Build a class inventory of local changes across multiple domains using sources before moving to causal analysis.

nodes.label: Causes and effects of change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why a change happened in the local community and what happened as a result.
criteria: States at least one cause of a community change
States at least one effect of that change
nodes.hinge_reason: Cause-effect reasoning is new at Year 3 — students who cannot identify causes cannot connect them to diverse contributors in Node 3.

width.minimum: Explain one cause and one effect of a specific change to the local community.
width.typical: Investigate reasons for change in the local community (why change was brought about) and what happened because of it; connect causes to effects for at least two changes.
wider: Investigate multiple causes for a single change and rank them by importance
Trace a chain of effects from one community change through to present day consequences

modes.reason: Model cause-effect reasoning explicitly using 'because' and 'as a result' sentence frames before expecting independent causal analysis.

nodes.label: Diverse contributors to community change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify individuals and groups from diverse backgrounds who have contributed to the community's development and describe their contribution.
criteria: Names at least one contributor from a diverse background
Describes their contribution and connects it to a community change

width.minimum: Identify at least one individual or group from a diverse background who contributed to the local community and describe their contribution.
width.typical: Identify individuals and groups from diverse backgrounds (economic, social, cultural, civic, environmental) who have contributed to community development; connect their contributions to specific changes in the community.
wider: Compare contributions from First Nations Australian community members with those of settlers and migrants to the same local area
Investigate how a previously unrecognised contributor's story is now being told and why their recognition matters

modes.reason: The more diverse the range of contributors examined, the richer the understanding of community complexity — seek contributors across cultural, economic and civic domains.

descriptors.title: Significant Australian events, symbols and identity
descriptors.description: significant events, symbols and emblems that are important to Australia's identity and diversity, and how they are celebrated, commemorated or recognised in Australia, including Australia Day, Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week, National Sorry Day, Easter, Christmas, and other religious and cultural festivals
descriptors.knowledge: From Foundation (AC9HSFK02) and Y2 (AC9HS2K01): Students explored celebrations, commemorations and local significance. They understand social, cultural and spiritual significance.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and explain significant Australian events, symbols and emblems and describe how they are celebrated, commemorated or recognised, including multiple perspectives on their significance.

nodes.label: National celebrations and commemorations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify significant Australian celebrations and commemorations (Australia Day, Anzac Day, NAIDOC Week, National Sorry Day, Easter, Christmas, Lunar New Year, Diwali, Eid) and describe their historical origins.
criteria: Identifies at least three significant Australian celebrations or commemorations
Describes the historical origin of at least one
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need factual knowledge of what events and symbols exist before they can discuss their significance or the perspectives different groups hold.

width.minimum: Identify at least three significant Australian celebrations or commemorations and describe the historical origin of at least one.
width.typical: Identify and discuss historical origins of important Australian celebrations and commemorations; recognise multiple perspectives on some events (e.g. 'Invasion Day' perspectives on Australia Day); explore local, state/territory, national and religious events.
wider: Compare how Australia Day is viewed by different community groups and discuss why the date is contested
Investigate the origins of NAIDOC Week and National Sorry Day and explain their significance to First Nations Australians

modes.reason: Build a class calendar of events with associated origins before moving to significance analysis.

nodes.label: Symbols and emblems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a range of Australian symbols and emblems, describe their origins and use, and explain what they represent about Australia's identity.
criteria: Identifies at least three symbols or emblems from different contexts
Explains what at least one symbol represents about identity

width.minimum: Identify at least three symbols or emblems and describe what each represents.
width.typical: Generate a list of local, state/territory, national and religious symbols and emblems; discuss their origins, use and significance; examine symbolism in flag design and positioning; identify when flags are flown.
wider: Examine the symbolism in the design of the Australian flag and First Nations Australian flags, comparing what each represents
Investigate the protocols around flag flying and the roles, rights and responsibilities of community members

modes.reason: Symbols from different cultural and religious traditions in the class community give genuine breadth to the concept of identity symbols.

descriptors.title: Australia's representation: states, territories and countries/places
descriptors.description: the representation of contemporary Australia as states and territories, and as the Countries/Places of First Nations Australians prior to colonisation, and the locations of Australia's neighbouring regions and countries
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2K03): Students located their home within geographical divisions from local to state/territory and explored interconnections across scales.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify how Australia can be represented as states/territories and as Countries/Places of First Nations Australians, and locate Australia's neighbouring regions and countries.

nodes.label: States, territories and capitals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name and locate Australian states and territories and their capital cities on a map.
criteria: Names at least four states or territories correctly
Locates at least four on a map
nodes.hinge_reason: Locating states and territories is prerequisite to comparing them with Countries/Places of First Nations Australians — you cannot compare boundaries you cannot locate.

width.minimum: Name at least four states or territories and locate them on a map.
width.typical: Use geographical tools (globe, wall map, digital source) to locate and name all states and territories and their capital cities; label them on a map.
wider: Research differences between states and territories in terms of population, size and climate
Locate Australian states and territories on a globe and discuss Australia's position relative to the equator and hemispheres

modes.reason: Accurate map knowledge requires repeated practice — use map quizzes, labelling and digital tools to build locational fluency.

nodes.label: Countries/Places of First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use the AIATSIS Map of Indigenous Australia to compare Aboriginal Countries and Torres Strait Islander Places with surveyed state/territory boundaries.
criteria: Identifies at least two Aboriginal Countries or Torres Strait Islander Places on the AIATSIS map
Describes at least one difference between the AIATSIS map and the states/territories map

width.minimum: Use the AIATSIS map to identify at least two Aboriginal Countries or Torres Strait Islander Places and compare their boundaries with state/territory lines.
width.typical: Compare the AIATSIS map of Indigenous Australia with a states and territories map; identify how boundaries differ; gain an appreciation of the different ways Australia can be represented; discuss what the two maps reveal about different understandings of land.
wider: Investigate why Aboriginal Country boundaries differ from state/territory lines and what determined each type of boundary
Explore how the existence of two different maps of Australia reflects two different ways of belonging to and organising land

modes.reason: The comparison of two fundamentally different map representations requires scaffolded reasoning — what does each map show, why do they differ, what does each represent?

nodes.label: Neighbouring regions and countries
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate Australia's neighbouring regions and countries and identify the direction of each from Australia.
criteria: Locates at least three neighbouring countries on a map or globe
Identifies the direction of at least two neighbouring countries from Australia

width.minimum: Locate at least three neighbouring countries (e.g. Papua New Guinea, New Zealand, Indonesia) on a globe or digital source and identify their direction from Australia.
width.typical: Use a globe or digital source to locate Pacific Island nations, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea, Timor-Leste, Indonesia and other relevant countries; label them on a map; identify direction from Australia.
wider: Investigate one neighbouring country in depth and describe its relationship with Australia
Compare Australia's location relative to its neighbours with the location of another country relative to its neighbours

modes.reason: Locating neighbouring countries requires map practice — use interactive digital tools and repeated labelling exercises.

descriptors.title: First Nations Australians' interconnections with country/place
descriptors.description: the ways First Nations Australians in different parts of Australia are interconnected with Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2K04): Students explained interconnections of First Nations Australians to a local Country/Place and the relationship between language, Country/Place and spirituality.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the diverse ways First Nations Australians in different parts of Australia are interconnected with Country/Place.

nodes.label: Multiple connections to Country/Place
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that First Nations Australians can have connections to multiple Countries/Places and describe how these connections are formed.
criteria: Explains that a person can have connections to more than one Country/Place
Names at least two ways connections to Country/Place are formed (e.g. birth, marriage, residence)
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding multiple connection types is prerequisite to appreciating the diversity of interconnections across Australia — the next node requires this conceptual flexibility.

width.minimum: Explain that First Nations Australians can have connections to more than one Country/Place and give at least one reason why.
width.typical: Explain that some First Nations Australians have connections to many Countries/Places through marriage, birth, parents, residence and chosen or forced movement; discuss how some people are connected to one Country because it is Mother's or Father's Country.
wider: Investigate how forced removal and the Stolen Generations disrupted Country/Place connections and what efforts are made to restore them
Explore how First Nations Australian people maintain connections to Country/Place when living away from it

modes.reason: The concept of belonging to multiple Countries/Places challenges conventional notions of 'one home' — scaffold carefully using concrete examples from stories and community members.

nodes.label: Diverse expressions of connection
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explore how First Nations Australians from different groups express their connections to Country/Place through poems, songs, paintings and stories.
criteria: Identifies at least one way a First Nations Australian group expresses connection to Country/Place
Describes what this expression reveals about the group's relationship with their Country/Place

width.minimum: Identify at least one way a First Nations Australian group expresses their connection to Country/Place through an artistic or cultural form.
width.typical: Read and view poems, songs, paintings and stories from First Nations Australian groups outside the local area; discuss how these expressions reveal connection to Country/Place; compare expressions from different groups.
wider: Compare how two different First Nations Australian groups express connection to Country/Place and identify similarities and differences
Explore what these expressions reveal about the relationship between cultural practice and land

modes.reason: Engaging with expressions from multiple groups — not just the local group — broadens understanding of the diversity of First Nations Australian connections to Country/Place.

descriptors.title: Similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries
descriptors.description: the similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries in terms of their natural, managed and constructed features
descriptors.knowledge: From Y1 (AC9HS1K03): Students classified local place features as natural, managed and constructed. From Y2 (AC9HS2K03): Students explored geographical scales from local to state/territory.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and describe similarities and differences between places in Australia and neighbouring countries in terms of natural, managed and constructed features.

nodes.label: Climatic types and natural features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the main climatic types in Australia and neighbouring countries and describe the natural features associated with each.
criteria: Names at least two climatic types
Describes one natural feature associated with each climatic type
nodes.hinge_reason: Climate is the primary driver of natural feature variation — without climate knowledge, comparisons of natural features lack explanatory power.

width.minimum: Identify at least two climatic types and describe one natural feature associated with each.
width.typical: Identify and locate examples of equatorial, tropical, arid, semi-arid and temperate climatic types in Australia and neighbouring countries; describe features of each climate type and their impact on other natural features.
wider: Compare how climate affects the natural features of a place in Australia with those in a contrasting country (e.g. Indonesia or a Pacific Island nation)
Investigate how animals and plants have adapted to specific climatic conditions in Australia and a neighbouring country

modes.reason: The relationship between climate and natural features is causal — model the connection explicitly before expecting students to apply it in comparisons.

nodes.label: Comparing Australia with a neighbouring country
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare Australia with at least one neighbouring country in terms of natural, managed and constructed features, identifying similarities and differences.
criteria: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference between Australia and a neighbouring country
Comparison covers at least two feature types (natural, managed or constructed)

width.minimum: Compare at least two features (natural, managed or constructed) between Australia and one neighbouring country, identifying one similarity and one difference.
width.typical: Identify and describe similarities and differences in natural features (rocks, landforms, water bodies, climate, vegetation, animal life) and in housing, settlement types and built/managed environments between Australia and a neighbouring country.
wider: Compare settlement patterns and classify them into hierarchical categories (isolated dwellings to large cities) for both Australia and a neighbouring country
Investigate why similar natural environments in different countries have been developed differently by their inhabitants

modes.reason: Comparing across multiple feature categories (natural, managed, constructed) gives richer comparison than focusing on one type.

descriptors.title: Rules: who makes them and why they matter
descriptors.description: who makes rules, why rules are important in the school and/or the local community, and the consequences of rules not being followed
descriptors.knowledge: No direct prior HASS civics standard. Students have lived experience of rules from home and school.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain who makes rules, why rules are important, and describe the consequences of rules not being followed.

nodes.label: Who makes rules and why
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify who makes rules in different contexts (parents, teachers, coaches, councils) and explain why rules differ across contexts.
criteria: Names at least two rule-making authorities
Explains why each authority has the right to make rules in their context
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding who makes rules is prerequisite to explaining why specific rules exist — cause and consequence analysis requires knowing the source.

width.minimum: Identify at least two rule-making authorities in different contexts and explain why each has that authority.
width.typical: Explore who has authority to make rules in different contexts (school, home, sport, community); consider why rules differ across contexts; examine cultural norms behind some rulemaking.
wider: Investigate how rules are made differently in different cultural contexts; for example, First Nations Australian cultural lore and how it governs community life
Research how community members can influence rule-making at school or local government level

modes.reason: Rule-making authority is contextual and relational — use concrete scenarios from students' own experience before generalising.

nodes.label: Importance of rules and consequences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why rules are important (protecting rights, enabling fairness, maintaining safety) and describe consequences when rules are not followed.
criteria: Explains why at least one rule is important
Describes at least one consequence of breaking a rule

width.minimum: Explain why at least one rule is important and describe at least one consequence of breaking it.
width.typical: Identify familiar rules; explain how rules protect the rights of others and define responsibilities; describe consequences of not following rules; discuss situations where one rule for all is unfair (e.g. students with disability).
wider: Develop and justify a set of fair rules for the class, considering different student needs
Discuss whether all rules are always fair and what should be done when a rule seems unfair

modes.reason: Connecting the importance of rules to the consequences of breaking them integrates authority, rights and responsibility into a coherent civics framework.

descriptors.title: Community participation
descriptors.description: why people participate within communities and how students can actively participate and contribute to communities
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 civics context: Students have explored rules and authority (AC9HS3K06). No direct prior standard on participation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain why people participate in communities and describe how they can actively contribute.

nodes.label: Why people participate in communities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify groups that participate in the local community, describe their purpose and explain why individuals choose to contribute.
criteria: Names at least two community participation groups
Explains why individuals participate in each
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding motivation for participation is prerequisite to students identifying their own possible contribution — without understanding why others participate, proposals for own participation lack rationale.

width.minimum: Identify at least two community groups and explain why each participates or contributes.
width.typical: Identify groups that actively participate in the local or virtual community and explore their purpose; investigate the motivations of individuals who contribute (volunteers, leaders, Elders); examine how individual contributions can be recognised.
wider: Investigate how an individual's contribution has been officially recognised (e.g. Order of Australia) and what criteria are used
Explore how online and virtual communities enable participation beyond geographic boundaries

modes.reason: Diverse examples of participation (volunteering, cultural leadership, community service) give richer understanding than a single type.

nodes.label: How students can participate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe ways they could participate in a school or community project and explain what contribution they could make.
criteria: Identifies at least one way they could contribute to a community project
Explains what the contribution would involve and who it would benefit

width.minimum: Identify one specific way they could contribute to a school or community project and explain what the contribution would involve.
width.typical: Explore how they could participate in a school or community project (raising money for aid, protecting a bird habitat, community clean-up); identify resources needed; connect participation to community benefit.
wider: Develop an action plan for a class participation project including roles, resources and expected outcomes
Investigate how a student-led initiative has made a difference in a community and discuss what made it successful

modes.reason: Student participation proposals integrate community knowledge, civic motivation understanding and personal agency — the integration of civics knowledge into action.

descriptors.title: Develop questions to guide investigations
descriptors.description: develop questions to guide investigations about people, events, places and issues
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S01): Students developed inquiry questions about historical sites and places using factual and perspective-seeking stems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop questions to guide investigations about people, events, places and issues, including consequential and ethical questions.

nodes.label: Expanded question types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a range of question types including 'Why there?' location questions, 'What might happen?' consequence questions, and 'What ought to happen?' ethical questions.
criteria: Develops at least three questions of different types
At least one question goes beyond factual recall to consequence or ethics
nodes.hinge_reason: Consequential and ethical question types are new at Year 3 and are required for the civics and evaluating demands of the curriculum — without them, inquiry stays factual.

width.minimum: Develop at least three questions of different types (location, consequence, ethical or comparative) about a HASS topic.
width.typical: Develop inquiring questions including: 'Why there?' about location; 'What might happen?' about consequences; 'What ought to happen?' about ethics; 'How have things changed?' comparative questions; probing questions during investigation.
wider: Evaluate a set of student-generated questions for a HASS investigation by type and usefulness and revise the least useful ones
Generate questions that could be investigated using different inquiry methods (fieldwork, interview, documentary analysis) and discuss which method suits each question

modes.reason: Ethical and consequential question types require explicit modelling — students need examples and practice before generating these independently.

descriptors.title: Locate, collect and record information
descriptors.description: locate, collect and record information and data from a range of sources, including annotated timelines and maps
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S02): Students collected from a range of source types and recorded on unscaled timelines and labelled maps.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, collect and record information from a range of sources including annotated timelines and maps using appropriate cartographic conventions.

nodes.label: Locating and evaluating sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate sources suited to a specific inquiry purpose and begin to assess their usefulness.
criteria: Identifies at least two sources suited to an inquiry purpose
Explains why each source is suitable
nodes.hinge_reason: Source selection is now a distinct skill at Year 3 — without being able to locate appropriate sources, fieldwork and annotation tasks cannot be executed.

width.minimum: Identify at least two sources suited to a specific inquiry purpose and explain why each is suitable.
width.typical: Locate historical sources (photographs, interviews, newspapers, digital media, stories, maps); collect information through fieldwork (photographs, sketches, natural objects, interviews, surveys); gather from maps, aerial photographs and satellite images.
wider: Compare sources from different perspectives on the same topic and discuss how perspective affects what sources are created
Investigate how the internet can be used as a source and evaluate reliability of different online sources

modes.reason: Source selection requires understanding inquiry purpose — model the reasoning 'I need this type of information, therefore this type of source is best suited'.

nodes.label: Annotated timelines and maps with conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct and annotate timelines and maps using appropriate cartographic conventions including map symbols, title and north point.
criteria: Constructs an annotated map or timeline
Includes at least one cartographic convention accurately

width.minimum: Construct an annotated map or timeline that includes at least one cartographic convention (title, north point, map symbols, legend).
width.typical: Sequence local people and events in annotated timelines to show change; acquire and record geographical information by constructing and annotating maps using map symbols, title and north point; create tables and graphs to show patterns.
wider: Compare a student-constructed annotated map with a professionally produced map of the same area and discuss differences in detail and conventions
Create an annotated timeline that includes both written annotations and visual evidence

modes.reason: Cartographic conventions (north point, legend, title, scale) require deliberate practice — use scaffolded map-making tasks before expecting independent production.

descriptors.title: Interpret information displayed in different formats
descriptors.description: interpret information and data displayed in different formats
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S03): Students interpreted distance and location on maps and compared objects and activities across places and time.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret information and data displayed in different formats including climate data, maps, graphs and photographs.

nodes.label: Distinguishing fiction from non-fiction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between fiction and non-fiction texts in relation to their representation of places, environments and past events.
criteria: Correctly identifies a given text as fiction or non-fiction
Gives at least one reason for the classification
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish fiction from non-fiction cannot correctly assess the evidentiary value of sources — this is a prerequisite for all subsequent analysis.

width.minimum: Identify whether a given text about a place or past event is fiction or non-fiction and explain one reason for the distinction.
width.typical: Distinguish fiction from non-fiction in texts about places, environments and past events; discuss how each type of text can be useful in HASS inquiry for different purposes.
wider: Identify how a historical fiction text uses factual details and which elements are invented
Explore how point of view affects whether a source presents events as fact or interpretation

modes.reason: The fiction/non-fiction distinction requires criteria — explicitly teach the features that distinguish each type in HASS contexts.

nodes.label: Interpreting climate data, graphs and maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret climate data, graphs, maps and photographs to identify patterns and features.
criteria: Interprets at least one data display accurately
Identifies at least one pattern or feature from the display

width.minimum: Interpret at least one data display (graph, table, map or photograph) to identify one pattern or feature.
width.typical: Interpret climate data to describe temperature and rainfall for a place; interpret data to identify patterns of change over time; use maps, aerial photographs and satellite images to identify and describe features including cartographic elements.
wider: Compare climate data from two contrasting places and draw conclusions about how climate affects human activity
Interpret building date data to make inferences about changing architectural styles and materials

modes.reason: Interpreting across multiple data formats (graphs, maps, photographs, tables) builds transferable analytical skill.

descriptors.title: Analyse information and identify perspectives
descriptors.description: analyse information and data, and identify perspectives
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S03-S04): Students compared objects and activities and discussed perspectives of different groups.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse information and data to identify evidence of change and identify perspectives in sources.

nodes.label: Comparing sources to identify change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare information across different sources to identify evidence of change and continuity.
criteria: Compares at least two sources on the same topic
Identifies at least one piece of evidence of change or continuity
nodes.hinge_reason: Comparative source analysis is the foundational move for all historical analysis — students who cannot compare sources for evidence cannot identify perspectives or draw sound conclusions.

width.minimum: Compare at least two sources on the same topic and identify at least one piece of evidence of change or continuity.
width.typical: Compare images and maps of the local area over time; compare accounts of historic events to determine effects of changes; use visible thinking strategies to examine paintings and maps across time periods.
wider: Compare three or more sources from different time periods on the same topic and describe the trajectory of change
Evaluate which sources are most reliable for understanding a specific change and explain why

modes.reason: Source comparison requires a structured approach — use visible thinking protocols (See-Think-Wonder, compare-contrast matrices) to scaffold before expecting independent analysis.

nodes.label: Identifying perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify different perspectives in sources and explain what shapes each perspective.
criteria: Identifies at least two different perspectives on the same topic
Explains what might shape each perspective

width.minimum: Identify at least two different perspectives on the same event or issue from provided sources.
width.typical: Analyse information from interviews with different people about rules and decisions; compare different accounts of historic events; identify whose perspective is represented in a source and what it might omit.
wider: Identify whose perspectives are absent from a set of sources and discuss why they might be missing
Analyse a set of paintings and maps to explore evidence of whose worldview is represented

modes.reason: Multiple perspectives on the same topic reveal the constructed nature of historical accounts — use interviews, photographs and written sources together for genuine breadth.

descriptors.title: Draw conclusions based on analysis
descriptors.description: draw conclusions based on analysis of information
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S05): Students drew evidence-based conclusions about significance, technology change and place connections.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions about community change, place features and people's connections with places, based on analysis of information.

nodes.label: Drawing evidence-based conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions about how their place and community have changed, the preservation of environmental features, and how people are connected to places, based on analysed data and information.
criteria: States at least one conclusion supported by at least two pieces of evidence
Conclusion responds to an inquiry question rather than restating a fact

width.minimum: Draw at least one conclusion about community change, an environmental feature or a place connection, supported by at least two pieces of analysed evidence.
width.typical: Reach conclusions about: how place and community have changed based on settlement patterns, local species changes, historic events or cultural celebrations; preservation of unique natural features; similarities and differences of places in Australia and neighbouring countries.
wider: Draw conclusions that connect community change to broader patterns (e.g. immigration, environmental policy) beyond the local area
Compare conclusions drawn from different source types on the same topic and discuss which are strongest

modes.reason: Year 3 conclusions must be grounded in analysis, not just impression — use structured evidence-to-conclusion templates to make the reasoning visible.

descriptors.title: Propose actions or responses
descriptors.description: propose actions or responses to an issue or challenge that consider possible effects of actions
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S05): Students proposed positive futures for familiar places. From Y1 (AC9HS1S05): Students made proposals for caring for places.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose actions or responses to an issue or challenge, considering possible effects of those actions.

nodes.label: Considering effects of actions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can anticipate the effects of proposed actions before committing to them, distinguishing between positive and negative effects.
criteria: Identifies at least one positive effect of a proposed action
Identifies at least one negative or unintended effect
nodes.hinge_reason: Considering effects before proposing action is the new Year 3 cognitive demand — without this, proposals are wishes rather than considered responses.

width.minimum: Identify at least one positive and one negative effect of a proposed action for a community challenge.
width.typical: Consider anticipated effects of actions designed to protect or improve places; identify who would be affected by proposed actions and how; distinguish between intended and unintended effects.
wider: Use a consequence wheel to map first- and second-order effects of a proposed action
Compare the effects of two different responses to the same challenge and argue which is better

modes.reason: Effect-consideration requires students to think beyond their preferred outcome — use 'What would happen if...?' scaffolding and consequence wheels.

nodes.label: Proposing and justifying responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a plan of action for a community challenge and argue for their proposal using persuasive reasoning.
criteria: Proposes at least one action for a community challenge
Supports the proposal with at least one persuasive reason

width.minimum: Propose at least one action for a community challenge and give at least one reason why it would help.
width.typical: Develop plans of action for community challenges (recycling, protecting endangered species, preserving a heritage place, community festival participation); argue a point of view using persuasive language ('I think', 'I dis/agree that').
wider: Develop a group response to a community challenge that considers the perspectives of at least two different community groups
Present a proposal to a real audience (school council, local community member) and respond to questions

modes.reason: Action proposals integrate issue analysis, effect consideration, perspective awareness and persuasive communication — the full civic and evaluating demand.

descriptors.title: Present descriptions and explanations
descriptors.description: present descriptions and explanations, using ideas from sources and relevant subject-specific terms
descriptors.knowledge: From Y2 (AC9HS2S06): Students developed narratives and shared observations using time and place vocabulary.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present descriptions and explanations using ideas from sources and relevant subject-specific terms from history, geography and civics.

nodes.label: Subject-specific vocabulary — three disciplines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use appropriate subject-specific terms from history, geography and civics in speech and writing.
criteria: Uses at least two terms from at least two different HASS disciplines
Terms are used accurately in context (not just listed)
nodes.hinge_reason: Cross-disciplinary vocabulary is required for Y3 HASS communication across history, geography and civics — students without this vocabulary cannot produce descriptions and explanations that meet the descriptor.

width.minimum: Use at least two terms from at least two different HASS disciplines accurately in describing or explaining a topic.
width.typical: Use historical terms (immigration, exploration, development, settlement, commemoration, emblems), geographical terms (climate, environment, natural, constructed) and civic terms (community, decision-making, participation) when speaking, writing and illustrating.
wider: Create a multi-disciplinary glossary for a HASS investigation topic that includes terms from all three disciplines
Identify which discipline's terms are most useful for explaining a specific event or issue and explain why

modes.reason: Three-discipline vocabulary requires deliberate, sustained practice — use word walls, glossaries and explicit embedding in all inquiry outputs.

nodes.label: Presenting using sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present descriptions and explanations that select relevant ideas from sources and use subject-specific terms throughout.
criteria: Incorporates at least one source idea in the presentation
Uses at least two subject-specific terms accurately

width.minimum: Present a description or explanation that uses at least one idea from a source and at least two subject-specific terms.
width.typical: Select ideas from sources (graphs, tables, timelines, photographs, pictures) to support descriptions and explanations; use subject-specific terms from all three HASS disciplines in speech, writing and illustration.
wider: Create a multimodal explanation that integrates visual sources, data displays and written description with accurate subject-specific vocabulary
Present an explanation to an audience and evaluate whether the vocabulary used was appropriate for that audience

modes.reason: Communicating integrates source ideas with subject-specific vocabulary into a coherent explanation — the communication is the integration of all Year 3 inquiry skills.

descriptors.title: Diversity and continuity of First Nations Australians
descriptors.description: the diversity of First Nations Australians, their social organisation and their continuous connection to Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3K04): Students explored the ways First Nations Australians in different parts of Australia are interconnected with Country/Place through poems, songs, paintings and stories.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the diversity of First Nations Australians, their social organisation and their continuous connection to Country/Place.

nodes.label: Diversity within First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that First Nations Australians include two distinct cultural groups (Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples) and that there is considerable diversity within these groups.
criteria: Explains that Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are distinct groups
Describes at least one way diversity exists within these groups
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that First Nations Australians are not a single homogeneous group is prerequisite to discussing their social organisation and connection to Country/Place meaningfully.

width.minimum: Explain that Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples are distinct groups and give at least one way they differ.
width.typical: Recognise the diversity between and within Aboriginal Peoples and Torres Strait Islander Peoples; explore diversity in language, culture, social organisation and connection to Country/Place across different groups.
wider: Research the significant diversity of language groups across Australia and investigate one group in depth
Compare social organisation in two contrasting First Nations Australian groups

modes.reason: Students often have a unified 'Aboriginal Australians' mental model — explicitly challenge this with evidence of linguistic, cultural and geographic diversity.

nodes.label: Continuous connection to Country/Place — archaeological evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how archaeological sites show the continuous connection of early First Peoples of Australia to Country/Place.
criteria: Names at least one archaeological site
Explains what the site reveals about continuous connection to Country/Place

width.minimum: Identify at least one archaeological site (e.g. Nauwalabila, Devil's Lair, Lake Mungo) and explain what it shows about continuous connection to Country/Place.
width.typical: Investigate archaeological sites that show continuous connection of early First Peoples to Country/Place and early lifestyles; explore the connection of First Nations Australians to land and water and how they manage these resources.
wider: Investigate the significance of Lake Mungo specifically and what its evidence tells us about the antiquity of human presence in Australia
Explore how archaeologists work with First Nations communities to investigate these sites respectfully

modes.reason: Multiple archaeological sites from different regions demonstrate that continuous connection is not a local phenomenon — breadth strengthens the evidence base.

nodes.label: Trade and exchange of ideas
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the diversity and significance of trade and exchange of ideas among First Nations Australians, including with groups outside Australia.
criteria: Describes at least one example of trade or exchange
Explains the significance of that trade or exchange for First Nations Australian society

width.minimum: Describe at least one example of trade or exchange involving First Nations Australians and explain its significance.
width.typical: Investigate the diversity and significance of trade and exchange of ideas among First Nations Australians, including with groups outside Australia such as the Macassans; connect trade to broader social organisation.
wider: Research the Macassan-First Nations Australian trading relationship in depth and discuss what it reveals about economic and social organisation
Compare First Nations Australian trade networks with those of other cultures in the same historical period

modes.reason: Trade and exchange connects social organisation, geographical knowledge and cross-cultural interaction — it integrates multiple aspects of the First Nations Australian descriptor.

descriptors.title: Establishment of the first british colony
descriptors.description: the causes of the establishment of the first British colony in Australia in 1788
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3: Students explored community change and diversity of contributions. At Y4 students begin studying colonisation of Australia.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the causes of the establishment of the first British colony in Australia in 1788.

nodes.label: European exploration as a precondition
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how European exploration of sea routes and the Australian coastline created the conditions that made British colonisation possible.
criteria: Names at least one explorer who contributed to knowledge of Australia's coastline
Explains one way their exploration enabled the possibility of colonisation
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding exploration as a precondition, the causes of colonisation appear disconnected from historical context — the causal chain requires this prior context.

width.minimum: Describe the journey of at least one explorer who contributed to knowledge of routes to Australia and explain how it enabled later colonisation.
width.typical: Examine journeys of explorers who sailed routes to Australia (Vasco da Gama, Magellan) and Australian coastline (Hartog, Tasman, Cook, Jansz, de la Perouse) using navigation maps; reconstruct journeys; explain how exploration enabled possible settlement.
wider: Compare what different European explorers knew about Australia and discuss how accumulated knowledge enabled colonisation
Investigate how First Nations Australians encountered early European explorers and what accounts of these encounters exist

modes.reason: The causal connection between exploration and colonisation is not obvious to Year 4 students — build the causal chain explicitly through map-based reconstruction.

nodes.label: Reasons for colonisation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the reasons for British colonisation of Australia including the need for a penal colony, the American War of Independence, strategic interests and resources.
criteria: Explains at least two reasons for British colonisation
At least one reason goes beyond 'needing a penal colony'

width.minimum: Explain at least two reasons why Britain colonised Australia.
width.typical: Investigate the reasons for colonisation: Britain needing a penal colony; impact of American War of Independence; creating a strategic base in the global south; resources; describe the roles of Cook, Banks and the 'secret instructions'.
wider: Evaluate which cause was most significant in the decision to colonise Australia and argue for a position with evidence
Investigate how the decision to colonise Australia was viewed differently in Britain and by other European powers

modes.reason: Multiple causes give richer historical explanation than a single cause — the penal colony cause is widely known but strategic and economic causes are equally significant.

descriptors.title: Experiences of individuals in establishing the first british colony
descriptors.description: the experiences of individuals and groups, including military and civilian officials, and convicts involved in the establishment of the first British colony
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K02: Students explained causes of the first British colony. They now examine who was involved and what they experienced.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the experiences of diverse individuals and groups involved in establishing the first British colony.

nodes.label: Who was on the First Fleet
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the different groups of people on the First Fleet and describe the range of backgrounds and reasons for their presence.
criteria: Names at least three different groups on the First Fleet
Describes the role or reason for each group's presence
nodes.hinge_reason: Knowing who was on the First Fleet is prerequisite to describing their experiences — without this population knowledge, individual account analysis lacks context.

width.minimum: Identify at least three different groups on the First Fleet (e.g. convicts, marines, officials, chaplain) and describe each group's role.
width.typical: Describe events around the establishment of the First Fleet and key people (Captain Phillip, marines, Reverend Johnson, convicts); examine the range of crimes punishable by transportation; investigate social standing of all groups who travelled.
wider: Research the experiences of a specific individual on the First Fleet (convict, marine or official) in depth
Investigate the particular experiences of children, families and women on the First Fleet

modes.reason: Students need to know who the groups were and why they were there before they can engage with individual experiences.

nodes.label: Experiences during the journey and early settlement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the experiences of specific groups and individuals on the journey of the First Fleet and in the early Port Jackson settlement.
criteria: Describes at least two challenges experienced by people in early settlement
Identifies at least one difference in experience between two different groups

width.minimum: Describe at least two challenges experienced by people on the First Fleet journey or in early settlement.
width.typical: Describe events and experiences of groups and individuals on the First Fleet journey; investigate daily life in the Port Jackson penal settlement; examine challenges experienced and how they were managed; investigate attitudes to the poor and social standing.
wider: Compare experiences of convicts with those of marines or officials during the same period
Investigate how the extreme conditions of early settlement affected different groups differently

modes.reason: Comparison across groups (convicts vs marines vs officials) reveals that the 'same' historical event was experienced very differently depending on social position.

descriptors.title: Effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians
descriptors.description: the effects of contact with other people on First Nations Australians and their Countries/Places following the arrival of the First Fleet and how this was viewed by First Nations Australians as an invasion
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K01-K03: Students have explored First Nations Australian diversity and First Fleet establishment. They now examine contact from First Nations Australian perspectives.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the effects of contact following 1788 on First Nations Australians, including how colonisation was experienced as an invasion.

nodes.label: Contact before 1788
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe contact between First Nations Australians and people from Asia and Europe before 1788, including trade and conflict.
criteria: Describes at least one example of pre-1788 contact between First Nations Australians and non-British visitors
Identifies the nature of that contact (e.g. trade, conflict, exchange)
nodes.hinge_reason: Establishing that First Nations Australians had prior agency in contact situations provides essential context for understanding the qualitative shift that British colonisation represented.

width.minimum: Describe at least one example of contact between First Nations Australians and non-British visitors before 1788.
width.typical: Investigate contact between First Nations Australians and people from different continents (Asia, Europe) before 1788; examine examples of trade, sharing of ideas and technologies; explore the repulsion of the Dutch at Cape Keerweer (1606).
wider: Compare First Nations Australian interactions with Macassans and with early European visitors, noting differences in the nature of contact
Investigate rock paintings depicting contact with Macassans and discuss what these reveal from a First Nations perspective

modes.reason: Pre-1788 agency must be established explicitly or students will naturalise colonial disruption as inevitable — this counter-narrative framing requires conscious scaffolding.

nodes.label: Effects of colonisation — perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effects of British colonisation on First Nations Australians (dispossession, disease, frontier conflict, dislocation, loss of food sources) and explain how colonisation was experienced as an invasion.
criteria: Describes at least two effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians
Explains why colonisation was experienced as an invasion from a First Nations perspective

width.minimum: Describe at least two effects of colonisation on First Nations Australians and explain why colonisation was experienced as an invasion.
width.typical: Examine paintings and accounts to explore impact of British colonisation on First Nations Australians; describe dispossession, dislocation, loss of lives, disease, loss of food sources and medicines; consider differing perspectives of interactions; explain the invasion perspective.
wider: Research the perspectives of specific First Nations Australian individuals (Pemulwuy, Windradyne, Bennelong) on early colonial contact
Examine paintings and compare what European and First Nations Australian accounts reveal about the same events

modes.reason: Multiple First Nations Australian voices and experiences give richer understanding of colonisation's effects than a single narrative.

descriptors.title: Importance of environments to people and animals
descriptors.description: the importance of environments, including natural vegetation and water sources, to people and animals in Australia and on another continent
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3K05): Students compared Australia with a neighbouring country in terms of natural, managed and constructed features. From Y3 (AC9HS3K04): Students explored First Nations Australian connections to Country/Place.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the importance of natural environments, including vegetation and water, to people and animals in Australia and on another continent.

nodes.label: Types and roles of vegetation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the main vegetation types (forest, savannah, grassland, woodland, desert) and explain the important roles vegetation plays in sustaining environments.
criteria: Identifies at least three vegetation types
Explains at least two functional roles of vegetation in the environment
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding vegetation types and roles is prerequisite to explaining the importance of environments — functional role knowledge grounds the importance claim.

width.minimum: Identify at least three vegetation types and explain at least two roles vegetation plays in the environment.
width.typical: Identify forest, savannah, grassland, woodland and desert vegetation types in Australia and another continent; explore how vegetation produces oxygen, prevents erosion, retains rainfall, provides habitat, shelters crops, cools urban places, provides medicines and materials.
wider: Compare vegetation types in Australia with those of another continent (e.g. Africa or South America) and explain similarities and differences
Investigate how vegetation change (e.g. clearing for farming) has affected a specific environment

modes.reason: Students need to know what vegetation types exist and what they do before they can explain importance — build the knowledge base through maps and images before the explanatory demand.

nodes.label: Importance of water
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the importance of water to the environment and to sustaining the lives of people and animals.
criteria: Explains at least two ways water is important to people and animals
Includes at least one functional and one non-functional dimension of importance

width.minimum: Explain at least two ways water is important to people and animals in Australia.
width.typical: Identify the importance of water to the environment and human and animal survival; explore how people's connections to environments are aesthetic, emotional and spiritual as well as functional; investigate strategies to protect environments.
wider: Compare water availability and management in Australia with a contrasting continent (e.g. Africa) and discuss implications
Investigate First Nations Australian knowledge of water sources and management practices

modes.reason: Water importance varies enormously across Australian environments — comparing arid and tropical regions reveals the full range.

descriptors.title: Sustainable use of resources
descriptors.description: sustainable use and management of renewable and non-renewable resources, including the custodial responsibility First Nations Australians have for Country/Place
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K05: Students explained the importance of environments and vegetation to people and animals. From Y3 (AC9HS3K06): Students explored rules and community responsibility.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how resources can be used and managed sustainably, including First Nations Australian custodial responsibility for Country/Place.

nodes.label: Renewable and non-renewable resources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between renewable and non-renewable resources and describe sustainable and non-sustainable ways resources are used.
criteria: Classifies at least four resources as renewable or non-renewable
Describes one sustainable and one non-sustainable use of resources
nodes.hinge_reason: The renewable/non-renewable distinction underpins all sustainability analysis — without it, students cannot evaluate whether specific practices are sustainable.

width.minimum: Classify at least four resources as renewable or non-renewable and describe one sustainable and one non-sustainable use.
width.typical: Explore how resources are used sustainably and non-sustainably (auditing classroom use, recycling, waste disposal, managing timber); distinguish renewable from non-renewable; investigate local recycling and waste systems.
wider: Audit resource use in the school and propose sustainable alternatives for the least sustainable practices
Research how a specific renewable resource (timber, water) is managed in Australia and evaluate whether the management is sustainable

modes.reason: Renewable vs non-renewable is a conceptual distinction requiring clear criteria — use concrete examples and classification exercises before sustainability analysis.

nodes.label: First Nations Australian custodial responsibility
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australians have practised sustainable resource use through knowledge and practices linked to custodial responsibility for Country/Place.
criteria: Describes at least one First Nations Australian sustainable resource practice
Explains how it demonstrates custodial responsibility for Country/Place

width.minimum: Describe at least one First Nations Australian practice of sustainable resource use and explain how it demonstrates custodial responsibility.
width.typical: Investigate how First Nations Australians adapted sustainable resource use through rotational harvesting, fire management, endemic plant use for food/shelter/medicine/tools, and how this knowledge is transmitted through stories and songs.
wider: Compare First Nations Australian sustainable land management practices (e.g. fire, rotational use) with contemporary conservation practices and discuss complementarities
Investigate how a specific First Nations Australian sustainable practice (e.g. mutton-bird harvesting in Tasmania) works in detail

modes.reason: Multiple First Nations Australian sustainable practices from different regions reveal the breadth and sophistication of Indigenous land management across Australia.

descriptors.title: Rules and laws
descriptors.description: the differences between 'rules' and 'laws', why laws are important and how they affect the lives of people
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3K06): Students explored who makes rules, why rules are important and the consequences of not following them.
descriptors.endpoint: Students distinguish between rules and laws, explain why laws are important and describe how they affect people's lives.

nodes.label: Distinguishing rules from laws
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between rules (contextual, limited scope) and laws (universal, enforceable) and give examples of each.
criteria: Gives at least two examples each of rules and laws
Explains at least one key difference between rules and laws
nodes.hinge_reason: The rule/law distinction is the conceptual foundation of civics understanding at Year 4 — without it, students cannot analyse how laws affect people's lives in Node 2.

width.minimum: Give at least two examples of rules and two of laws and explain the key difference between them.
width.typical: Distinguish between laws (not speeding in school zones) and rules (sun safety at school); explore examples of laws and their purposes; recognise that laws apply to everyone in society.
wider: Investigate how a rule at school compares with a similar law in the community and discuss what makes the difference in scope and enforcement
Explore First Nations Australian customary lore and discuss how it functions like law within communities

modes.reason: Rule vs law is a conceptual distinction requiring explicit criteria — use a comparison matrix with scope, maker, enforcer and applicability columns.

nodes.label: How laws affect people's lives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how specific laws affect the lives of people, including the impact of environmental and native title laws on First Nations Australians.
criteria: Describes how at least one specific law affects people's lives
Identifies that laws can affect different groups differently

width.minimum: Describe how at least one law affects the daily life of people.
width.typical: Investigate the impact of laws on students' lives; explore how environmental laws, native title laws and laws concerning sacred sites affect specific groups including First Nations Australians.
wider: Investigate native title law in depth and explain how it was established and what it means for First Nations Australian communities
Research the customary lore of a specific First Nations Australian group and discuss how it governs community life
