modes.reason: Laws affecting different groups (general community vs First Nations Australians vs environmental users) reveal that laws have differential impacts.

descriptors.title: Roles of local government
descriptors.description: the roles of local government and how members of the community use and contribute to local services
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3K07): Students explored why people participate in communities and how they can contribute. From Y3 (AC9HS3K06): Students explored rule-making authority.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the roles of local government and describe how community members use and contribute to local services.

nodes.label: How local government is chosen and what it does
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how local government is chosen and explain the range of services it provides.
criteria: Describes how local government is chosen
Names at least four services provided by local government
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need to know what local government does before they can explain how community members use and contribute to those services.

width.minimum: Describe how local government is chosen and list at least four services it provides.
width.typical: Examine how local government is chosen and by whom; explore what local government does — environment and waste management, libraries, health, parks, cultural events, pools, sports facilities, arts and pet management.
wider: Research the specific services provided by the local council in the school's area and compare with another council
Investigate how local councillors are elected and what their responsibilities are

modes.reason: Students need a comprehensive picture of local government services before they can analyse community use and contribution patterns.

nodes.label: Community use and contribution to local services
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how local government services affect students' lives and discuss how community members — including children — can influence those services.
criteria: Describes how at least two local services affect their life
Identifies at least one way community members can influence local services

width.minimum: Describe how at least two local government services affect their own life and identify one way community members can contribute to or influence them.
width.typical: Describe how local government services impact students' lives; discuss how groups, organisations and children can use their voice to make responsible choices about services affecting them and their environment.
wider: Research a recent local government decision about community services and evaluate whether it served the community well
Investigate how a community group successfully influenced a local government decision and what strategies they used

modes.reason: Community participation in local government integrates civic knowledge, participation skills and personal agency — the integration of Y4 civics knowledge.

descriptors.title: Cultural, religious and social groups and identity
descriptors.description: diversity of cultural, religious and/or social groups to which they and others in the community belong, and their importance to identity
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3K02): Students explored significant Australian events, symbols and identity. From Foundation-Y2: Students explored celebrations, family structures and community connections.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the diversity of cultural, religious and social groups to which they and others belong and describe their importance to identity.

nodes.label: Groups people belong to
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the different social, cultural and religious groups they and others in their community belong to and describe what makes them feel part of each group.
criteria: Identifies at least three groups they belong to
Describes what creates belonging in at least one group
nodes.hinge_reason: Students need to identify and describe the groups they belong to before they can analyse how those groups shape identity — the identity analysis in Node 2 requires this foundation.

width.minimum: Identify at least three groups they belong to and describe what makes them feel part of each.
width.typical: Identify diversity through different social, cultural and religious groups students belong to; describe what creates belonging; list and compare different beliefs, traditions and symbols used by different groups.
wider: Compare how belonging to different groups simultaneously can sometimes create tensions or enrich identity
Investigate how immigration has diversified the cultural groups present in the local community

modes.reason: Students benefit from exploring the full range of group types (cultural, religious, interest, community) before analysing any in depth.

nodes.label: Groups and identity
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how membership of groups shapes identity, including how First Nations Australian identity is shaped by Country/Place, language and knowledge traditions.
criteria: Explains how at least one group shapes their identity
Recognises that First Nations Australian identity is specifically shaped by Country/Place, language and knowledge traditions

width.minimum: Explain how at least one group shapes their own identity.
width.typical: Recognise that identity is shaped by membership of multiple groups; recognise that First Nations Australian identity is specifically shaped by Country/Place, language and knowledge traditions.
wider: Compare how identity is shaped by voluntary groups (interest groups) and ascribed groups (cultural, religious, national) and discuss differences
Investigate how First Nations Australian language and knowledge traditions shape identity and what is at risk when these traditions are not maintained

modes.reason: The breadth of group types that shape identity — including First Nations groups — gives richest understanding of identity as constructed and multiple.

descriptors.title: Develop questions to guide investigations
descriptors.description: develop questions to guide investigations about people, events, places and issues
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S01): Students developed location, consequence and ethical questions using inquiring question types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop questions to guide investigations about people, events, places and issues, including discipline-specific and 'How do we know?' questions.

nodes.label: Discipline-specific inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop questions that address disciplinary concepts from history, geography and civics, including 'What was the cause?', 'What are the characteristics of this place?' and 'How can we manage resources sustainably?'
criteria: Develops at least three questions from at least two HASS disciplines
At least one question targets disciplinary evidence ('How do we know?')

width.minimum: Develop at least three inquiry questions using disciplinary question types from at least two different HASS disciplines.
width.typical: Develop questions addressing: cause ('What was the cause?'), significance ('Why was this event significant?'), change ('How did daily life change?'), place ('What are the characteristics of this place?'), sustainability ('How can we manage resources sustainably?'), rules ('What rules are used by...?') and evidence ('How do we know?').
wider: Evaluate whether a set of inquiry questions adequately covers all disciplinary perspectives on a topic
Develop questions that link historical, geographical and civic aspects of the same issue (e.g. colonisation affects history, geography and civic rights)

modes.reason: Discipline-specific questions are the most sophisticated question type at Year 4 — practise across multiple disciplines before expecting fluent integration.

descriptors.title: Locate, collect and record information
descriptors.description: locate, collect and record information and data from a range of sources, including annotated timelines and maps
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S02): Students located and evaluated sources and constructed annotated timelines and maps using cartographic conventions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, collect and record information from discipline-appropriate sources using annotated timelines, maps, graphs and tables.

nodes.label: Discipline-appropriate sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify source types suited to different inquiry contexts (historical, geographical, civic) and explain why each is appropriate.
criteria: Identifies appropriate source types for at least two different inquiry contexts
Explains why each source type suits that context
nodes.hinge_reason: Discipline-appropriate source selection is the Year 4 research capability — without being able to match sources to inquiry contexts, the graphing and organisation tasks in Node 2 lack methodological grounding.

width.minimum: Identify at least one appropriate source type for each of two different inquiry contexts and explain why each is suited.
width.typical: Identify sources suited to historical (paintings, maps, written accounts), geographical (thematic maps, satellite imagery, field data) and civic inquiry (newspaper articles, databases, interviews with local government); discuss why particular sources suit particular contexts.
wider: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of different source types for a specific inquiry question
Compare what information is available from digital vs non-digital sources for the same inquiry topic

modes.reason: Source-context matching requires explicit reasoning: 'For a historical question I need... for a geographical question I need...' — scaffold with worked examples.

nodes.label: Organising information in multiple formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use graphic organisers, timelines, maps, graphs and tables to display collected data and information.
criteria: Organises information in at least two different formats
Format choice is appropriate for the type of information being displayed

width.minimum: Organise collected information in at least two different formats (e.g. a timeline and a table).
width.typical: Use food webs, consequence wheels, timelines of the First Fleet, maps of vegetation or peoples' movement, graphs of cultural groups in Australian society, and tables of data — selected appropriately for the type of information.
wider: Create a connected multi-format presentation where a map, timeline and table each present different aspects of the same inquiry
Evaluate which format best communicates specific types of information and argue for a choice

modes.reason: Multi-format organisation integrates research with data literacy — the matching of data type to display format is the integration task.

descriptors.title: Interpret information in different formats
descriptors.description: interpret information and data displayed in different formats
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S03): Students distinguished fiction from non-fiction and interpreted climate data, graphs and maps.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret information and data from symbols, graphs, maps, satellite images and other display formats.

nodes.label: Decoding symbols and map conventions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can decode the meaning of symbols and emblems associated with Australian history, geography and civic life and apply understanding of conventions when interpreting large-scale maps.
criteria: Interprets at least three symbols from different contexts
Applies at least one map convention correctly when reading a map

width.minimum: Interpret at least three symbols from different contexts (historical, geographical, civic) and apply at least one map convention correctly.
width.typical: Decode meaning of symbols associated with Australian history, geography and civic life; apply understanding of conventions, vocabulary and symbols when interpreting large-scale maps; interpret thematic maps and online satellite images to describe environmental characteristics.
wider: Compare the symbols used in maps from different time periods and discuss how map conventions have changed
Interpret a thematic map of a continent and draw conclusions about the environmental characteristics it reveals

modes.reason: Map conventions and symbol systems require practice across multiple examples before fluent interpretation.

nodes.label: Interpreting graphs and comparing environments
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret data in graphs to identify trends and compare environments across continents.
criteria: Interprets at least one graph and identifies one trend
Uses the trend to explain something about the topic being studied

width.minimum: Interpret at least one graph to identify one trend and explain what it means.
width.typical: Interpret picture, line, bar or column graphs to identify trends; explain survey results about waste or community participation; compare environments in places of similar climate on different continents.
wider: Compare environments with similar climates on different continents (e.g. sandy deserts of Australia, Africa and South America) and explain similarities and differences
Interpret multiple graph types about the same topic and compare what each reveals

modes.reason: Interpreting across graph types (line, bar, column, picture) builds transferable data literacy.

descriptors.title: Analyse information and identify perspectives
descriptors.description: analyse information and data, and identify perspectives
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S04): Students compared sources for evidence of change and identified perspectives, including whose perspectives may be absent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse information across sources and identify multiple perspectives including those of First Nations Australians and diverse groups.

nodes.label: Multi-source analysis
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare information across multiple sources to identify evidence of continuity and change, and draw analytical inferences.
criteria: Analyses at least two sources on the same topic
Identifies evidence of change or continuity that appears in the sources

width.minimum: Analyse at least two sources on the same topic and identify evidence of change or continuity that appears in both.
width.typical: Compare information to find First Nations Australian, Dutch and French place names; analyse interviews with different people about the same management issue; use visible thinking to examine paintings across time periods; compare written information from a historian with visual sources.
wider: Analyse a set of sources that present conflicting information about the same event and decide which is more reliable and why
Compare what paintings of First Nations Australian rock art depicting Macassan contact reveal alongside written historical accounts

modes.reason: Multi-source analysis requires a systematic comparison approach — use analysis matrices to structure the comparison before expecting free-form analysis.

nodes.label: Multiple perspectives on the same event
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain different perspectives on a historical event or contemporary issue, including perspectives of diverse groups.
criteria: Identifies at least two different perspectives on the same event
Explains what shapes each perspective (experience, position, cultural background)

width.minimum: Identify at least two different perspectives on the same event and explain what shapes each perspective.
width.typical: Explore perspectives of convicts, soldiers, free settlers and First Nations Australians on the arrival of the First Fleet; explore contemporary perspectives on school issues or environmental issues.
wider: Compare how perspectives on the First Fleet have changed over time (how historians now tell the story differently from how it was told 50 years ago)
Explore how the perspectives of the same event differ between its portrayal in Australian national narrative vs First Nations Australian accounts

modes.reason: Multiple perspectives from diverse groups on the same historical event is the most important analytical skill at Year 4 — use the First Fleet as the central case.

descriptors.title: Draw conclusions based on analysis
descriptors.description: draw conclusions based on analysis of information
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S05): Students drew evidence-based conclusions about community change, environmental features and place connections.
descriptors.endpoint: Students draw conclusions from analysis of information about risks, resources, exploration, ecosystems and civic issues.

nodes.label: Drawing analytical conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions about historical, geographical and civic topics by analysing sources, with conclusions grounded in evidence rather than opinion.
criteria: States at least one conclusion grounded in analysis of sources
Conclusion goes beyond restating facts to explain a relationship or pattern

width.minimum: Draw at least one conclusion from analysis of at least two sources on a HASS topic.
width.typical: Describe risks in past times (sea travel, exploration, colonisation); explain how seeking resources connects to trade, exploration, colonisation and environmental change; analyse sources to answer questions about ecosystems, local government services and school rules.
wider: Draw conclusions that connect historical events (e.g. colonisation) to present-day circumstances (e.g. land ownership, environmental change)
Compare conclusions drawn from historical and geographical sources about the same topic and identify where they converge or diverge

modes.reason: Year 4 conclusions must integrate multi-source analysis — use structured templates that require evidence from at least two sources before a conclusion can be stated.

descriptors.title: Propose actions or responses
descriptors.description: propose actions or responses to an issue or challenge that consider possible effects of actions
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S06): Students considered effects of actions before proposing them and developed action plans with persuasive justification.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose actions or responses to environmental, local government or cultural issues, considering effects and forecasting futures.

nodes.label: Forecasting probable and preferred futures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can forecast a probable future and a preferred future for an issue and explain the difference between them.
criteria: Describes a probable future for an issue
Describes a preferred future and identifies what would need to change to achieve it
nodes.hinge_reason: The probable/preferred future distinction is new at Year 4 — without it, proposals are wishes rather than evidence-based interventions.

width.minimum: Describe one probable future and one preferred future for a specific issue and explain one action that could shift from the probable to the preferred.
width.typical: Forecast probable and preferred futures for environmental, local government or cultural issues (e.g. ocean plastics, habitat loss); identify resources needed; forecast outcomes of actions.
wider: Develop a detailed preferred future scenario for an issue with a multi-step action plan
Evaluate the realism of a preferred future scenario by identifying what would need to change to achieve it

modes.reason: Probable vs preferred future requires students to distinguish what IS likely from what SHOULD happen — explicitly contrast the two before expecting students to reason across them.

nodes.label: Responsible decision-making and action
nodes.checkpoint: Students can reflect on personal behaviours, identify attitudes that affect their environment and propose awareness-raising strategies.
criteria: Identifies at least one personal behaviour affecting the environment
Proposes a specific action or awareness-raising strategy with a reason

width.minimum: Identify at least one personal behaviour that affects the environment and propose one change to that behaviour.
width.typical: Reflect on personal behaviours affecting the environment at local or global level; identify resources needed for proposed actions; propose solutions to waste management, endangered species protection or cultural issues; participate in cooperative decision-making.
wider: Develop an awareness-raising strategy for a specific environmental issue, including identifying the audience, the message and the medium
Evaluate whether a proposed action would genuinely achieve its goal and revise it if needed

modes.reason: Responsible decision-making integrates reflection, forecasting, effect analysis and communication — the full Year 4 civic and evaluating capability.

descriptors.title: Present descriptions and explanations
descriptors.description: present descriptions and explanations, using ideas from sources and relevant subject-specific terms
descriptors.knowledge: From Y3 (AC9HS3S07): Students presented using ideas from sources and subject-specific terms from history, geography and civics.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present descriptions and explanations using ideas from sources and subject-specific terms from Year 4 HASS disciplines.

nodes.label: Year 4 subject-specific vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use accurate Year 4 subject-specific terms from history, geography and civics in speech, writing and illustration.
criteria: Uses at least two subject-specific terms from at least two disciplines accurately
Terms are used in disciplinary context (not just listed)
nodes.hinge_reason: Year 4 introduces significantly more complex and specific vocabulary across all three disciplines — without this vocabulary, students cannot communicate at the level the descriptor demands.

width.minimum: Use at least two terms from each of two HASS disciplines accurately in a description or explanation.
width.typical: Use historical terms (exploration, navigation, trade, penal, transportation, contact, colonisation); geographical terms (continents, countries, natural resources, vegetation, environments, ecosystems, sustainability, consumption, waste, management); civic terms (local government, decision-making, services, roles, responsibilities, rules, laws, belonging).
wider: Use subject-specific vocabulary to write a multi-disciplinary explanation of a single event (e.g. colonisation) from historical, geographical and civic perspectives
Create a subject-specific vocabulary resource that includes definitions, examples and images for Year 4 HASS

modes.reason: Year 4 vocabulary includes many abstract and discipline-specific terms requiring sustained practice — use word walls, explicit instruction and vocabulary-embedded inquiry tasks.

nodes.label: Describing relative location and direction
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the relative location of different features in a place by distance and compass direction.
criteria: Describes the location of at least two features using distance and compass direction
At least one compass direction is used correctly

width.minimum: Describe the location of at least two places or features using distance and at least one compass direction.
width.typical: Describe relative location using distance and compass direction (e.g. the distance from home to local waste management site; the route of a navigator); incorporate spatial descriptions into presentations about historical events and geographical features.
wider: Describe a complete route from one place to another using compass directions and distance estimates
Incorporate a map with compass directions into a presentation and explain location using both the map and verbal description

modes.reason: Relative location description with compass direction integrates spatial literacy with HASS communication — the presentation is the integration task.

descriptors.title: Causes of british colonies after 1800
descriptors.description: the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K02 (Causes of the first British colony): Students explain the causes of the establishment of the first British colony in Australia.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, distinguishing between different colony types and the reasons for each.

nodes.label: Types of colonies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify that different types of British colonies were established in Australia after 1800, including penal colonies and colonies for free settlers, and name examples of each.
criteria: Students identify at least two types of British colonies and give a named example of each.
Students explain the intended purpose of each colony type in one or two sentences.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't distinguish colony types will conflate the economic, political and social causes that follow — causes were not uniform across all colonies. The distinctions underpin all subsequent causal reasoning.

width.minimum: Identify two types of colonies (penal and free settler) and provide one example of each.
width.typical: Distinguish between penal colonies (e.g. Moreton Bay, Van Diemen's Land) and free settler colonies (e.g. South Australia, Victoria), explaining the intended purpose of each.
wider: Investigate how the type of colony influenced its early social structure, laws and treatment of First Nations Australians in that location
Explore how colony type shaped the economy and land use practices in the early decades of settlement

modes.reason: Use sorting activities (e.g. card sorts by colony type) and explicit classification frameworks to ensure students can categorise examples before moving to causes.

nodes.label: Economic causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain economic reasons for the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, including acquisition of land and resources, and economic conditions in Britain.
criteria: Students name at least two economic causes and explain how each contributed to establishing colonies.
Students connect British economic conditions (e.g. unemployment, overcrowding) to the decision to colonise.

width.minimum: Explain one economic cause (e.g. land and resource acquisition or economic hardship in Britain).
width.typical: Explain the range of economic causes: acquisition of land and resources, high unemployment and poverty in Britain, and the economic potential of Australian land for farming and resource extraction.
wider: Investigate how global trade interests and competition between European powers shaped British economic motivations for colonisation
Examine the role of specific industries (e.g. wool, whaling, grain) in the economic argument for expanding Australian colonies

modes.reason: Economic causes are best understood by comparing the British economic context with the colonial opportunity — use both perspectives to deepen understanding rather than a single causal story.

nodes.label: Political causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain political reasons for the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, including expanding the British Empire and strategic concerns about competing nations.
criteria: Students explain at least one political cause and link it to a decision to establish a specific colony or expand settlement.
Students distinguish political causes from economic and social causes.

width.minimum: Explain one political cause (e.g. expanding the British Empire).
width.typical: Explain that political causes included expanding the British Empire's global reach and concern that other colonial powers (e.g. France) might claim Australian territory.
wider: Investigate the geopolitical context of European colonialism in the late 18th and 19th centuries, comparing British motivations with those of France and other powers
Explore how colonial policy was influenced by British parliamentary politics and competing interests within British government

modes.reason: Political causes become more meaningful when set against the broader European colonial context — comparative framing helps students see British motives as deliberate strategic choices rather than inevitable events.

nodes.label: Social causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain social reasons for the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, including overcrowded British cities, high crime rates and overflowing prisons.
criteria: Students name at least two social causes and explain how they contributed to transportation and colonisation.
Students explain the connection between social conditions in Britain and the decision to use Australia for transportation.

width.minimum: Explain one social cause (e.g. overcrowded British prisons).
width.typical: Explain the range of social causes: overcrowded cities, high crime rates, overflowing prisons, and the use of transportation as a solution to Britain's social problems.
wider: Investigate the lives of transported convicts — who they were, their crimes, and their experiences of the voyage and arrival in the colony
Examine First Nations Australian perspectives on the arrival of convicts and settlers as a social and cultural disruption to established ways of life

modes.reason: Social causes are most vivid when explored through case studies of real transported individuals — concrete human stories ground abstract social conditions in ways that support understanding.

nodes.label: Integrating multiple causes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the economic, political and social causes of the establishment of British colonies in Australia after 1800, identifying how different causes applied to different colony types.
criteria: Students explain at least one economic, one political and one social cause in an integrated account.
Students show how the mix of causes differed between at least two colony types.
Students' explanation uses relevant historical terminology (e.g. 'penal colony', 'free settlers', 'transportation').

width.minimum: Explain at least one cause from each category (economic, political, social) and link each to the establishment of at least one colony.
width.typical: Explain the full range of economic, political and social causes, distinguishing how different causes applied more strongly to penal versus free settler colonies, and identify which causes were most significant.
wider: Construct a comparative analysis of two different colonies, examining how the combination of causes shaped the character of each colony differently
Evaluate which category of cause (economic, political or social) was most significant overall, using evidence from multiple colonies to support the argument

modes.reason: The integration node requires students to bring all three cause categories together into a coherent explanation. Use structured tasks such as cause-and-effect matrices or comparative colony profiles to support this synthesis.

descriptors.title: Impacts of colonial development
descriptors.description: the impact of the development of British colonies in Australia on the lives of First Nations Australians, the colonists and convicts, and on the natural environment
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K03 (Experiences of colonisation) and AC9HS4K04 (Effects of contact and invasion): Students explain the experiences of colonisation for First Nations Australians and early colonists, and the effects of contact and invasion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the impact of the development of British colonies in Australia on the lives of First Nations Australians, colonists and convicts, and on the natural environment, identifying both intended and unintended consequences.

nodes.label: Impact on First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the impact of colonial development on the lives of First Nations Australians, including dispossession, conflict, disruption to cultural practices and loss of life.
criteria: Students explain at least two specific impacts on First Nations Australians with reference to historical evidence.
Students describe how colonial development changed the relationship between First Nations Australians and their Country/Place.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand colonial impacts only from a settler perspective will struggle to engage with the multi-perspective analysis required in subsequent nodes and in later HASS learning. A thin account here distorts the historical record and limits the sophistication of future causal analysis.

width.minimum: Explain at least two impacts of colonial development on First Nations Australians.
width.typical: Explain the range of impacts on First Nations Australians: dispossession from Country, frontier conflict, disruption to cultural and spiritual practices, loss of life, and the destruction of established economic systems (including food sources and land management).
wider: Investigate the experience of a particular First Nations community or nation during colonial expansion, using primary and secondary sources to describe changes to their way of life
Examine First Nations Australian perspectives and responses to colonisation, including resistance movements and efforts to maintain cultural practices

modes.reason: Multiple First Nations perspectives and case studies are essential — not as enrichment but as the corrective to a default settler-centred account. Use sources that foreground First Nations voices and experiences.

nodes.label: Impact on colonists and convicts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the impact of colonial development on the daily lives of different groups of colonists and convicts, including differences in their clothing, food, work, housing and social position.
criteria: Students describe the daily life of at least two different colonial groups and identify at least one key difference between them.
Students use relevant historical terms (e.g. 'convict', 'free settler', 'squatter') accurately in their account.

width.minimum: Describe the daily life of one colonial group (e.g. convicts or free settlers) including at least three aspects of daily life.
width.typical: Compare the daily lives of different groups — convicts, free settlers, squatters, indentured labourers, and different migrant groups — across several aspects: clothing, food and water access, work (paid and unpaid), housing, leisure, and children's lives.
wider: Investigate the experiences of a specific migrant group (e.g. Chinese miners, Afghan cameleers, Pacific Islander labourers) and compare their colonial experience with that of British free settlers
Examine the role of women in colonial society, including both the constraints they faced and the agency they exercised across different social positions

modes.reason: The range of colonial groups is the key width dimension here — students benefit from comparing across multiple social positions rather than studying one group in depth. The elaborations explicitly name this range.

nodes.label: Impact on the natural environment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the impact of colonial settlement on the natural environment, including changes to vegetation, land use, fauna and ecosystems.
criteria: Students describe at least two ways colonial settlement changed the natural environment.
Students explain how settlement patterns were influenced by geographical features.

width.minimum: Explain at least one way colonial settlement changed the natural environment.
width.typical: Explain how colonial settlement patterns were shaped by geographical factors (land for farming, water, transport) and how these patterns impacted local environments through vegetation clearance, introduction of grazing livestock, drainage, and the effects on local flora, fauna and ecosystems.
wider: Compare the present and past landscape of a local area to identify changes in vegetation and fauna since European colonisation, using maps, photographs or local data
Examine the contrasting approaches to land management of First Nations Australians (e.g. firestick farming) and British colonists, and evaluate the long-term environmental consequences of each

modes.reason: Environmental impact is strongest when explored through local or regional examples — connecting abstract land-use changes to a specific place makes the impact tangible and supports geographical thinking.

nodes.label: Integrating multiple perspectives on impact
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the impact of colonial development in Australia on First Nations Australians, colonists and convicts, and the natural environment, presenting a multi-perspective account that acknowledges intended and unintended consequences.
criteria: Students explain the impact on at least three groups or entities (e.g. First Nations Australians, convicts, environment) in an integrated account.
Students distinguish between intended and unintended consequences of colonial development.
Students demonstrate awareness that different groups experienced colonial development very differently.

width.minimum: Describe the impact on at least two different groups and on the environment, and identify at least one unintended consequence.
width.typical: Explain the contrasting impacts on First Nations Australians, different colonial groups, and the environment; identify which impacts were intended by colonial authorities and which were unintended; acknowledge different perspectives on these impacts.
wider: Evaluate which group experienced the most significant negative impact from colonial development and justify the claim with evidence
Investigate how the long-term environmental impacts of colonial settlement continue to affect Australia today, and how First Nations land management practices are now being recognised and applied

modes.reason: This integration node requires students to hold multiple perspectives simultaneously — use structured comparison tasks (e.g. perspective matrices) that make visible the different experiences and their causes.

descriptors.title: Individuals and groups in colonial development
descriptors.description: the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations Australians and those who migrated to Australia, in the development of events in an Australian colony
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K04 (Effects of contact and invasion): Students explain the effects of contact and invasion on First Nations Australians and early colonists. Students have prior understanding of colonial figures and events from Year 4.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the role of a significant individual or group, including First Nations Australians and migrants, in the development of a key event or industry in an Australian colony, and assess the economic, social or political impact of that event or development.

nodes.label: What makes a role significant?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain what makes the role of an individual or group historically significant — that is, that their actions influenced the development of events or changed outcomes for others.
criteria: Students name at least two criteria for historical significance.
Students apply at least one criterion to explain why a colonial figure or group is considered significant.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot apply criteria for significance will describe events rather than explain roles — they'll list what happened without assessing why a particular person or group mattered. This conceptual framing is the prerequisite for the analysis required in subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Identify at least two criteria for historical significance and apply them to one colonial figure or group.
width.typical: Explain the concept of historical significance — that significance involves influence on events, consequences for others, and lasting effects — and apply these criteria to evaluate the role of at least one individual or group from the colonial period.
wider: Explore the concept of historical significance across different perspectives — questioning whose roles tend to be recorded and whose are overlooked in historical accounts
Examine how different historians have assessed the significance of the same colonial figure or event, and what this reveals about historical interpretation

modes.reason: Use an explicit significance framework (e.g. SECON: Significance, Evidence, Causes, Outcomes, Now) or a simplified two-criteria model to scaffold the move from description to analysis.

nodes.label: Roles of key individuals
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the role of at least one significant individual from a colonial event or development, including their actions and the economic, social or political impact of those actions.
criteria: Students explain the role of at least one significant individual and describe at least one specific action they took.
Students assess the economic, social or political impact of that individual's role on the colony.

width.minimum: Describe the role of one significant individual and explain one economic, social or political impact of their actions.
width.typical: Explain the role of a significant individual (e.g. Bennelong, Peter Lalor, Elizabeth Macarthur, a colonial governor) and assess the economic, social or political impact of their role on the development of the colony.
wider: Investigate an individual whose historical role has been reassessed over time (e.g. how Ned Kelly or Governor Macquarie has been viewed differently across eras) and explain why interpretations have changed
Examine a First Nations individual (e.g. Windradyne, Bennelong, Truganini) and explain their role from both First Nations and colonial perspectives

modes.reason: The range of individuals in the elaborations is substantial — students benefit from exposure to figures across different social groups (not just white male colonial leaders) to build a representative picture of colonial development.

nodes.label: Roles of groups including migrants and First Nations Australians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the role of a significant group, including First Nations Australians and migrant groups, in the development of events or industries in an Australian colony.
criteria: Students explain the role of at least one migrant or First Nations group in a colonial event or industry.
Students describe the significance of that group's contribution and any challenges they faced.

width.minimum: Describe the role of one group (migrant or First Nations) in a colonial event or industry.
width.typical: Explain the experiences and contributions of at least one migrant group (e.g. Chinese miners, German settlers, Pacific Islanders) or a First Nations group in a colonial event or industry, and assess their role's significance.
wider: Compare the experiences of two different migrant groups in colonial Australia and explain why their contributions have been treated differently in historical accounts
Investigate the development of a primary industry (e.g. wool, pearling, sugar cane, mining) and assess the contribution of First Nations Australians or a specific migrant group to that industry

modes.reason: Group roles are enriched by comparison across groups — particularly comparing the treatment and experience of migrant groups with that of First Nations Australians in the same period and location.

nodes.label: Assessing impact and 'what if' reasoning
nodes.checkpoint: Students can assess the economic, social or political impact of a significant individual or group on an Australian colony, and reason about how events might have developed differently.
criteria: Students explain the economic, social or political impact of their chosen individual or group with reference to evidence.
Students construct a plausible 'what if' scenario and explain why the actual outcome occurred instead.
Students use appropriate historical terms (e.g. 'significance', 'impact', 'consequence') in their response.

width.minimum: Explain the impact of one individual or group and identify one alternative outcome that might have occurred if events had been different.
width.typical: Assess the economic, social or political impact of a chosen individual or group; construct a 'what if' scenario that explores an alternative outcome for a key event; evaluate which factors made the actual outcome more likely than the alternative.
wider: Evaluate the relative significance of multiple individuals or groups in shaping the same colonial event, and justify a claim about whose role was most significant
Examine how 'what if' thinking is used by historians to understand causation, and apply this method to assess the role of contingency versus inevitability in colonial history

modes.reason: The 'what if' reasoning and impact assessment require explicit scaffolding — provide sentence frames or structured planning templates that distinguish between describing what happened and reasoning about what might have been different and why.

descriptors.title: People shape places
descriptors.description: the influence of people, including First Nations Australians and people in other countries, on the characteristics of a place
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K05 (Importance of environments): Students explain the importance of environments and the connections people have to them. Students understand that places have natural and human characteristics.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the influence of people, including First Nations Australians and people in other countries, on the characteristics of a place, evaluating both positive and negative effects of human influence.

nodes.label: How people change place characteristics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that people influence the characteristics of places through land use, resource management and development decisions, and give examples of how this happens.
criteria: Students name at least two ways people influence the characteristics of places.
Students give a specific example for at least one of these influences.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand only physical/natural characteristics of places (from earlier years) need to clearly grasp that human decisions actively and intentionally reshape places. This conceptual shift from 'places have characteristics' to 'people create characteristics' is foundational for the evaluative work in subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Explain two ways people change the characteristics of a place.
width.typical: Explain the range of ways people change place characteristics: vegetation clearance, fencing, urban development, drainage, irrigation, farming, introduction of livestock, mining, and forest plantations, with examples drawn from Australian contexts.
wider: Investigate how the characteristics of a local place have changed over time by comparing historical and current photographs, maps or records
Explore examples of human influence on place characteristics in countries in Asia, Europe or North America, and compare with Australian examples

modes.reason: Use a 'before and after' framework to make the human influence visible — explicitly connecting the decision (what people did) to the characteristic change (what the place became).

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and place management
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how First Nations Australians have influenced place characteristics through land and resource management practices such as firestick farming.
criteria: Students explain at least one First Nations land management practice and describe its effect on a place.
Students distinguish First Nations land management from post-colonial approaches in at least one example.

width.minimum: Explain one way First Nations Australians managed land or resources and describe the effect on the place's characteristics.
width.typical: Explain First Nations Australian land management practices including firestick farming, and describe how these practices sustained environments and shaped place characteristics over thousands of years.
wider: Investigate a specific First Nations community's land management practices and compare them with post-colonial land use in the same area
Explore how contemporary land management in Australia is incorporating First Nations knowledge and practices, and the effect this is having on the characteristics of specific places

modes.reason: First Nations land management is a distinct and important context — treating it as equivalent enrichment to other land use examples risks reducing it to tokenism. Give it dedicated time and treat the knowledge system as significant in its own right.

nodes.label: Positive and negative influences
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate positive and negative human influences on place characteristics, giving examples of each and explaining why some actions are considered beneficial or harmful.
criteria: Students give at least one example each of a positive and negative human influence on a place.
Students explain the reasoning behind categorising each influence as positive or negative.

width.minimum: Give one example each of a positive and a negative human influence on a place and explain why each is categorised that way.
width.typical: Evaluate a range of positive influences (e.g. reforestation, land-care, rehabilitation of mining sites) and negative influences (e.g. vegetation clearance, urban sprawl, pollution) on place characteristics, and explain the criteria used to categorise them.
wider: Investigate a specific land rehabilitation project (e.g. rehabilitated mine site, wetland restoration) and evaluate its success in restoring place characteristics
Examine an example of positive or negative human influence on places in another country (including Asia, Europe or North America) and compare the context and consequences with an Australian example

modes.reason: Evaluation of positive/negative influence depends heavily on whose perspective is centred — present multiple stakeholder views (environmental, economic, community) to avoid oversimplified good/bad categorisation.

nodes.label: Evaluating human influence on place characteristics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the influence of diverse groups of people on the characteristics of a place, evaluating the range of positive and negative effects and considering different perspectives on those effects.
criteria: Students explain the influence of at least two different groups on the characteristics of a place.
Students evaluate the positive and/or negative effects of these influences with reference to evidence.
Students acknowledge that different groups may view the same influence differently.

width.minimum: Explain the influence of at least two different groups of people on a place and evaluate whether the overall effect has been positive or negative.
width.typical: Explain the influence of multiple groups (including First Nations Australians, colonists/settlers, and people in other countries) on the characteristics of a place, evaluating the economic, environmental and social effects and acknowledging that perspectives on these effects differ.
wider: Construct an argument for a particular course of action to manage human influence on a specific place, drawing on evidence about current and historical impacts
Evaluate the long-term sustainability of current human influences on a chosen place, considering what characteristics might be lost if current practices continue

modes.reason: This node brings together the full range of human influences, including First Nations, colonial and international contexts, into an evaluative account. Use a structured comparison or evaluation matrix to support synthesis.

descriptors.title: Managing environments and hazards
descriptors.description: the management of Australian environments, including managing severe weather events such as bushfires, floods, droughts or cyclones, and their consequences
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K06 (Resource management and sustainability): Students explain why environments are important and how communities manage resources for sustainability. Students understand that environments can be affected by human actions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how Australian environments are managed, including the management of severe weather events such as bushfires, floods, droughts and cyclones, and evaluate the consequences of both events and management responses.

nodes.label: How environments are used and managed
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how Australian environments are managed through practices and laws designed to balance human use with environmental protection.
criteria: Students name at least two environmental management approaches and explain the purpose of each.
Students give a specific Australian example for at least one management approach.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand that environments are actively managed through deliberate decisions will treat environmental hazards as purely natural events disconnected from human choice. The concept of management is the prerequisite for evaluating management responses in subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Explain one way Australian environments are managed (e.g. national parks, zoning, wildlife corridors) and why that management is needed.
width.typical: Explain the range of environmental management approaches: protective laws and practices, zoning systems, creation of wildlife corridors and national parks, and land-use planning that aims to balance economic use with environmental protection.
wider: Investigate the management of a specific Australian national park or protected area, including the rules, zoning and management challenges it faces
Explore how First Nations Australian management practices (e.g. cultural burning, seasonal harvesting protocols) are being incorporated into contemporary environmental management frameworks

modes.reason: Use a framework that distinguishes 'what the environment provides', 'how humans use it', and 'how management balances these' — this three-part structure scaffolds the conceptual move from environment as given to environment as managed.

nodes.label: Types of severe weather events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the types of severe weather events that affect Australian environments — bushfires, floods, droughts and cyclones — and explain their causes and typical locations.
criteria: Students name at least three types of severe weather events that affect Australia and the regions at risk.
Students explain at least one cause of a severe weather event and its typical consequences.

width.minimum: Describe one type of severe weather event, explain where in Australia it typically occurs, and identify one consequence.
width.typical: Describe the range of severe weather events affecting Australia (bushfires, floods, droughts, cyclones), explain the environmental and geographical factors that cause them, and identify the typical regions most at risk from each.
wider: Investigate how climate patterns and climate variability (including El Niño and La Niña) affect the frequency and intensity of severe weather events in Australia
Compare the experience of severe weather events in Australia with those in other countries, and explain why different regions face different types of natural hazards

modes.reason: Students often have uneven prior experience of different hazard types depending on where they live — deliberately addressing all four types ensures the breadth needed for comparative management analysis.

nodes.label: Management strategies for hazards
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how communities and governments manage the risks of severe weather events through preparation, mitigation and response strategies.
criteria: Students explain at least two management strategies for severe weather events with reference to how they reduce risk or harm.
Students distinguish between preparedness strategies (before an event) and response strategies (during and after).

width.minimum: Describe two management strategies for one type of severe weather event (e.g. building codes for cyclones, controlled burns for bushfires).
width.typical: Explain the range of management strategies for severe weather events: building codes and zoning regulations, controlled burns and firebreaks, water management and storage systems, evacuation plans, and early warning systems.
wider: Investigate the management of a recent Australian severe weather event (e.g. a specific bushfire, flood or cyclone) and evaluate the effectiveness of preparation and response
Explore how community organisations (e.g. Rural Fire Service, State Emergency Service) are structured to manage hazards, and assess the role of volunteers in this system

modes.reason: Management strategies are best understood through specific case studies — students need concrete examples of how strategies work in practice, not just abstract lists of approaches.

nodes.label: Consequences and evaluating responses
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the consequences of severe weather events on communities and environments, and evaluate how effectively management approaches reduce those consequences.
criteria: Students explain at least two consequences of a severe weather event across different domains (e.g. environmental, economic, social).
Students evaluate the effectiveness of at least one management strategy with reference to evidence.
Students use relevant geographic and environmental terms accurately.

width.minimum: Explain two consequences of a severe weather event and assess whether one management strategy was effective in reducing harm.
width.typical: Explain the environmental, social and economic consequences of severe weather events; evaluate how effective management strategies (e.g. building codes, controlled burns, irrigation) have been in reducing harm; acknowledge that not all consequences can be mitigated.
wider: Evaluate the long-term consequences of a recurring environmental hazard (e.g. drought) on a specific community or industry, and propose management improvements

Examine how environmental mismanagement can create or intensify hazards (e.g. fire fuel loads from lack of burning, flood risk from inadequate drainage planning), and propose how management practices should change

modes.reason: Evaluation requires students to bring together their understanding of hazard types, management strategies, and consequences. Use structured evaluation criteria (e.g. economic cost, lives saved, environmental protection) to scaffold judgment.

descriptors.title: Democracy, elections and representatives
descriptors.description: the key values and features of Australia's democracy, including elections, and the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K07 (Rules and laws) and AC9HS4K08 (Local government and services): Students explain why rules and laws exist and how local government provides services to communities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the key values and features of Australia's democracy, including the electoral system, and describe the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives at different levels.

nodes.label: What is democracy?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the meaning of democracy and identify the key values underpinning Australian democracy, including freedom of election, assembly, speech and religion, the rule of law, and human rights.
criteria: Students explain what democracy means and name at least three key values of Australian democracy.
Students give an example of how at least one democratic value applies in a context they are familiar with.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't understand the core values of democracy will treat elections as a procedural mechanism without understanding what they protect or enable. The values framework is the conceptual foundation for understanding why elections, representatives and citizenship responsibilities exist.

width.minimum: Define democracy and name two key values of Australian democracy.
width.typical: Explain the meaning of democracy and describe the range of key values: freedom of election and being elected, freedom of assembly and political participation, freedom of speech and religious belief, rule of law, and basic human rights. Illustrate how these values apply in familiar contexts.
wider: Compare Australian democratic values with those of a non-democratic system of government to highlight what distinguishes democracy
Explore the Australian citizenship pledge and the federal government's statement of Australian values, evaluating what these documents reveal about the ideals of Australian democracy

modes.reason: Use concrete, familiar examples (class vote, school council, local election) to illustrate each value. Abstract democratic values become accessible when applied to contexts students already understand.

nodes.label: Features of Australia's electoral system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key features of Australia's electoral system, including the secret ballot, compulsory voting, preferential voting, and the role of the Australian Electoral Commission.
criteria: Students describe at least two features of Australia's electoral system and explain the purpose of each.
Students explain the role of the Australian Electoral Commission.

width.minimum: Describe two features of Australia's electoral system and explain the purpose of each.
width.typical: Explain all key features of Australia's electoral system: the secret ballot, compulsory voting, preferential voting system, and the role of the Australian Electoral Commission in administering free and fair elections.
wider: Investigate how Australia's voting system has changed over time, including when women and First Nations Australians were first allowed to vote, and evaluate what these changes reveal about democracy as an evolving system
Compare Australia's electoral system with that of another country, identifying similarities and differences in features such as voting age, compulsory voting and vote-counting methods

modes.reason: The historical expansion of voting rights (women, First Nations Australians) adds essential context to understanding electoral features as choices made and contested, not natural givens.

nodes.label: Roles and responsibilities of elected representatives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives, including making laws, representing constituents and being accountable to voters.
criteria: Students describe at least two roles or responsibilities of elected representatives.
Students give an example of how a representative is accountable to voters.

width.minimum: Describe two responsibilities of an elected representative at one level of government.
width.typical: Describe the roles and responsibilities of elected representatives at different levels (local, state/territory, federal), including making and debating laws, representing the views of their constituents, and being accountable through elections.
wider: Investigate the work of a specific elected representative (e.g. a local councillor or federal MP) over a period of time, and evaluate how effectively they have represented their community
Explore what characteristics make for a 'good' representative at different levels of government, and consider whether current representatives meet these criteria

modes.reason: The distinction between levels of government (local, state, federal) is important groundwork for Year 6 content — ensure students can differentiate roles and responsibilities across levels, not just describe them in the abstract.

nodes.label: Responsibilities of citizens in a democracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the responsibilities of citizens in a democracy, including enrolling to vote, being informed, voting responsibly, and participating in civic life.
criteria: Students explain at least two responsibilities of citizens in a democracy.
Students connect at least one citizen responsibility to a democratic value (e.g. being informed connects to freedom of election).
Students use correct civic terms (e.g. 'elector', 'representative', 'electoral roll').

width.minimum: Name two responsibilities of citizens in a democracy and explain why each matters.
width.typical: Explain the responsibilities of citizens in a democracy: enrolling to vote, being informed about candidates and issues, voting responsibly, and participating in civic life through community groups, advocacy or other means.
wider: Investigate how citizens participate in democracy beyond voting, including through petitions, public submissions, community groups and protest, and evaluate the effectiveness of different forms of participation
Examine examples of citizens working together to achieve a democratic goal (connecting to AC9HS5K07) and assess the role of shared values in making collective civic action effective

modes.reason: This node connects the features and values of democracy to what they require of citizens. Use a structured reflection on how democratic values (Node 1) are enacted through specific citizen responsibilities — make the conceptual link explicit.

descriptors.title: Citizens working for civic goals
descriptors.description: how citizens (members of communities) with shared beliefs and values work together to achieve a civic goal
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K09 (Community identity and diversity): Students explain how communities are diverse and how people within communities have shared identities and belonging. Students understand that community groups serve different purposes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain how citizens with shared beliefs and values work together to achieve a civic goal, giving examples of community groups that pursue shared goals and evaluating the importance of civic participation.

nodes.label: What is a civic goal?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the concept of a civic goal — a shared aim that benefits a community or society — and distinguish civic goals from personal or commercial goals.
criteria: Students explain the meaning of 'civic goal' and distinguish it from personal or commercial goals.
Students give at least one example of a community pursuing a civic goal.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish civic goals from personal or commercial goals will describe community groups without understanding what makes their aims distinctively civic. This distinction is the conceptual foundation for understanding citizenship and collective action.

width.minimum: Define 'civic goal' and give one example of a community pursuing a civic goal.
width.typical: Explain what a civic goal is — an aim that benefits the broader community or society — and give examples of civic goals pursued by different types of community groups, distinguishing these from personal goals (benefiting an individual) or commercial goals (benefiting a business).
wider: Investigate the relationship between civic goals and democratic values — how do shared values motivate citizens to work together for community benefit?
Explore examples of civic goals at different scales: local (school/neighbourhood), regional, national and global, and compare the challenges of pursuing civic goals at each scale

modes.reason: Use a three-column sorting framework (personal / commercial / civic) with real examples to make the distinction concrete before moving to analysis of how civic goals are pursued.

nodes.label: How citizens organise and work together
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how citizens with shared beliefs and values organise themselves into groups and work collectively to pursue civic goals, including through volunteering and community organisations.
criteria: Students describe how at least one community group is organised around shared values and goals.
Students explain at least two ways members of the group work together to pursue their civic goal.

width.minimum: Describe how one community group organises itself and works toward a civic goal.
width.typical: Explain how different types of community groups (religious and other charities, rural fire services, surf life-saving clubs, emergency services, First Nations community groups, youth groups) organise themselves around shared values and work collectively to achieve civic goals.
wider: Investigate a First Nations Australian community organisation and explain the services it provides, the values it is built around, and how it supports community goals
Examine how digital platforms and social media are used by citizens to organise around shared civic goals at local, national and global levels

modes.reason: The range of community group types in the elaborations is important — students benefit from seeing how civic organisation occurs across very different contexts, from emergency services to cultural organisations to digital advocacy.

nodes.label: Why citizens participate in civic life
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why citizens choose to participate in civic life and community groups, including the connection between shared beliefs and values and the motivation to act for community benefit.
criteria: Students explain at least two reasons citizens participate in civic organisations.
Students connect at least one motivating reason to a shared value or belief.

width.minimum: Explain two reasons why citizens might volunteer or participate in a civic organisation.
width.typical: Explain the motivations for civic participation: shared values and beliefs, concern for community wellbeing, cultural and religious obligation, desire to make a difference, and the social benefits of belonging to a community organisation.
wider: Survey members of a local community organisation to investigate their motivations for participation, and compare their responses with the elaboration examples
Explore how civic participation is connected to broader democratic values — making the link between individual participation and the health of democracy explicit

modes.reason: The link between values and motivation is an inferential move students may not make automatically — use examples that make the value-to-action pathway explicit (e.g. 'We believe in protecting life, so we volunteer with the SES').

nodes.label: Evaluating civic participation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the importance of civic participation in a democratic society, explaining how citizens working together for civic goals contributes to community wellbeing and democratic health.
criteria: Students explain why civic participation matters for community wellbeing and democracy.
Students give at least one example of citizens working together to achieve a civic goal.
Students use relevant civic terms accurately (e.g. 'civic', 'volunteer', 'community organisation', 'shared values').

width.minimum: Explain why civic participation is important in a democracy, using at least one example.
width.typical: Evaluate the importance of civic participation for community wellbeing and democracy, explaining how collective action around shared values achieves goals that individuals or governments acting alone cannot, and give examples from Australian and global contexts.
wider: Investigate how civic participation has changed over time in Australia (e.g. changes in volunteering rates, new forms of civic action) and evaluate what this means for the health of Australian democracy
Assess whether digital forms of civic participation (e.g. online petitions, social media campaigns) are as effective as traditional forms, and what each contributes differently to civic goals

modes.reason: Evaluation of civic participation connects the concept of civic goals, the mechanics of collective action, and the motivation of citizens into a single analytical judgment. Support students with a structured argument frame.

descriptors.title: Resources, needs and wants
descriptors.description: types of resources, including natural, human and capital, and how they satisfy needs and wants
descriptors.knowledge: Foundation–Year 4 HASS concepts: Students have prior understanding of communities, places, and basic ideas about goods and services. Year 4 content introduces government and services, providing indirect context for economic concepts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the types of resources — natural, human and capital — and how they are used in production to satisfy the needs and wants of communities, including consideration of sustainable resource use.

nodes.label: Needs and wants
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between needs (essential for survival and wellbeing) and wants (desirable but not essential), and give examples of each.
criteria: Students define 'needs' and 'wants' and give two examples of each.
Students explain why the distinction between needs and wants matters for thinking about resource use.
nodes.hinge_reason: The needs/wants distinction is conceptually foundational for understanding scarcity, resource allocation, and the purpose of production. Students who conflate the two will not understand why resources must be allocated or why sustainability is necessary.

width.minimum: Define 'needs' and 'wants', give two examples of each, and explain the difference.
width.typical: Explain the distinction between needs (food, water, shelter, safety) and wants (entertainment, luxury goods, non-essential services), and discuss that the boundary between needs and wants can vary by context, culture and community.
wider: Explore how needs and wants differ between communities in high-income and low-income countries, and evaluate whether all needs are currently being met globally
Investigate how advertising shapes people's perceptions of what they 'need', and discuss the distinction between manufactured wants and genuine needs

modes.reason: Use a sorting activity with concrete items to establish the distinction, including some genuinely ambiguous cases (e.g. is a phone a need or a want in contemporary life?) to build nuanced understanding rather than a rigid binary.

nodes.label: Types of resources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can categorise resources as natural, human or capital, give examples of each type, and explain how each type contributes to the production of goods and services.
criteria: Students correctly categorise at least two examples of each resource type.
Students explain how each type of resource contributes to producing a named good or service.

width.minimum: Name and define three types of resources (natural, human, capital) and give one example of each.
width.typical: Categorise resources as natural (water, coal, wheat), human (workers, business owners, volunteers, managers) and capital (tools, machines, technologies), and explain how each type is used in the production of goods and services that satisfy needs and wants.
wider: Investigate the factors of production used in a specific local industry (e.g. farming, manufacturing, services) and explain how natural, human and capital resources combine to produce goods or services
Explore how technology is changing the role of human resources in production, and discuss what this means for workers and communities

modes.reason: The three-category resource classification is a prerequisite vocabulary for economic analysis — students need fluency with the categories and examples before they can analyse production or evaluate sustainability.

nodes.label: How resources satisfy needs and wants
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how natural, human and capital resources are combined in production to satisfy the needs and wants of communities.
criteria: Students trace the three resource types used in producing at least one good or service.
Students explain which need or want the production satisfies.

width.minimum: Trace how resources (natural, human, capital) are combined to produce one good or service and explain which need or want it satisfies.
width.typical: Explain how the three types of resources are combined in the production of goods and services for a local community, identifying the factors of production used and the needs or wants satisfied by several different examples.
wider: Map the full supply chain for a common consumer product and identify all three resource types at each stage of production
Compare resource use in subsistence economies with market economies, and discuss how each system satisfies community needs and wants

modes.reason: Students benefit from tracing the resource-to-satisfaction pathway across multiple different goods and services — this builds transferable economic reasoning rather than a single worked example.

nodes.label: Sustainable resource use
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why sustainable resource use is important, and describe how resources might be used more sustainably to meet current and future needs and wants.
criteria: Students explain what sustainable resource use means and why it matters.
Students describe at least one strategy for using resources more sustainably.
Students connect sustainable resource use to meeting both current and future needs and wants.

width.minimum: Explain what 'sustainable resource use' means and give one example of a more sustainable practice.
width.typical: Explain why sustainable resource use is important — that resources are finite and that current use patterns affect future availability — and describe strategies for using resources more sustainably, with examples from natural, human and capital resource categories.
wider: Investigate a specific resource management challenge (e.g. water scarcity, soil degradation, energy transition) and evaluate proposed solutions for sustainability

Explore how First Nations Australian resource management practices (e.g. seasonal harvesting, firestick farming) model sustainable use, and consider what modern economies can learn from these approaches

modes.reason: Sustainable resource use integrates the needs/wants distinction (Node 1), the resource types (Node 2), and the production process (Node 3). Students need to connect all three to make a reasoned sustainability judgment.

descriptors.title: Develop system investigation questions
descriptors.description: develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S01 (Develop guided investigation questions): Students develop questions to guide investigations of people, events, places and communities with teacher support. Students have practised formulating basic investigation questions in Year 4.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop a range of purposeful questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems, selecting question types appropriate to the inquiry purpose and disciplinary focus.

nodes.label: Question types and purposes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between different types of questions used in HASS inquiry (probing, open-ended, practical, financial) and explain the purpose of each type.
criteria: Students name at least two question types and explain the purpose of each.
Students give an example of a question from each type they name.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish question types will default to closed factual questions for all inquiry stages. Understanding that different question types serve different stages and purposes is foundational for purposeful investigation across HASS disciplines.

width.minimum: Name two types of inquiry questions and explain when each is most useful.
