width.typical: Explain the range of question types used in HASS inquiry: probing questions (to seek specific details), open-ended questions (to elicit ideas and multiple perspectives), and practical questions (to guide action, financial choices or investigation logistics); explain when each type is appropriate.
wider: Explore how question type selection varies across HASS disciplines — compare the questions a historian uses with those a geographer or economist would use for the same event or phenomenon
Investigate how disciplinary concepts (history, geography, economics, civics) should shape question design — and practice generating questions that frame inquiry from a specific disciplinary angle

modes.reason: Use a question classification exercise — sort sample questions into types and explain the purpose of each. Model question design explicitly before students write their own.

nodes.label: Framing inquiry questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop questions that address relevant disciplinary concepts and frame the stages of an inquiry, from initial investigation through to conclusions.
criteria: Students develop at least three questions that together frame a HASS inquiry.
Students use at least two different question types and explain why each is appropriate for its stage of inquiry.

width.minimum: Develop at least three questions that frame a HASS inquiry from start to finish, using at least two different question types.
width.typical: Develop a set of inquiry questions that address relevant disciplinary concepts, frame investigation stages (before, during, after), and include probing, open-ended and practical question types appropriate to the inquiry topic.
wider: Develop inquiry questions for a multi-disciplinary HASS topic (e.g. combining historical, geographic and economic angles on colonial settlement) that reveal connections across disciplines
Refine an initial set of inquiry questions based on preliminary research — modelling the iterative nature of professional inquiry

modes.reason: Question design improves through practice across multiple topics. Build a bank of strong inquiry questions that students can use as models — diversity of examples is more valuable than perfecting a single question set.

nodes.label: Questions to locate and evaluate sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop practical questions to identify, locate and evaluate sources useful for an investigation, including questions about source usefulness, reliability and access.
criteria: Students develop at least two questions designed to locate or evaluate sources for an inquiry.
Students explain how answering these questions would improve their investigation.

width.minimum: Develop two questions to guide the identification or evaluation of sources for an investigation.
width.typical: Develop practical questions to guide source location and evaluation: 'Is this source useful?', 'Who can help with this project?', 'What protocols must be followed for this inquiry?', 'What resources do we need?' — and explain the purpose of each question in the investigation process.
wider: Develop a source evaluation checklist framed as a set of questions, and apply it to evaluate the usefulness of several different source types for the same inquiry
Explore how the questions posed at the start of an inquiry shape which sources are sought — and how finding unexpected sources can prompt new questions

modes.reason: Source-evaluation questions are best practised across a range of source types (primary, secondary, digital, oral) — each type raises different evaluative questions. Breadth of source types matters more than depth on one.

nodes.label: Developing a complete inquiry question set
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a complete set of purposeful questions for a HASS inquiry that spans investigation stages, addresses relevant disciplinary concepts, and guides source selection and action.
criteria: Students develop at least four inquiry questions that cover different stages and purposes.
Students use at least two distinct question types and explain the role of each in their inquiry.
Questions address relevant HASS disciplinary concepts rather than generic factual queries.

width.minimum: Develop a set of at least four questions for a HASS inquiry that cover different stages and purposes.
width.typical: Develop a complete inquiry question set for a HASS topic that: frames initial investigation, probes for detail, guides source selection, and leads toward conclusions and action; addresses relevant disciplinary concepts; and uses a range of question types appropriate to their purpose.
wider: Evaluate the quality of a question set by testing it against a completed inquiry — assess which questions were most valuable and revise questions that did not generate useful inquiry

Develop questions that connect multiple HASS disciplines to explore a complex topic (e.g. 'How do purchasing decisions affect the environment and community?' — connecting economics, geography and civics)

modes.reason: A complete inquiry question set requires students to coordinate all question types across all stages of inquiry — the integration challenge is designing a coherent sequence, not just a list of questions.

descriptors.title: Organise primary and secondary sources
descriptors.description: locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S02 (Collect information from source ranges): Students collect and record information from provided sources including timelines, maps and models. Students have practised sorting and recording data at Year 4 level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, collect and organise information and data from a range of primary and secondary sources in multiple formats, selecting appropriate organisational tools and applying cartographic and graphing conventions.

nodes.label: Primary vs secondary sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between primary and secondary sources, give examples of each relevant to HASS contexts, and explain the value of each type for different inquiry purposes.
criteria: Students correctly classify at least three examples as primary or secondary sources.
Students explain why each type of source is useful for a specific inquiry purpose.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without the primary/secondary distinction, students cannot evaluate the provenance or reliability of sources in subsequent nodes, and cannot apply the source evaluation skills in AC9HS5S04. This distinction is the prerequisite for purposeful source work across Year 5.

width.minimum: Define primary and secondary sources and give one example of each from a HASS context.
width.typical: Distinguish between primary sources (e.g. maps, diaries, official documents, photographs, artefacts, newspapers of the day, oral histories, fieldwork observations) and secondary sources (e.g. books, internet articles, reports), and explain when each type is most useful for an inquiry.
wider: Investigate a historical event using both a primary source and a secondary source on the same topic, and compare what each reveals and what it omits

Explore how digital technologies have changed the availability of primary sources — consider how sources like social media posts, government datasets and satellite imagery function as primary sources for contemporary investigations

modes.reason: Students often confuse primary and secondary sources — and errors in applying this distinction flow through all source evaluation work. Use repeated classification practice across varied examples to build fluency.

nodes.label: Collecting and organising using graphic tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect and organise information and data using a range of digital and non-digital graphic organisers, selecting the tool appropriate to the purpose.
criteria: Students use at least one graphic organiser to organise information for an inquiry purpose.
Students explain why the chosen organiser is appropriate for the information and purpose.

width.minimum: Use one graphic organiser (e.g. flow chart, Venn diagram, timeline) to organise information for an inquiry purpose.
width.typical: Select and use appropriate graphic organisers (flow charts, consequence wheels, futures timelines, Venn diagrams, decision-making matrices, bibliography templates) to organise information, explaining why each tool suits the purpose.
wider: Evaluate the effectiveness of two different graphic organisers for the same data and justify which is more useful for the inquiry purpose
Design a custom graphic organiser for a specific inquiry task and explain the design decisions that make it fit for purpose

modes.reason: Students need a varied toolkit of graphic organisers and the judgment to select the right one. Build repertoire by practising with multiple tool types rather than mastering one deeply.

nodes.label: Constructing maps, timelines, tables and graphs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct timelines, maps, tables and graphs using appropriate digital applications and conventions, to display information and data.
criteria: Students construct at least one map, timeline, table or graph displaying HASS data.
Students apply relevant conventions correctly (e.g. title, legend, scale for maps; labelled axes for graphs).

width.minimum: Construct one map, timeline, table or graph using appropriate conventions to display data.
width.typical: Construct timelines, maps, tables and graphs using appropriate digital applications and cartographic conventions (border, source, scale, legend, title, north point) to display data relevant to HASS investigations such as movement of peoples, population growth, key event sequences, and cultural group distributions.
wider: Create a digital map using a geospatial tool (e.g. Google Maps, ArcGIS Online) to display HASS data, applying all cartographic conventions correctly
Compare a map, graph and timeline of the same dataset and evaluate how each display choice shapes what the viewer understands about the data

modes.reason: Cartographic and graphing conventions are precise skills that require practice — errors in conventions (missing north point, unlabelled axis) undermine the communication of findings. Fluency matters here.

nodes.label: Integrating multiple sources and formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate, collect and organise information from multiple primary and secondary sources in a range of formats, selecting appropriate organisational tools and conventions for the inquiry purpose.
criteria: Students collect information from at least one primary and one secondary source.
Students organise collected information using an appropriate tool and apply conventions correctly.
Students explain why they selected the organisational tools and formats they used.

width.minimum: Collect information from at least two source types (one primary, one secondary) and organise it using appropriate tools for the inquiry purpose.
width.typical: Locate, collect and organise information and data from a range of primary and secondary sources in multiple formats (including geospatial tools, surveys, digital and non-digital sources), selecting appropriate organisational tools and applying relevant conventions.
wider: Conduct fieldwork or a survey to gather primary data, then organise and integrate this data with secondary source findings to produce a multi-source investigation
Evaluate the completeness of a source collection for an inquiry — identify what types of sources are missing and explain how adding them would improve the investigation

modes.reason: The integration challenge is coordinating multiple source types and formats into a coherent organised collection — students need to make deliberate decisions about which tool organises which information and why.

descriptors.title: Evaluate patterns and trends
descriptors.description: evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, or to infer relationships
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S03 (Interpret information displays): Students interpret information and data from a range of sources including maps and timelines. Students can read and describe what information in displays shows.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, and to infer relationships between phenomena.

nodes.label: Patterns and trends vs isolated facts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between isolated factual observations and patterns or trends that emerge across multiple data points, and explain what it means to 'identify a pattern' in HASS data.
criteria: Students distinguish between an isolated fact and a pattern or trend in HASS data.
Students identify at least one pattern from a provided data source and describe what it shows.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who treat data as a collection of isolated facts cannot make the inferential move to pattern recognition. Pattern identification is the prerequisite for inferring relationships, which is the central analytical skill in this descriptor.

width.minimum: Explain the difference between an isolated fact and a pattern or trend, using one HASS example.
width.typical: Explain what patterns and trends mean in HASS contexts — that patterns appear across multiple cases or data points, that trends show change over time — and distinguish these from one-off facts. Apply this understanding to interpret at least one visual data source.
wider: Compare pattern analysis in different HASS disciplines: how patterns are identified in historical evidence versus geographical data versus economic data
Explore how sample size and data completeness affect the reliability of identified patterns — and discuss what makes a pattern convincing versus speculative

modes.reason: Use a series of data examples where students explicitly name what they see (individual data points) versus what they infer (the pattern across them) — scaffold the inferential move explicitly before applying it to complex data.

nodes.label: Reading and analysing graphs and maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret data presented in line, bar, column and pie graphs, and extract patterns and trends relevant to HASS investigations.
criteria: Students correctly read and describe the pattern shown in at least one graph.
Students use specific data values or proportions to support their description of the pattern.

width.minimum: Read and describe the pattern shown in one type of graph (e.g. bar or line graph) using HASS data.
width.typical: Interpret line, bar, column and pie graphs presenting HASS data (e.g. election results, colonial population growth, resource use, economic trends), describing patterns and trends and making simple comparisons between data sets.
wider: Compare data from two different graph types showing the same information, and evaluate which representation makes the pattern more visible
Interpret graphs from First Nations Australians' language and Country/Place data to describe patterns in the diversity and distribution of First Nations peoples

modes.reason: Fluency in reading multiple graph types is built through repeated practice — each graph type makes different features of data visible. Students need repertoire across types, not deep expertise in one.

nodes.label: Inferring relationships from visual and written sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine visual and written sources to infer relationships — explaining what a relationship means and how evidence supports it.
criteria: Students infer at least one relationship from a visual or written source.
Students explain the evidence in the source that supports their inferred relationship.

width.minimum: Identify one relationship inferred from a visual or written source and explain the evidence that supports it.
width.typical: Examine photographs, maps and written sources to infer relationships: how drought shapes enterprising behaviour, how place characteristics correlate with settlement patterns, how colonial social structures were shaped by economic roles. Explain how the evidence supports each inferred relationship.
wider: Examine maps and sources showing First Nations Australians' language groups and Countries/Places, and explain the diversity of connections to Country/Place that these sources reveal
Investigate multiple sources on the same phenomenon and compare the relationships each source implies — identifying where sources agree and where they suggest different causal patterns

modes.reason: The move from 'observation' to 'inferred relationship' is inferential and requires explicit scaffolding — students need to practise articulating 'I see X, which suggests Y because Z' as a structured reasoning step.

nodes.label: Evaluating information to identify patterns and infer relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate information and data from multiple formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, and infer relationships, explaining how the evidence supports their analysis.
criteria: Students identify at least one pattern or trend from information in multiple formats.
Students infer at least one relationship and explain what evidence supports it.
Students use appropriate analytical language (e.g. 'pattern', 'trend', 'relationship', 'suggests').

width.minimum: Identify a pattern or trend and infer one relationship from information in at least two different formats.
width.typical: Evaluate information and data from a range of formats (graphs, maps, written sources, photographs) to identify and describe patterns and trends across a HASS topic, and infer relationships between phenomena with reference to supporting evidence.
wider: Evaluate the reliability of an inferred relationship by checking it against additional sources — and revise the inference where evidence is contradictory
Analyse data showing patterns in a current HASS issue (e.g. environmental change, migration trends, voting patterns) and explain what the patterns reveal about the underlying relationships

modes.reason: The integration challenge is moving fluidly across data formats to build a multi-source analytical account — not just reading each source in isolation but drawing on several to construct a coherent analysis.

descriptors.title: Evaluate source purpose and perspective
descriptors.description: evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S04 (Analyse data and perspectives): Students analyse data and identify different perspectives in sources. Students can identify viewpoints in sources, but at Year 4 level do not yet evaluate origin and purpose systematically.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine their origin, purpose and the perspectives they present, identifying bias, stereotypes and differences between accounts.

nodes.label: Origin and purpose of sources
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the origin of a source (who created it, when, where) and explain its likely purpose (to inform, persuade, entertain, record), and explain how origin and purpose might affect the information a source contains.
criteria: Students identify the origin (creator, date) and purpose of at least one source.
Students explain how the source's origin and purpose might affect what it shows or omits.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify origin and purpose cannot evaluate perspective or bias — the evaluative skills in the rest of this descriptor and in AC9HS5S05 depend on understanding that sources are created by someone for a reason that shapes their content.

width.minimum: Identify the origin and purpose of one provided source and explain how these might affect what the source shows.
width.typical: For a range of primary and secondary sources, identify origin (creator, date, context) and purpose (informative, persuasive, record-keeping), and explain how origin and purpose affect the reliability, completeness and perspective presented in each source.
wider: Compare a primary source (e.g. a colonial-era newspaper article) and a secondary source (e.g. a modern history book) on the same topic, and evaluate how origin and purpose result in different accounts
Investigate how to verify source details — checking publication dates, authorship and institutional affiliation — and evaluate what this reveals about the reliability of different source types

modes.reason: Use a source analysis frame (e.g. Who? When? Why? What does this mean for the information?) to scaffold the move from describing what a source says to analysing what it is and why it was created.

nodes.label: Identifying bias and stereotypes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify inferred messages, stereotypes and over-generalisations in historical and contemporary sources, explaining how these reflect the perspective and possible bias of the source's creator.
criteria: Students identify at least one example of bias or a stereotype in a source.
Students explain what perspective the bias or stereotype reflects and whose viewpoint it represents.

width.minimum: Identify one example of bias or a stereotype in a provided source and explain what perspective it reflects.
width.typical: Examine visual and written sources (e.g. colonial-era newspaper caricatures, historical photographs, contemporary social media opinions) to identify inferred messages, stereotypes and over-generalisations relating to age, gender, ethnicity, ability, religion or politics; explain what perspective these elements reflect.
wider: Compare a colonial-era source and a contemporary source on the same group (e.g. First Nations Australians, Chinese migrants, women) and explain how the perspectives and stereotypes have changed — or persisted
Analyse how a modern media source about a current issue (e.g. environmental policy, immigration) uses language, image selection and framing to reflect a particular perspective

modes.reason: Identifying bias in historical sources — particularly colonial-era sources — requires students to hold a critical distance from the source's viewpoint. Scaffold explicitly: 'What does the creator assume? What is left out? Who might disagree?'

nodes.label: Comparing accounts and perspectives
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare primary and secondary sources on the same topic to identify similarities and differences in their accounts, explaining why different sources present different perspectives.
criteria: Students compare at least two sources on the same topic and identify at least one similarity and one difference.
Students explain why the sources might present different accounts.

width.minimum: Compare two sources on the same topic and identify at least one similarity and one difference in their accounts.
width.typical: Compare sources of evidence (primary and secondary, from different creators and perspectives) to identify similarities and differences in accounts of the past or present; explain why sources differ and what each perspective reveals; give examples from historical events (e.g. Eureka Stockade, colonial exploration, gold rush).
wider: Compare how an event is described in a source created at the time with how it is described in a recently published account, and evaluate what has changed in the interpretation and why
Examine accounts of the same event from First Nations Australian and European perspectives, and evaluate what each perspective reveals that the other omits

modes.reason: Comparing perspectives across multiple source types and historical actors is the core skill — students benefit from practising comparisons across different kinds of differences (time period, cultural background, social position, source type).

nodes.label: Evaluating sources for accuracy and perspective
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the accuracy of sources, identify the perspectives they present, and explain how origin, purpose and perspective together affect a source's usefulness for inquiry.
criteria: Students evaluate at least one source for accuracy and perspective with reference to its origin and purpose.
Students explain whether the source is useful for their inquiry and why.
Students use relevant source analysis terminology (e.g. 'origin', 'purpose', 'perspective', 'bias', 'reliability').

width.minimum: Evaluate one source for accuracy and perspective, and explain whether it is useful for a specific inquiry purpose.
width.typical: Evaluate the accuracy and perspectives in a range of primary and secondary sources (checking publication details, author expertise, evidence used, perspectives represented), and explain how origin, purpose and perspective together determine a source's usefulness for inquiry.
wider: Develop and apply a systematic source evaluation criteria framework (e.g. CRAAP test adapted for HASS) to a set of sources on a HASS topic
Evaluate a contested historical event using sources with conflicting accounts, and explain how the conflict between sources can itself be used as evidence of different perspectives

modes.reason: Source evaluation at this level requires students to hold multiple analytical frames simultaneously — origin, purpose, perspective, accuracy, and usefulness all interact. Scaffold with structured evaluation protocols before expecting independent application.

descriptors.title: Develop evidence-based conclusions
descriptors.description: develop evidence-based conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S05 (Conclude from analysis): Students draw basic conclusions from their analysis of information. Students can state what information shows but may not yet explicitly ground conclusions in cited evidence.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop evidence-based conclusions that reflect their inquiry questions, understanding of disciplinary concepts, and evaluation of primary and secondary sources.

nodes.label: What makes a conclusion evidence-based?
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the difference between a conclusion based on evidence and a conclusion based on personal preference, limited sources, or unsupported opinion.
criteria: Students explain what makes a conclusion 'evidence-based'.
Students identify the difference between at least two contrasting conclusions (one evidence-based, one not).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't distinguish evidence-based from opinion-based conclusions will conflate personal judgment with analytical finding throughout their HASS work. This conceptual distinction is the prerequisite for all evidence-based reasoning in Year 5 and beyond.

width.minimum: Explain what 'evidence-based' means and give an example of an evidence-based conclusion versus one that is not.
width.typical: Explain the distinction between conclusions based on identified evidence (from valid primary and secondary sources), conclusions based on personal preference, and conclusions based on limited or unreliable sources. Apply these criteria to evaluate examples of student conclusions.
wider: Explore how historians and geographers judge the quality of conclusions in academic writing, and apply these criteria to evaluate the conclusions in a secondary source
Investigate cases where initial evidence suggested one conclusion but additional evidence changed it — discussing what this means for inquiry practice

modes.reason: Use concrete examples — two conclusions on the same topic, one evidence-based and one opinion-based — and use explicit criteria to identify the difference. The contrast makes the distinction tangible.

nodes.label: Identifying valid evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify valid evidence from primary and secondary sources that can be used to form a conclusion, explaining why some evidence is more valid than other evidence for a specific inquiry purpose.
criteria: Students select at least two pieces of valid evidence from sources for an inquiry question.
Students explain why each piece of evidence is relevant and reliable.

width.minimum: Select two pieces of valid evidence from provided sources and explain why each is relevant to the inquiry question.
width.typical: Identify valid evidence from primary and secondary sources (e.g. images, posters, newspaper articles, books, websites) for a HASS inquiry; explain why some sources are more valid than others; consider the reliability, recency and relevance of each source as evidence.
wider: Compare the validity of evidence from a government agency website versus a private blog on the same topic — evaluate the criteria for judging reliability in digital sources
Investigate how the date a secondary source was created affects its validity — exploring how a history textbook written in 1960 may reflect different values from one written in 2020

modes.reason: Evidence validity requires applying source evaluation criteria (from AC9HS5S04) in an argument-building context — scaffold the move from 'this source is reliable' to 'this source provides valid evidence for my conclusion because...'

nodes.label: Forming conclusions from evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can draw conclusions from identified evidence that consider differing information, reflect disciplinary concepts, and address their inquiry question.
criteria: Students write at least one conclusion that addresses an inquiry question.
Students cite at least two sources as evidence for their conclusion.
Students distinguish their conclusion from personal opinion.

width.minimum: Write one conclusion grounded in identified evidence that addresses an inquiry question.
width.typical: Draw conclusions from primary and secondary sources that: address the inquiry question, reflect understanding of disciplinary concepts (historical, geographic, civic, economic), consider evidence from different sources including those with differing viewpoints, and are clearly distinguished from personal preference.
wider: Draw conclusions about a community or environment (e.g. changing democratic values, patterns of human consumption, environmental change) using evidence from multiple source types
Construct conclusions that explicitly acknowledge uncertainty or conflicting evidence, and explain how this affects confidence in the conclusion

modes.reason: Writing evidence-based conclusions is a precision skill — students need practice forming conclusions that make the evidence-to-claim link explicit. Errors (missing citation, over-claiming, under-claiming) need targeted feedback loops.

nodes.label: Evaluating the inquiry and conclusions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can consider how the sources they used affected the validity of their conclusions, and identify how additional or different sources would improve the inquiry.
criteria: Students identify how the sources they used affected the validity of their conclusions.
Students suggest at least one way their inquiry could be improved through different or additional sources.
Students use relevant inquiry terms (e.g. 'conclusion', 'evidence', 'validity', 'reliability').

width.minimum: Reflect on two sources used in an inquiry and explain how each affected the validity of the conclusions.
width.typical: Consider the primary and secondary sources used in an inquiry and evaluate how the choice of sources may have influenced the validity and completeness of conclusions; identify what types of sources were missing; explain how including them would improve the investigation.
wider: Evaluate a completed inquiry by assessing whether the conclusions would change if different sources had been used — and identify any gaps or biases introduced by the source selection
Reflect on how the inquiry questions shaped which sources were sought and which perspectives were included or excluded

modes.reason: This reflective evaluation node connects source selection, evidence validity and conclusion quality into a metacognitive judgment about the inquiry as a whole. Use structured reflection prompts to scaffold this reflective move.

descriptors.title: Assess effects using criteria
descriptors.description: propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to assess the possible effects
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S06 (Propose responses with effects): Students propose responses to issues and identify possible effects. Students can suggest actions but do not yet apply formal criteria to assess effects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to systematically assess the possible effects of those actions.

nodes.label: Identifying issues and proposed actions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a HASS issue or challenge, describe why it matters, and propose at least one possible action or response.
criteria: Students identify a specific HASS issue or challenge and explain why it matters.
Students propose at least one possible action or response to the issue.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who propose actions without clearly identifying the issue first tend to address symptoms rather than causes — their effects assessment will be shallow because they have not established what problem the action is meant to solve. Issue identification is the prerequisite for meaningful effect assessment.

width.minimum: Identify one HASS issue or challenge and propose one possible action in response to it.
width.typical: Identify a current or historical HASS issue or challenge (environmental, civic, economic, historical), describe its significance, and propose a range of possible actions or responses, including actions taken in the past and possible future actions.
wider: Investigate a specific contemporary challenge (e.g. environmental hazard, community need, democratic issue) using a problem-finding process that examines causes before proposing actions
Compare how different groups have proposed different responses to the same challenge, explaining why their proposed actions differ

modes.reason: Use a problem-framing scaffold (What is the issue? Who is affected? What causes it? What would a good response address?) before students propose actions — this prevents the common error of jumping to solutions before understanding the problem.

nodes.label: Using criteria to assess effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and apply criteria to assess the possible effects of proposed actions, explaining what each criterion measures and why it matters.
criteria: Students identify at least two criteria for assessing the effects of an action.
Students apply each criterion to a proposed action and describe the likely effect.

width.minimum: Name two criteria for assessing the effects of an action and apply each to one proposed action.
width.typical: Identify a set of criteria (e.g. economic factors: needs, wants and costs; environmental factors; health factors; social factors) and apply them to assess the possible effects of proposed actions or responses to a HASS challenge.
wider: Investigate how criteria are used in real decision-making contexts (e.g. council planning decisions, government environmental policies) and evaluate whether the criteria used reflect the right values
Develop and justify a custom set of criteria for a specific HASS challenge, explaining why these criteria are more appropriate than a generic set

modes.reason: Applying criteria requires students to hold the action, the criterion, and the likely effect in mind simultaneously — use a structured evaluation table (action × criterion = likely effect) to make this thinking visible.

nodes.label: Forecasting probable and preferred futures
nodes.checkpoint: Students can forecast probable futures for a HASS issue and distinguish probable from preferred futures, proposing actions that move toward preferred outcomes.
criteria: Students describe one probable future and one preferred future for a HASS issue.
Students explain at least one action that would help move toward the preferred future.

width.minimum: Describe one probable future for a HASS issue and propose one action that would move toward a preferred future.
width.typical: Forecast probable futures for a HASS issue (what is likely to happen if current patterns continue), describe preferred futures (what outcome would be best), and propose specific actions that would move from the probable toward the preferred future.
wider: Construct a futures wheel or consequence map for a HASS challenge, tracing second and third-order effects of proposed actions
Evaluate the effectiveness of a past response to a challenge (e.g. a colonial response to hardship, or a government environmental policy) and assess whether the preferred future was achieved

modes.reason: The distinction between probable and preferred futures is an explicit futures thinking move — scaffold it clearly. Students often default to describing only what they want (preferred) without analysing what is likely (probable).

nodes.label: Integrated action proposal and effects assessment
nodes.checkpoint: Students can propose an action or response to a HASS issue or challenge and use a set of criteria to systematically assess its possible effects, drawing on evidence and disciplinary understanding.
criteria: Students propose a specific action in response to a HASS issue.
Students apply at least two criteria to assess the possible effects of their proposed action.
Students acknowledge potential unintended effects or limitations of their proposed action.

width.minimum: Propose one action for a HASS issue and use at least two criteria to assess its possible effects.
width.typical: Propose a coherent action or response to a HASS issue; use a defined set of criteria (economic, environmental, social, health) to systematically assess possible effects; draw on evidence from inquiry to support the assessment; acknowledge that different criteria may lead to different conclusions.
wider: Participate in a democratic decision-making process (e.g. class vote, mock community consultation) about a proposed action, and evaluate the outcome using the criteria developed
Evaluate how effectively a past challenge was addressed (e.g. a colonial or environmental challenge) using the same criteria framework, and assess whether the response achieved its goals

modes.reason: The integrated proposal brings together issue identification, criteria selection, futures thinking and evidence-based assessment. Use a structured proposal format (issue → action → criteria assessment → recommendation) to support synthesis.

descriptors.title: Present findings and viewpoints
descriptors.description: present descriptions and explanations, drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, and using relevant terms and conventions
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4S07 (Present sourced explanations): Students present descriptions and explanations drawing on sources and using subject-specific terms. Students can present basic sourced accounts at Year 4 level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present descriptions and explanations that draw ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, using relevant subject-specific terms and conventions appropriate to the HASS disciplines.

nodes.label: Drawing from sources in presentations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and reference ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources in their descriptions and explanations, distinguishing their own ideas from source material.
criteria: Students reference at least one source within their description or explanation.
Students distinguish source-derived information from their own interpretation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who present findings without referencing sources cannot demonstrate evidence-based thinking or the distinction between personal opinion and sourced finding. Explicit source attribution is foundational for credible HASS communication.

width.minimum: Present one description or explanation that references at least one source, distinguishing the source's viewpoint from their own.
width.typical: Select and reference ideas and viewpoints from a range of sources (letters, graphs, tables, timelines, photographs, pictures) in descriptions and explanations, clearly indicating the sources of ideas and distinguishing sourced information from personal interpretation.
wider: Construct a description that synthesises information from three or more sources, weaving together multiple viewpoints into a coherent account
Evaluate how selecting different sources changes the account that can be presented — exploring how source selection is itself a form of perspective-taking

modes.reason: Consistent source attribution is a practice skill that requires reinforcement — students often need repeated feedback to habituate citing sources within their explanations rather than treating references as an afterthought.

nodes.label: Using subject-specific terms accurately
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use accurate, subject-specific terms from relevant HASS disciplines in their presentations, applying terms correctly in context.
criteria: Students use at least four subject-specific HASS terms correctly in context.
Terms are drawn from at least two HASS discipline areas.

width.minimum: Use at least four subject-specific HASS terms correctly in a description or explanation.
width.typical: Use accurate and subject-appropriate terms across HASS disciplines: historical terms (colonial, gold era, migration, penal), geographic terms (characteristics, environmental, human, ecosystems, sustainable, settlement, management), civics terms (electoral process, democracy, shared beliefs), and economic terms (scarcity, choices, resources, needs and wants).
wider: Develop a HASS glossary of key terms for a unit and use the glossary to improve the precision of a draft explanation
Compare how the same concept is named differently across HASS disciplines (e.g. 'community' in history versus geography versus civics) and explain why disciplinary vocabulary matters

modes.reason: Subject-specific vocabulary is a precision skill — incorrect or inconsistent use undermines the credibility of explanations. Students benefit from targeted vocabulary practice embedded in content rather than isolated word lists.

nodes.label: Descriptions and explanations in different formats
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present HASS descriptions and explanations in a range of formats appropriate to purpose and audience, selecting format based on content and communication goals.
criteria: Students present findings in a format appropriate to the inquiry purpose.
Students explain why their chosen format suits the content and audience.

width.minimum: Present findings in one format (written, oral or visual) appropriate to the inquiry purpose.
width.typical: Present descriptions and explanations in formats suited to purpose: written descriptions, oral explanations, visual displays (maps, timelines, graphs), or multimodal presentations that combine text, image and data.
wider: Produce a multimodal presentation (combining written, oral and visual formats) that communicates HASS findings to a specific audience
Evaluate how different presentation formats (e.g. a written report versus a visual display versus an oral presentation) communicate different aspects of the same findings, and justify a format choice

modes.reason: Varied presentation formats build communicative flexibility — students who only practise written formats are poorly equipped for oral or visual communication tasks. Build repertoire across formats across the year.

nodes.label: Presenting evidence-supported descriptions and explanations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can present descriptions and explanations that draw ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, use subject-specific terms accurately, and are communicated in a format appropriate to purpose and audience.
criteria: Students reference at least two sources in their description or explanation.
Students use subject-specific HASS terms accurately across at least two discipline areas.
Students present in a format that is appropriate for the content and clearly communicated.

width.minimum: Present a description or explanation that references at least two sources, uses appropriate subject-specific terms, and is in a format suited to the purpose.
width.typical: Present descriptions and explanations that: draw on sourced ideas and viewpoints across a HASS topic, use accurate subject-specific terms from relevant disciplines, apply appropriate conventions for the chosen format, and communicate findings in a way suited to purpose and audience.
wider: Present findings from an extended HASS inquiry in a form suitable for a real audience (e.g. a school assembly presentation, an article for a school newsletter, a letter to a local council)
Reflect on the effectiveness of a completed presentation — evaluate what communicated well and what could be improved, and identify specific revisions that would strengthen it

modes.reason: The integrated presentation task brings together source referencing, disciplinary vocabulary and format selection. Students need to coordinate all three simultaneously — scaffold with a planning template before drafting.

descriptors.title: Federation and democracy
descriptors.description: significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation, the Constitution and democratic system of government
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students explain the key values and features of Australia's democracy, including elections and the roles of elected representatives. Students understand democratic values and electoral features.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation, the Constitution and democratic system of government, identifying the origins and influences that shaped Australia's constitutional framework.

nodes.label: The path to Federation — key individuals and events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the roles of key individuals and events in Australia's path to Federation, including Henry Parkes, Edmund Barton, Alfred Deakin, the Tenterfield Oration and the Corowa Conference.
criteria: Students identify at least two key individuals and two key events in Australia's path to Federation.
Students explain the role each individual or event played in the Federation process.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without understanding the actors and events that drove Federation, students cannot explain why the Constitution was designed as it was, or what ideas the founders drew on. This factual and narrative foundation is the prerequisite for the constitutional and democratic analysis in subsequent nodes.

width.minimum: Explain the role of one key individual and one key event in Australia's path to Federation.
width.typical: Explain the roles of key individuals (Henry Parkes, Edmund Barton, Alfred Deakin, George Reid, John Quick) and key events (Tenterfield Oration, Corowa Conference, 1898–1900 referendums) in Australia's path to Federation.
wider: Investigate the perspectives of those who opposed Federation and explain their objections — examining why Federation was not universally welcomed
Explore the role of women and First Nations Australians in the Federation debate, and assess whose voices were included or excluded from the constitutional drafting process

modes.reason: Use a timeline of key events alongside brief profiles of key individuals to build the chronological foundation before moving to analysis of the ideas and influences that shaped Federation.

nodes.label: The ideas and influences behind Australia's Constitution
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key ideas and influences behind Australia's Constitution, including the influence of the Westminster system, the US federal model and the Magna Carta.
criteria: Students identify at least two influences on the design of Australia's Constitution.
Students explain how each influence shaped a specific feature of the Constitution (e.g. separation of powers, constitutional monarchy).

width.minimum: Explain one idea or influence that shaped the design of Australia's Constitution.
width.typical: Explain the range of ideas and influences that shaped Australia's Constitution: origins in Magna Carta, the English Civil War and Westminster system (explaining constitutional monarchy and separation of powers); the influence of the American federal model (Washington system) on Andrew Clark's first draft.
wider: Compare the Australian Constitution with the Westminster system and the US Constitution, identifying specific features borrowed from each
Investigate what separation of powers means in practice — examine a real example of the legislature, executive and judiciary operating independently to illustrate the concept

modes.reason: The international influences on the Australian Constitution (British and American) are best understood comparatively — students need enough context about each source to understand what was borrowed and why.

nodes.label: Australia's democratic system of government
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key features of Australia's democratic system of government that emerged from Federation, including the constitutional monarchy, federal structure and separation of powers.
criteria: Students explain at least two key features of Australia's system of government established at Federation.
Students explain how each feature is related to the Constitution.

width.minimum: Explain two key features of Australia's system of government established at Federation.
width.typical: Explain the key features of Australia's democratic system of government: constitutional monarchy, federal structure (Commonwealth and States), separation of powers (legislative, executive, judiciary), and how these features are embedded in the Constitution.
wider: Investigate the Australian Constitution document itself — identify specific sections that establish key features of government and explain what each means in practice
Explore the ongoing debate about Australia becoming a republic, and assess what would need to change in the Constitution and system of government if this occurred

modes.reason: The relationship between Federation, the Constitution and the system of government is a complex layered concept — use a diagram or flowchart to make visible how the constitutional text produces the governmental structure.

nodes.label: Integrating the Federation story
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the significant individuals, events and ideas that led to Australia's Federation and constitutional democratic system, identifying connections between the historical circumstances, the influential ideas and the resulting constitutional design.
criteria: Students explain contributions of at least one individual, one event and one idea to Federation.
Students describe the democratic system of government that resulted from Federation.
Students use relevant historical and civics terms accurately (e.g. 'Federation', 'Constitution', 'constitutional monarchy', 'separation of powers').

width.minimum: Explain how at least one key individual, one key event and one key idea each contributed to Federation and the Constitution.
width.typical: Explain the connections between the key individuals, events and ideas that led to Federation; describe how historical circumstances in the colonies created the conditions for Federation; explain how international ideas shaped the Constitution's design; and describe the democratic system of government that resulted.
wider: Evaluate which factor — individuals, events or ideas — was most significant in bringing about Federation, and justify the claim with reference to evidence
Assess how the founding principles and constitutional design of Australia have shaped its democratic system today — examining what has changed and what has remained constant

modes.reason: The integration task requires students to connect the narrative (who did what, when) to the analytical (why it happened and what it produced). Use a structured essay plan or annotated timeline to support this synthesis.

descriptors.title: Citizenship and political change
descriptors.description: changes in Australia's political system and to Australian citizenship after Federation and throughout the 20th century that impacted First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students understand the key values and features of Australian democracy. From AC9HS6K01 (Federation and democracy): Students have just studied the founding of Australia's democratic system.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the changes in Australia's political system and citizenship that impacted First Nations Australians, migrants, women and children after Federation and throughout the 20th century, assessing the significance of key changes.

nodes.label: First Nations Australians and political rights
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the significance of the 1962 right to vote federally and the 1967 referendum for First Nations Australians, and explain what these changes meant for citizenship and political recognition.
criteria: Students explain what changed for First Nations Australians in 1962 and 1967.
Students describe why these changes were significant for citizenship and political recognition.
nodes.hinge_reason: The exclusion and then inclusion of First Nations Australians in civic and political life is foundational to understanding Australia's democratic history — students who treat democracy as having always been inclusive will misunderstand both the struggles that created change and the significance of what was achieved.

width.minimum: Explain what happened in 1962 and 1967 for First Nations Australians and why these events were significant.
width.typical: Describe the significance of the 1962 right to vote federally and the importance of the 1967 referendum for First Nations Australians — what changed, what had been in place before, and why these changes mattered for citizenship, political recognition and the relationship between First Nations peoples and the Australian state.
wider: Investigate the campaign for the 1967 referendum — who organised it, what arguments were made, and how the Yes vote result was achieved
Explore the ongoing campaign for constitutional recognition of First Nations Australians, and assess what further changes advocates argue are still needed

modes.reason: Use a before/after framework to make the political exclusion visible before the change — students need to understand what the situation was before 1962 and 1967 to appreciate the significance of the change.

nodes.label: Women and the advance of democracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain key developments in advancing democracy and citizenship for women in Australia across the 20th century, including the suffragette movement, right to vote, equal pay and anti-discrimination legislation.
criteria: Students describe at least two developments that advanced democratic rights for women.
Students place each development in approximate chronological context and explain its significance.

width.minimum: Describe two developments that advanced the rights of women in Australia and explain why each was significant.
width.typical: Explain key developments in advancing democracy for women: the suffragette movement and winning the right to vote, the bar on married women working in the public service, the equal pay campaign, and the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 — placing each in chronological context and explaining its significance.
wider: Investigate the life and contribution of a specific figure in the Australian women's rights movement and explain their role in achieving a particular change
Compare the pace and nature of democratic change for women in Australia with that in another country, and assess what factors influenced the timing and form of change

modes.reason: The timeline of change for women spans the full 20th century — students benefit from placing individual developments in chronological sequence to understand that democratic inclusion was a long, contested process.

nodes.label: Migrants, children and expanding citizenship
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain changes to citizenship and democratic participation for migrants and children in Australia across the 20th century, including the minimum wage, anti-discrimination legislation and multicultural policy.
criteria: Students describe at least two changes that expanded citizenship rights for migrants or children.
Students explain the significance of each change for the groups affected.

width.minimum: Describe two changes that expanded democratic rights or citizenship for migrants or children.
width.typical: Explain key developments advancing democracy for all citizens, including migrant groups: establishment of the minimum wage, anti-discrimination legislation, official multicultural policy — and for children: experiences in orphanages and homes, protections introduced over time.
wider: Investigate the experience of a specific migrant group in Australia during the 20th century and assess how legislation and policy affected their citizenship rights
Explore the history of child welfare legislation in Australia, including the Stolen Generations, and evaluate the long-term impacts on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities

modes.reason: The range of groups whose citizenship expanded across the 20th century is the key breadth dimension — students benefit from comparison across groups to see democratic change as a broad social process rather than isolated events.

nodes.label: Democracy as an evolving system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that Australia's political system and citizenship have changed significantly since Federation, assessing the significance of key changes for different groups and describing the nature of democracy as an evolving rather than fixed system.
criteria: Students explain changes to Australia's democratic system for at least two different groups.
Students assess the significance of at least one change for the group affected.
Students describe democracy as an evolving system rather than a fixed one.

width.minimum: Explain two changes to Australia's democratic system or citizenship since Federation and assess the significance of each for the group most affected.
width.typical: Explain the range of changes to Australia's democratic system and citizenship since Federation for First Nations Australians, women, migrants and children; assess the significance of each change; describe how these changes reflect democracy as a system that evolves in response to social movements and changing values.
wider: Evaluate which change to Australian citizenship or the political system since Federation was most significant overall, constructing and defending an argument with evidence
Assess what further changes to Australian democracy might be needed today, drawing on the pattern of 20th century change as a guide to what remains unfinished

modes.reason: The integration challenge is moving from a series of individual changes to a coherent understanding of democratic evolution. Support students to identify the pattern across cases — that democratic inclusion has expanded over time through advocacy and legislation.

descriptors.title: Migration and Australian society
descriptors.description: the motivation of people migrating to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, their stories and effects on Australian society, including migrants from the Asia region
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K03 (Individuals and groups in colonial development): Students understand the contributions and experiences of different groups in colonial Australia, including some migrant groups. Students understand historical significance and multi-perspective analysis.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the motivations of people who migrated to Australia since Federation and throughout the 20th century, describe their stories and experiences, and assess the effects of migration on Australian society, including contributions of migrants from the Asia region.

nodes.label: Push and pull factors for migration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the push and pull factors that have motivated people to migrate to Australia since Federation, including economic factors, conflict and political refuge.
criteria: Students identify at least two push factors and two pull factors for migration to Australia.
Students apply push/pull factors to at least one specific historical migrant group.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish push from pull factors will describe migration as a single undifferentiated movement. The push/pull distinction is the analytical foundation for understanding why specific groups migrated when they did.

width.minimum: Identify two push factors and two pull factors that have driven migration to Australia and give one historical example of each.
width.typical: Explain the push and pull factors that have driven migration to Australia since Federation: economic push factors (poverty, unemployment), conflict and political instability as push factors, and Australia's economic opportunities, political stability and immigration programs as pull factors. Apply to specific 20th century migrant groups (e.g. post-WWII Europeans, South-East Asian refugees, Assisted Passage).
wider: Compare the push and pull factors for two different migrant groups from different eras (e.g. post-WWII European migrants and South-East Asian refugees) and explain why their motivations differed
Investigate a specific immigration program (e.g. the Assisted Passage Migration scheme, Refugee and Humanitarian Program) and assess how it shaped who migrated and why

modes.reason: Use a push/pull T-chart with specific examples for at least two different migrant groups before moving to analysis. Visual scaffolding makes the distinction clear and avoids conflation.

nodes.label: Stories and experiences of migrants
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the journeys and experiences of migrants to Australia using primary sources including letters, documents, oral histories and objects, explaining the circumstances of arrival and early settlement.
criteria: Students describe the migration experience of at least one individual or group using primary source evidence.
Students identify at least two specific details from primary sources in their description.

width.minimum: Describe the journey and early experience of one migrant or migrant group using information from at least one primary source.
width.typical: Explore individual narratives using primary sources (letters, documents, historical objects, oral histories) to describe the journey, circumstances of arrival, and early experience of migrants to Australia from different groups and time periods.
wider: Conduct or analyse an oral history interview with a person from a migrant family (including family history connections) and present their migration story
Examine population data from different points in time to trace how the places of birth of Australia's people have changed, and connect this data to historical migration patterns

modes.reason: Individual migration stories are the key humanising layer for the push/pull analysis — students need to hear diverse stories across different groups and time periods rather than a single 'representative' narrative.

nodes.label: Effects of migration on Australian society
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the effects of migration on Australian society, including cultural changes, economic contributions and social impacts, with specific reference to contributions from migrant groups including those from the Asia region.
criteria: Students explain at least two effects of migration on Australian society.
Students give specific examples from at least one migrant group, including from the Asia region.

width.minimum: Describe two effects of migration on Australian society and give a specific example for each.
width.typical: Explain how migration has changed Australian society: cultural practices related to family life, beliefs and customs; contributions to industries (e.g. cattle, Snowy Mountains Scheme, pearling); contributions from notable Australians of migrant background; and the influence of Asian migration on Australian culture and society.
wider: Investigate the role of a specific cultural group in Australia's economic or social development and assess the significance of their contribution
Evaluate how Australian multicultural identity today reflects the history of migration since Federation, using contemporary data and examples

modes.reason: The effects of migration are best understood across multiple domains (cultural, economic, social) and multiple migrant groups — students who focus only on one group or one domain miss the cumulative picture.

nodes.label: Migration as a shaping force in Australian history
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how the motivations, stories and effects of migration since Federation have shaped Australian society, assessing migration's role as a significant force in Australia's social and cultural development.
criteria: Students explain migration motivations, describe migrant experiences, and assess effects on Australian society in an integrated account.
Students reference specific migrant groups including those from the Asia region.
Students use relevant terms (e.g. 'push factor', 'pull factor', 'refugee', 'multiculturalism') accurately.

width.minimum: Explain how migration has shaped Australian society by drawing on examples of motivation, individual stories and societal effects.
width.typical: Assess migration as a shaping force in Australian society — connecting motivations (push/pull), individual stories, and societal effects into a coherent explanation of how migration since Federation has contributed to Australia's identity, economy and culture.
wider: Evaluate how government migration policies have shaped the composition and character of Australian society, assessing both intended and unintended social effects
Compare the experience of recent migrants to Australia with those from earlier 20th century waves of migration, identifying what has changed and what remains similar

modes.reason: The integration requires connecting the analytical framework (push/pull), the human scale (stories), and the social scale (effects) into a coherent historical argument. Use a structured essay or presentation framework.

descriptors.title: Asia region diversity and location
descriptors.description: the geographical diversity and location of places in the Asia region, and its location in relation to Australia
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K04 (People shape places): Students understand how people influence the characteristics of places. Students can describe and locate places at a general level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the geographical diversity and location of places in the Asia region, describe its location in relation to Australia, and use latitude and longitude to describe absolute location.

nodes.label: Location of the Asia region in relation to Australia
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the location of the Asia region in relation to Australia, including the main sub-regions (North-East, South-East, South Asia) and Australia's proximity to and connections with each.
criteria: Students identify the Asia region and its main sub-regions on a map.
Students describe Australia's location in relation to the Asia region.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a secure geographical foundation for the location and structure of the Asia region, students cannot develop meaningful understanding of diversity, connections or comparisons within the region.

width.minimum: Describe where the Asia region is in relation to Australia and name at least two sub-regions.
width.typical: Describe the Asia region's location in relation to Australia, identify the main sub-regions (North-East, South-East, South Asia), and explain how Australia's location in the Asia-Pacific region shapes its relationships and connections.
wider: Use latitude and longitude to describe the absolute location of at least three countries in the Asia region, and compare these with Australia's coordinates
Investigate how Australia's geographic proximity to South-East and South Asia has shaped historical and contemporary connections (trade, migration, diplomacy)

modes.reason: Location knowledge requires repeated map practice — students need to build a reliable mental map of the Asia region through multiple encounters with atlases, digital maps and coordinate systems.

nodes.label: Absolute location using latitude and longitude
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the location of places in countries of the Asia region in absolute terms, using latitude and longitude.
criteria: Students correctly use latitude and longitude to describe the location of at least two places in Asia.
Students explain what latitude and longitude coordinates mean (which hemisphere, how far from equator/prime meridian).

width.minimum: Use latitude and longitude to describe the absolute location of at least two places in the Asia region.
width.typical: Describe the location of places in the Asia region using latitude and longitude; apply this to compare locations, explain hemispheric positions, and understand why latitude relates to climate and seasonal patterns.
wider: Use a digital geospatial tool to plot locations in the Asia region using coordinates, and explain what the coordinates reveal about relative position and climate
Investigate how latitude affects climate across the Asia region, comparing countries at different latitudes

modes.reason: Reading and using latitude and longitude is a precision geographic skill requiring practice. Errors in coordinate notation (reversing lat/long, confusion about hemispheres) need targeted correction.

nodes.label: Geographical and cultural diversity of the Asia region
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the geographical and cultural diversity of the Asia region, including diversity of environments, settlement types, population, languages and ways of life.
criteria: Students describe at least two types of geographical or cultural diversity in the Asia region with specific examples.
Students identify at least two countries or sub-regions that illustrate different aspects of this diversity.

width.minimum: Describe two ways the Asia region is geographically or culturally diverse, with specific examples.
width.typical: Describe the geographical diversity of environments (mountains, tropical forests, deserts, densely populated coastal cities, agricultural plains) and cultural diversity (population sizes, life expectancy, daily life, food, housing, education, wealth distribution) across the Asia region.
wider: Compare the daily lives of people in two different countries in the Asia region, examining food, housing, education and economic conditions

Investigate the diversity of Indigenous peoples across the Asia region (e.g. Orang Asli, Tibetans, Mongols) and explore their sustainable ways of living and their cultural similarities and differences with First Nations Australians

modes.reason: Diversity is the core concept here — students who study only one country or sub-region will not grasp that 'Asia' encompasses extraordinary variation. Breadth across sub-regions and types of diversity is the learning goal.

nodes.label: Asia region: location, diversity and Australia's connections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the geographical diversity and absolute location of places in the Asia region, and explain its location in relation to Australia, drawing on population, environment and life expectancy data.
criteria: Students describe the Asia region's location in relation to Australia.
Students use latitude and longitude for at least one location in the region.
Students describe geographical and cultural diversity across at least two countries or sub-regions.

width.minimum: Describe the Asia region's location in relation to Australia, use latitude/longitude for at least one location, and describe the diversity of at least one country or sub-region.
width.typical: Describe the geographical diversity and location of places in the Asia region; use latitude and longitude to describe absolute locations; compare population size and life expectancy across selected countries; describe the range of environments and ways of life in the region; explain its location in relation to Australia.
wider: Analyse population and development data for countries across the Asia region, identifying patterns and explaining factors that account for differences
Evaluate how Australia's geographic position in relation to the Asia region has shaped its trade relationships, migration patterns and foreign policy

modes.reason: This integration node draws together location (coordinates), diversity (environment, culture, population) and Australia's relationship to the region. Use a structured comparison matrix or annotated map to support synthesis.

descriptors.title: Australia's international interconnections
descriptors.description: Australia's interconnections with other countries and how these change people and places
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K04 (People shape places): Students understand how people influence place characteristics. From AC9HS6K04 (Asia region diversity and location): Students have studied the Asia region's geography and location.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain Australia's interconnections with other countries, particularly in the Asia and Pacific regions, and describe how these interconnections change people and places.

nodes.label: Types of international interconnections
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and describe the types of interconnections Australia has with other countries, including migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence and cultural influences.
criteria: Students identify at least three types of interconnections Australia has with other countries.
Students give a specific example for at least two types.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a typology of interconnection types, students cannot distinguish between different kinds of relationships or understand how each type changes people and places in different ways. The typology is the analytical frame for all subsequent analysis.

width.minimum: Identify three types of interconnections Australia has with other countries and give one example of each.
width.typical: Describe the range of interconnections Australia has with countries in the Asia and Pacific regions: migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence and cultural influences — and use geospatial tools to identify geographical patterns in these connections.
wider: Investigate the volume and value of Australia's trade connections with the Asia region, and explain how these have changed over time
Examine Australia's development aid to a specific country in Asia or the Pacific, describing what the aid supports and how it affects people and places in that country

modes.reason: Use a classification framework (trade / migration / aid / cultural / education / defence) and map examples to the framework before students analyse effects — this prevents conflation of different connection types.

nodes.label: How interconnections change people and places
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how at least one of Australia's international interconnections changes people and places, both in Australia and in connected countries.
criteria: Students explain how at least one international interconnection changes people or places.
Students give specific examples of change in both an Australian and an overseas location.

width.minimum: Explain how one type of Australian interconnection changes people or places, with a specific example.
width.typical: Research connections between Australia and at least one country in the Asia or Pacific regions in terms of migration, trade, tourism, aid, education, defence or cultural influence, and explain the effects of at least one connection on a place in Australia and a place in another country.
wider: Investigate the effects of Australian government or non-government aid to a specific country, analysing how the aid has changed places and people's lives in that country
Examine how tourism between Australia and a specific Asian country has changed places and cultural practices in both countries, identifying both benefits and challenges

modes.reason: The effects of interconnections are best understood through specific case studies — choose connections with visible, concrete effects on places and communities rather than staying at the abstract level of 'trade' or 'migration'.

nodes.label: Geographical divisions and Australia's position
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the geographical divisions of the world including the Asia and Pacific regions, and explain Australia's position within these divisions.
criteria: Students correctly locate the Asia and Pacific regions on a world map.
Students describe Australia's geographical position in the Asia-Pacific.

width.minimum: Identify the Asia and Pacific regions on a world map and describe Australia's position in relation to them.
width.typical: Use geospatial tools (globe, wall map, digital applications) to identify the geographical divisions of the world, including the Asia and Pacific regions, and explain Australia's position within the Asia-Pacific — describing how this position shapes Australia's international relationships.
wider: Use a digital mapping application to visualise Australia's connections with the Asia and Pacific regions (e.g. shipping routes, flight paths, migration flows) and explain the geographical patterns
Investigate how Australia's membership of regional bodies (e.g. APEC, ASEAN dialogue partner) reflects its geographical position and interconnections

modes.reason: Geographical location knowledge for the Asia-Pacific region requires spatial practice — reinforce with regular map work rather than treating location as a one-off lesson.

nodes.label: Evaluating interconnections and their effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain Australia's interconnections with other countries and evaluate how these interconnections change people and places, considering different perspectives on these effects.
criteria: Students explain at least two types of Australia's international interconnections.
Students evaluate the effects of at least one interconnection on both Australian and overseas places or people.
Students use relevant geographic terms (e.g. 'interconnection', 'trade', 'aid', 'migration', 'cultural influence').

width.minimum: Explain two types of Australia's international interconnections and evaluate one positive and one negative effect on people or places.
width.typical: Explain Australia's range of international interconnections; evaluate how specific connections change people and places in Australia and in connected countries; acknowledge that different groups may experience the effects of interconnections differently.
wider: Evaluate whether Australia's interconnections with the Asia region are mutually beneficial or whether they produce unequal benefits, using evidence to support the assessment
Investigate a current issue in Australia's international relationships and assess how it illustrates the complexity of interconnections
