modes.reason: Evaluating interconnections requires students to hold the complexity of multi-directional effects — what changes for Australia and what changes for the other country, and how these may differ. Use structured comparison to support evaluation.

descriptors.title: Government institutions and democracy
descriptors.description: the key institutions of Australia's system of government, how it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students understand democratic values, electoral features and the roles of elected representatives. From AC9HS6K01 (Federation and democracy): Students understand how Federation established Australia's constitutional framework.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the key institutions of Australia's system of government, how it is based on the Westminster system, and the key values and beliefs of Western democracies.

nodes.label: Key institutions: monarchy, parliament and courts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the roles of the key institutions of Australia's system of government: the monarchy and its representatives, parliaments, and courts.
criteria: Students identify at least three key institutions and explain the role of each.
Students distinguish the roles of the parliament, the monarchy/Governor-General, and the courts.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot distinguish the key institutional actors (monarchy/Governor-General, parliament, courts) will conflate the roles of different branches of government and cannot understand the separation of powers that underpins Westminster-style democracy.

width.minimum: Explain the role of two key institutions in Australia's system of government.
width.typical: Explain the role of the monarchy and its representatives in Australia (including the Governor-General), the parliaments (Commonwealth and State/Territory), and the courts, as the three key institutional pillars of Australia's system of government.
wider: Investigate Parliament House and the High Court in Canberra (virtually or in situ) and explain how the physical design of these institutions reflects their roles in the democratic system
Explore a recent case where the judiciary has exercised its independence from parliament or the executive, and explain what this reveals about the role of courts in Australian democracy

modes.reason: Use an institutional roles framework (who they are / what they do / why they matter) for each institution before moving to how the Westminster system connects them.

nodes.label: Australia and the Westminster system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare Australia's system of government with the Westminster system, identifying similarities and differences between the Australian Parliament and the UK Parliament.
criteria: Students identify at least two similarities between Australia's parliament and the Westminster system.
Students identify at least one significant difference (e.g. elected Senate).

width.minimum: Describe two similarities and one difference between Australia's parliament and the Westminster system.
width.typical: Compare Australia's system of government with the Westminster system: explain that the House of Representatives and Senate parallel the House of Commons and House of Lords, but that the Australian Senate has elected members (unlike the UK Lords); describe the common features of constitutional monarchy, responsible government and parliamentary sovereignty.
wider: Investigate how Australia's constitutional development has modified the Westminster model to create a distinctively Australian hybrid system
Explore how bills move through the Australian parliament, including the role of parliamentary committees and public submissions — and compare this process with the Westminster equivalent

modes.reason: The comparison requires students to hold two systems simultaneously — use a structured comparison table before asking for an integrated explanation.

nodes.label: Values of Western democracies
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key values and beliefs of Western democracies — including freedom of speech, equality before the law, social justice, and the rule of law — and trace their origins.
criteria: Students name at least two values of Western democracies and explain what each means.
Students give one example of how each value is expressed in Australian law or institutions.

width.minimum: Name two key values of Western democracies and explain what each means in practice.
width.typical: Explain the key values of Western democracies: freedom of speech, equality before the law, social justice, and the rule of law; trace their origins in British and European democratic traditions (France, USA); explain how these values are reflected in Australian law and government.
wider: Investigate the influence of French and American democratic traditions on Australian constitutional values and identify specific features in Australian law that reflect these influences
Explore a current challenge to democratic values in Australia or another Western democracy and assess how institutions and citizens are responding to protect those values

modes.reason: Democratic values are abstract without concrete examples — students need to see each value instantiated in specific laws, events and institutions to understand what the value requires and protects.

nodes.label: How Australia's government reflects its Westminster origins and democratic values
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the key institutions of Australia's system of government, how it is based on the Westminster system, and how the system reflects key values of Western democracies.
criteria: Students explain at least two key institutions and their roles.
Students identify at least one Westminster feature of Australia's system.
Students connect at least one institutional feature to a democratic value it protects.

width.minimum: Explain two key institutions, identify one Westminster connection, and name one democratic value that the system upholds.
width.typical: Explain the key institutions of Australia's government; describe how the system is based on the Westminster system; identify the key values of Western democracies that the system reflects; and connect institutional design to value protection (e.g. how the judiciary's independence protects rule of law).
wider: Evaluate how effectively Australia's system of government upholds the values of Western democracy, identifying any gaps or tensions between the ideals and the practice
Investigate the role of the Executive in relation to policy development and legislation, and assess how the Executive's relationship to parliament reflects Westminster principles

modes.reason: The integration challenge is connecting institutional design, historical origins (Westminster), and democratic values into a coherent account. Use a structured framework that maps each institution to a democratic value it protects.

descriptors.title: Roles of government
descriptors.description: the roles and responsibilities of the 3 levels of government in Australia
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS4K08 (Local government and services): Students explain that local government provides specific services to communities. From AC9HS5K06 (Democracy, elections and representatives): Students know that elected representatives exist at different levels of government.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government in Australia — local, state/territory and federal — and understand how their responsibilities interact and sometimes overlap.

nodes.label: Three levels and their primary responsibilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the three levels of government and describe the primary roles and responsibilities of each level.
criteria: Students name the three levels of government.
Students correctly categorise at least two responsibilities for each level.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without a clear map of which level is responsible for what, students cannot analyse overlapping responsibilities, resolve confusion about who is accountable for specific issues, or understand how the federal system operates.

width.minimum: Name the three levels of government and describe at least two responsibilities of each.
width.typical: Sort and categorise the roles and responsibilities of local (roads, rubbish, parks, local planning), state/territory (schools, hospitals, police, state roads, public transport) and federal (defence, immigration, foreign affairs, social security, national laws) governments.
wider: Investigate the specific responsibilities of your local council and compare them with the responsibilities of your state government — identifying what is managed at each level and why
Examine a local community issue and identify which level of government is primarily responsible for addressing it, explaining the reasoning

modes.reason: Use a sorting activity (card sort or three-column table) to categorise responsibilities across the three levels — make the categories concrete before moving to analysis of overlap and interaction.

nodes.label: Overlapping powers and constitutional hierarchy
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify issues where multiple levels of government have overlapping powers, and explain that federal law overrides state law when they conflict on these issues.
criteria: Students give at least one example of overlapping federal and state powers.
Students explain that federal law overrides state law in cases of conflict.

width.minimum: Give one example of an area where federal and state governments both have the power to make laws, and explain what happens if they conflict.
width.typical: Identify areas of concurrent legislative power (e.g. environment, education, health) where federal and state parliaments both make laws; explain that federal law overrides state law when they conflict on concurrent issues; give examples of this happening.
wider: Investigate the Murray-Darling Basin water management as an example of multiple levels of government involvement, and evaluate the challenges of managing a shared resource across state and federal jurisdictions
Research a specific case where federal and state laws have conflicted on an environmental or social issue, and trace how the conflict was resolved

modes.reason: Concurrent powers and federal override are abstract constitutional concepts — students need concrete case examples (environment, Murray-Darling) to understand how the constitutional hierarchy operates in practice.

nodes.label: How new laws originate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how new laws originate in Australia, including from party policy, member or senator proposals, and interest group advocacy.
criteria: Students describe at least two sources of new law proposals.
Students explain one step in the pathway from proposal to legislation.

width.minimum: Describe two ways new laws can originate in Australia.
width.typical: Explain how new laws can originate: from party policy (announced during election campaigns), from suggestions by members and senators, and from interest groups and community organisations lobbying government — and trace the pathway a new law typically follows from idea to legislation.
wider: Investigate the passage of a specific piece of Australian legislation from its origins to its passing, tracing the individuals, groups and processes involved
Examine a community campaign that successfully led to new legislation, and assess what made the campaign effective

modes.reason: The law-making process involves multiple stages and actors — use a flowchart of the legislative process to make the sequence visible before students analyse how it works in specific cases.

nodes.label: The three-level system in practice
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the roles and responsibilities of the three levels of government, identify where responsibilities interact or overlap, and give examples of how each level makes and enforces laws in their community.
criteria: Students correctly describe the primary responsibilities of all three levels of government.
Students give one real-life example of each level's responsibility from their own community.
Students explain how governments at different levels interact on at least one issue.

width.minimum: Explain the roles of all three levels and give one example from daily life of each level's responsibility.
width.typical: Explain the responsibilities of local, state/territory and federal government; identify overlapping responsibilities in at least one area; describe the types of laws and regulations each level makes and who enforces them (e.g. road laws, health laws, pollution laws); connect to real examples from their own community.
wider: Map all three levels of government involvement in one community issue (e.g. environmental management, housing, transport) and evaluate whether the division of responsibilities is effective
Evaluate whether there are areas where the current distribution of responsibilities between levels could be improved, and propose a change with justification

modes.reason: The integration challenge is connecting the abstract framework (three levels, their roles) to concrete community reality (specific laws, services, enforcement). Local examples are essential for making the abstract system visible.

descriptors.title: Consumer and financial choices
descriptors.description: influences on consumer choices and strategies that can be used to help make informed personal consumer and financial choices
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5K08 (Resources, needs and wants): Students understand the types of resources and the distinction between needs and wants. Students understand that scarcity requires choices to be made about resource use.
descriptors.endpoint: Students explain the influences on consumer choices and describe strategies for making informed personal consumer and financial decisions.

nodes.label: Influences on consumer choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the range of factors that influence consumer purchasing decisions, including personal, social, economic, psychological, cultural, environmental and ethical factors.
criteria: Students identify at least three categories of consumer influence.
Students give a specific example of each category of influence they name.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who reduce consumer influence to a single factor (e.g. price) cannot analyse the complexity of real purchasing decisions or evaluate strategies for making better choices. The multi-factor framework is the prerequisite for understanding the range of strategies that follow.

width.minimum: Identify three different types of influences on consumer choices and give one example of each.
width.typical: Identify and explain the range of factors influencing consumer choices: personal preferences, social trends, economic factors (budgets, available money), psychological factors (advertising, peer pressure), and cultural, environmental, legal and ethical factors. Categorise examples of purchases using this framework.
wider: Investigate how a specific advertising or marketing strategy influences consumer behaviour — analyse an advertising campaign and assess what psychological or social levers it uses

Examine how ethical and environmental factors influence consumer choices (e.g. local vs imported products, fair trade, sustainable packaging) and evaluate whether these considerations are growing in significance

modes.reason: Use a personal spending reflection (what did you buy recently? what influenced that choice?) to make the framework concrete before applying it to case study examples.

nodes.label: Selling strategies and advertising
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare the influence of different selling and advertising strategies on consumer choices, and explain how these strategies are designed to shape purchasing decisions.
criteria: Students describe at least two selling or advertising strategies.
Students explain the technique each strategy uses to influence consumer choice.

width.minimum: Describe two selling or advertising strategies and explain how each influences consumer choices.
width.typical: Compare the influence of different advertising and selling strategies: TV and internet advertising, email promotions, peer recommendations, in-store tactics, social media influence — and explain the techniques each uses to shape consumer behaviour.
wider: Analyse a set of advertisements using media literacy tools — identifying the claims made, the techniques used, and the audience targeted
Investigate how digital advertising (including social media algorithms and targeted advertising) has changed the way businesses influence consumer choices compared with traditional advertising

modes.reason: Students benefit from analysing multiple advertising formats — the way advertising works differs significantly between TV, social media and in-store environments. Breadth across formats builds genuine critical consumer awareness.

nodes.label: Types of financial transactions and their implications
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain the different types of financial transactions (notes, coins, credit and debit cards, barter) and describe the advantages and disadvantages of each.
criteria: Students name at least three types of financial transactions.
Students explain at least one advantage and one disadvantage for at least two transaction types.

width.minimum: Name three types of financial transactions and explain one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
width.typical: Explain the range of financial transaction types: notes and coins, credit cards, debit cards, digital payments, and barter — describe the advantages and disadvantages of each type and consider how the type of transaction available may influence purchasing decisions.
wider: Investigate how digital and cashless payment systems have changed consumer behaviour, and assess the implications for record-keeping, budgeting and privacy
Explore the concept of credit and debt — when is using credit a sound financial decision and when might it lead to financial difficulty?

modes.reason: The advantages and disadvantages framework for transaction types requires careful analysis — avoid oversimplification (cash = bad, digital = good) by exploring real tradeoffs including access, privacy, spending behaviour and record-keeping.

nodes.label: Strategies for informed consumer and financial decisions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe strategies for making informed consumer and financial decisions, and evaluate how these strategies can improve personal financial choices.
criteria: Students describe at least two strategies for making informed consumer or financial decisions.
Students explain how applying these strategies leads to better financial outcomes.
Students use relevant economic terms (e.g. 'consumer', 'budget', 'advertising', 'credit', 'opportunity cost') correctly.

width.minimum: Describe two strategies for making informed consumer or financial decisions and explain how each leads to better decisions.
width.typical: Explain the strategies for making informed consumer and financial decisions: finding more information, comparing prices, keeping a record of money spent, saving for the future, and considering the effects on the family and community of purchase decisions.
wider: Develop a personal budget or spending plan that demonstrates application of informed decision-making strategies

Evaluate how purchasing decisions in a local supermarket have effects beyond the individual — on the family (opportunity cost), the local community (employment) and the environment (local vs imported products)

modes.reason: Informed financial decision-making integrates knowledge of influences (Node 1), advertising strategies (Node 2), transaction types (Node 3), and decision strategies (Node 4). Use a real or simulated purchasing decision as the integration task.

descriptors.title: Develop questions about systems
descriptors.description: develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5S01 (Develop system investigation questions): Students develop purposeful inquiry questions using probing, open-ended and practical question types. Students can frame inquiry questions across HASS stages.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop questions to investigate people, events, developments, places and systems, including ethical and system-level questions that reveal connections across economic, political and environmental dimensions.

nodes.label: Ethical and systemic question types
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop ethical questions about cultural protocol and sensitivity, and system-mapping questions that reveal connections between economic, political and environmental systems.
criteria: Students develop at least one ethical question relevant to a HASS inquiry.
Students develop at least one question that reveals a connection between two systems or disciplines.
nodes.hinge_reason: Ethical questions and system-level questions are the Year 6 extensions beyond Year 5 practice — students who cannot form these question types will conduct surface-level inquiries that miss the systemic connections that Year 6 content demands.

width.minimum: Develop one ethical question and one question that reveals a connection between two HASS systems.
width.typical: Develop a range of question types for Year 6 contexts: probing questions, open-ended questions, practical questions for enterprising behaviours, and ethical questions about cultural sensitivities and protocol. Develop questions that reveal connections across systems (e.g. 'How do the purchases my family makes influence the environment?').
wider: Mind-map a complex HASS concept (e.g. consumer decisions and environmental impact) and generate questions that reveal all significant system connections
Develop an inquiry question set that requires investigation across at least two HASS disciplines and explain how each question targets a different disciplinary lens

modes.reason: Model ethical and system-level questions explicitly, showing the difference between 'what happened?' and 'who is affected and why?' — students need to see the form of these questions before generating them independently.

nodes.label: Questions that guide all inquiry stages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a set of questions that frame and guide all stages of a HASS inquiry — before, during and after investigation — addressing relevant disciplinary concepts.
criteria: Students develop at least four inquiry questions covering different stages and purposes.
Students use at least two question types including at least one ethical or systemic question.

width.minimum: Develop a set of at least four questions that cover different stages of a HASS inquiry using at least two question types.
width.typical: Develop questions that address relevant disciplinary concepts before, during and after investigation; include probing, open-ended, practical and ethical question types; ensure questions guide investigation toward evidence-based conclusions.
wider: Develop questions for a multi-disciplinary inquiry that spans history, geography and economics, showing how each question targets a specific disciplinary concept
Evaluate a completed set of inquiry questions after investigation — assessing which questions generated the most productive inquiry and why

modes.reason: Build a question bank across multiple Year 6 inquiry topics — students improve at question design through varied practice, not repetition of the same topic.

nodes.label: Complete inquiry question set for Year 6 topics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can develop a complete inquiry question set for a Year 6 HASS topic that spans disciplines, addresses cultural sensitivities, and guides investigation from initial framing through to conclusions and action.
criteria: Students develop at least five questions covering different stages and types for a Year 6 HASS inquiry.
Questions include at least one ethical question and one question revealing system connections.
The question set addresses at least two HASS disciplines.

width.minimum: Develop a complete question set (minimum 5 questions) for a Year 6 HASS topic that includes at least one ethical question.
width.typical: Develop a complete inquiry question set for a Year 6 topic (e.g. Federation, migration, consumer choices, international interconnections) that: frames investigation stages, addresses disciplinary concepts across multiple HASS areas, includes ethical and systemic questions, and guides toward evidence-based conclusions.
wider: Design a question set for a community-based inquiry project that requires real data collection, and evaluate how each question supports the project's goals
Revisit and refine questions mid-inquiry based on what has been found so far — modelling iterative professional inquiry practice

modes.reason: A complete Year 6 inquiry question set requires integrating all question types across all disciplines — the quality measure is coherence and coverage, not just the number of questions.

descriptors.title: Organise information and data
descriptors.description: locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5S02 (Organise primary and secondary sources): Students can locate, collect and organise information from primary and secondary sources using a range of graphic organisers, maps, timelines and graphs with appropriate conventions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students locate, collect and organise information and data from primary and secondary sources in a range of formats, using appropriate methods including digital tools, fieldwork, surveys and spatial technologies.

nodes.label: Selecting appropriate methods for collecting information
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine the most appropriate method for finding information for a specific inquiry purpose, selecting from personal observation, interviews, surveys, internet searches, census data, and primary and secondary sources.
criteria: Students identify an appropriate collection method for at least two different inquiry purposes.
Students explain why each method is the best choice for the inquiry type.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who always default to internet search as their collection method will miss the richer data that surveys, interviews, fieldwork and census data provide. Method selection is the first decision that shapes what evidence is available for analysis.

width.minimum: Identify the most appropriate method for finding information for one inquiry purpose and explain why it is the best choice.
width.typical: Determine appropriate information-collection methods for different inquiry purposes: personal observation, interviews, surveys, internet searches, census data, library catalogues, excursions and field trips — and explain why different methods are more appropriate for different types of questions.
wider: Compare the information yielded by two different collection methods for the same inquiry question (e.g. survey vs interview) and evaluate what each reveals and omits
Plan and conduct a field trip or excursion (virtual or actual) to collect primary data for a HASS inquiry, applying appropriate observation and recording strategies

modes.reason: Use a method-selection decision framework: What kind of question is this? What kind of data would answer it? Which collection method produces that data? Apply to multiple inquiry examples before students make independent choices.

nodes.label: Evaluating sources and identifying key words
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use key words to search for relevant information and evaluate sources, recognising that domain names (com, edu, gov) indicate source provenance.
criteria: Students identify appropriate keywords for at least one HASS inquiry search.
Students correctly explain what edu, gov and com domain names indicate about a source.

width.minimum: Identify appropriate search keywords for an inquiry and explain what domain names (com, edu, gov) indicate about source provenance.
width.typical: Identify key words for effective information searches using search engines and library catalogues; evaluate sources using domain names as provenance indicators (com = commercial, edu = educational, gov = government); assess source relevance and reliability.
wider: Develop and apply an advanced search strategy (including Boolean operators and domain filtering) to find high-quality sources for a specific HASS inquiry
Evaluate the difference between search results from edu/gov sources versus com sources on the same topic — and assess what each reveals about perspective and reliability

modes.reason: Digital search skills degrade without consistent practice — key word selection and domain-based provenance evaluation need to be applied regularly across inquiry tasks, not just taught once.

nodes.label: Creating maps and spatial representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create maps using spatial technologies and cartographic conventions appropriate to the inquiry purpose, including flow maps and large-scale location maps.
criteria: Students create at least one map with all required cartographic conventions applied correctly.
The map communicates HASS data relevant to the inquiry purpose.

width.minimum: Create one map using appropriate cartographic conventions (border, source, scale, legend, title, north point) relevant to a HASS inquiry.
width.typical: Create maps using spatial technologies and cartographic conventions — including large-scale location maps (places and features in Australia and Asia) and flow maps (showing connections such as shipping routes or migration flows) — applying all required conventions correctly.
wider: Create a digital map using spatial technologies to display Year 6 inquiry data (e.g. Australia's connections with Asia, migration patterns, three levels of government jurisdictions) and explain the design choices made
Compare a hand-drawn map with a digital map of the same information and evaluate the advantages of each medium for communication

modes.reason: Cartographic conventions require precision and consistent practice — particularly flow maps, which are a new format at Year 6. Errors in conventions undermine geographic communication.

nodes.label: Organising multi-source information for a Year 6 inquiry
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate, collect and organise information and data from multiple primary and secondary sources in a range of formats, selecting appropriate tools and applying relevant conventions.
criteria: Students collect information from at least two source types for a HASS inquiry.
Students organise information using at least two appropriate tools with relevant conventions applied.
Students explain why they selected the tools they used.

width.minimum: Collect information from at least two different source types and organise it using at least two appropriate organisational tools.
width.typical: Locate, collect and organise information from a range of sources (internet, primary sources, surveys, census data, field work, visual materials) for a Year 6 HASS inquiry; select appropriate organisational tools (maps, timelines, flow charts, tables, bibliography templates); apply relevant conventions throughout.
wider: Design a complete information organisation system for a complex Year 6 inquiry — specifying which tools will be used for which information and why
Evaluate the organisation of a completed inquiry — assess whether the tools chosen made the information accessible and useful, and identify improvements

modes.reason: Organising multi-source information at Year 6 requires deliberate planning — students need to make conscious decisions about tools, formats and conventions before collecting, not after. Scaffold the planning phase.

descriptors.title: Identify patterns and relationships
descriptors.description: evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, or to infer relationships
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5S03 (Evaluate patterns and trends): Students can identify patterns and trends in information and data across a range of formats, and infer relationships. Students can read and analyse multiple graph types.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate information and data in a range of formats to identify and describe patterns and trends, and infer cause-effect relationships, including across historical, geographic and social domains.

nodes.label: Causes, effects and significance in historical data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine sources to identify the causes, effects and significance of past events and developments, using evidence to support their analysis.
criteria: Students identify at least one cause, one effect and one indicator of significance for a past event.
Students support each component with reference to source evidence.
nodes.hinge_reason: The move to cause-effect-significance analysis is more demanding than Year 5 pattern identification — students who cannot systematically identify causes AND effects AND significance will reduce complex historical analysis to simple description.

width.minimum: Identify the causes and effects of one past event or development using at least one source.
width.typical: Examine sources to identify causes, effects and significance of past events and developments — such as the Wave Hill walk-off, Wik decision, health policies and migration policies — and explain how these events have brought about change.
wider: Analyse the causes, effects and significance of two related events and assess how one contributed to the other (causal chain analysis)
Investigate how different historians have assessed the significance of the same event — and explain why significance assessments may differ

modes.reason: Use an explicit causes/effects/significance framework applied to a worked example before students apply it independently. The three-part structure requires deliberate scaffolding.

nodes.label: Identifying patterns using graphic organisers and maps
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use graphic organisers, maps and concept maps to identify patterns, trends and cause-effect relationships in HASS data.
criteria: Students use a graphic organiser or map to identify a pattern, trend or relationship.
Students describe what the pattern, trend or relationship shows about the HASS topic.

width.minimum: Use one graphic organiser or map to identify a pattern, trend or relationship in HASS data.
width.typical: Use graphic organisers (maps, concept maps, tables, charts) to identify patterns — such as settlement in regional agricultural areas — trends (e.g. changes in Australian immigration statistics) and cause-effect relationships (e.g. war and refugee movement, consumer decisions and environmental sustainability).
wider: Create a concept map that traces the system of causes and effects for a complex Year 6 topic (e.g. how consumer decisions affect environment and community), identifying second and third-order effects
Analyse Australian immigration statistics across multiple decades using a graph, identifying trends and proposing explanations for each change observed

modes.reason: Students benefit from using multiple graphic tools across different topics — each tool reveals different features of the data. Build a repertoire of analytical tools rather than deepening expertise in one.

nodes.label: Evaluating past attitudes and proposing reasons for change
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate attitudes and actions of the past that seem strange or unacceptable by contemporary standards, and propose reasons why values and social norms change over time.
criteria: Students identify at least one past attitude or practice that is no longer considered acceptable.
Students explain why it was accepted at the time and why values have changed.

width.minimum: Identify one past attitude or practice that is no longer acceptable and propose one reason why values changed.
width.typical: Evaluate attitudes and actions of the past that now seem unacceptable (e.g. deportation of South Sea Islanders, denial of voting rights, institutional child care practices), propose reasons why these were accepted at the time and why values changed; reflect on what aspects of current society might be viewed similarly in the future.
wider: Investigate a specific historical shift in social values (e.g. attitudes toward immigration, gender equality) and trace the events, movements and arguments that drove the change
Reflect on a current issue and propose which aspects of contemporary society might be judged negatively by future generations — and what this suggests about the nature of social progress

modes.reason: Evaluating past attitudes requires students to hold two temporal frames simultaneously (past context and present standards) — scaffold explicitly by asking students to explain both what was accepted then and why it is not now.

nodes.label: Evaluating data to identify patterns and infer relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate information and data from multiple formats to identify patterns and trends, and infer cause-effect relationships, using evidence to support their analysis.
criteria: Students identify at least one pattern and infer at least one cause-effect relationship from evidence.
Students support their analysis with reference to at least two sources or data formats.
Students acknowledge ambiguity or limitations in the evidence where appropriate.

width.minimum: Identify a pattern or trend and infer a cause-effect relationship from information in at least two formats.
width.typical: Evaluate information and data from a range of formats (maps, charts, written sources, graphic organisers, historical sources) to identify patterns, trends and cause-effect relationships across Year 6 HASS topics; support inferences with evidence; acknowledge where evidence is ambiguous or incomplete.
wider: Evaluate competing explanations for a historical pattern and assess which has stronger evidential support
Propose reasons why socially sustainable practices (negotiation, arbitration, reconciliation, cultural mediation) resolve issues peacefully — drawing on patterns identified from historical examples

modes.reason: Integrated pattern analysis across formats and topics requires students to bring together data literacy, historical thinking and cause-effect reasoning. Support with a structured analysis protocol.

descriptors.title: Evaluate sources and perspectives
descriptors.description: evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives
descriptors.knowledge: From AC9HS5S04 (Evaluate source purpose and perspective): Students can evaluate sources for origin, purpose and perspective, identify bias and stereotypes, and compare accounts from different sources. Students apply a source analysis framework independently.
descriptors.endpoint: Students evaluate primary and secondary sources to determine origin, purpose and perspectives, including identifying persuasive techniques, distinguishing fact from opinion, and assessing the relevance and context of sources.

nodes.label: Publication details and content evaluation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can examine a source's publishing details and content to clarify its purpose, distinguish fact from opinion, identify potential bias, assess its relevance, and contextualise its information.
criteria: Students examine at least one source using at least three evaluation criteria (purpose, fact/opinion, bias, relevance, context).
Students correctly distinguish at least one fact from one opinion in the source.
nodes.hinge_reason: Source evaluation at Year 6 requires integrating multiple criteria simultaneously — students who evaluate on one criterion only (e.g. just checking for bias) will miss the complex interplay between origin, purpose, content and context that determines usefulness.

width.minimum: For one source, examine publishing details and content to identify purpose, one example of fact vs opinion, and one indicator of potential bias.
width.typical: For a range of primary and secondary sources, examine publishing details (author, publisher, date, type) and content to: clarify purpose, distinguish fact from opinion, identify potential bias, assess relevance, and place information in historical or geographic context.
wider: Apply a systematic source audit protocol to a set of sources used in an inquiry — document findings for each source and assess how source quality affects inquiry reliability
Investigate how publication date affects interpretation — compare a government report from the 1950s with a contemporary one on the same social topic and explain what has changed and why

modes.reason: Use a multi-criteria evaluation frame (purpose / fact vs opinion / bias / relevance / context) applied consistently to each source — the Year 6 challenge is applying all criteria to every source, not just one at a time.

nodes.label: Identifying persuasive techniques
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify persuasive techniques in sources, including modality language and passive voice, and explain why writers use these techniques.
criteria: Students identify at least one persuasive technique in a source.
Students explain why the writer used the technique and what effect it has on the reader.

width.minimum: Identify one persuasive technique in a source and explain how it is used to shape the reader's view.
width.typical: Identify persuasive techniques in sources: modality language (would, could, may, might — hedging claims), passive voice ('It is claimed that...' versus active 'The government claims...'), and other techniques — and explain what each technique does and why the writer chose it.
wider: Compare a factual report and a persuasive text on the same HASS topic, identifying all persuasive techniques in the second text and evaluating their effectiveness
Analyse a political speech or campaign material for persuasive techniques and assess how the techniques shape the audience's perception of the issue

modes.reason: Modality and passive voice are linguistic concepts that require explicit instruction — model these techniques with annotated examples before students identify them independently.

nodes.label: Discussing contested perspectives and proposing reasons
nodes.checkpoint: Students can discuss issues explored in sources where there were or are a range of views, and propose reasons for why perspectives differ.
criteria: Students identify at least two perspectives on a contested issue.
Students propose at least one reason why perspectives differ.

width.minimum: For one contested issue, describe two different perspectives and propose one reason why they differ.
width.typical: Discuss issues explored through sources where there are or were multiple views (e.g. deportation of South Sea Islanders, women's vote, sustainable environment management, migration) — identify the perspectives represented, explain what each view involves, and propose reasons for why perspectives differ.
wider: Evaluate points of view about a sustainability issue using sources representing producers' and consumers' perspectives, and assess the expertise of each source expressing a view

Investigate a historically contested decision (e.g. deportation of Pacific Islanders, immigration restriction) from multiple perspectives and evaluate which perspective has stronger evidential support

modes.reason: Contested perspectives are best understood by comparing multiple different viewpoints — not just 'for and against' but examining what different groups valued and why. Breadth of perspectives is the key enrichment direction.

nodes.label: Integrated source evaluation across a Year 6 inquiry
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a range of primary and secondary sources for origin, purpose and perspectives, applying persuasive technique analysis and multi-criteria evaluation to assess each source's usefulness.
criteria: Students evaluate at least two sources using at least three evaluation criteria each.
Students identify persuasive technique in at least one source.
Students assess each source's usefulness for the inquiry and explain the reasoning.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two sources using multiple criteria (origin, purpose, perspective, persuasive technique) and assess the usefulness of each for an inquiry.
width.typical: Evaluate a set of primary and secondary sources across a Year 6 inquiry: examine publishing details, distinguish fact from opinion, identify persuasive techniques, assess bias and relevance, consider historical and geographic context, and explain how each source's origin, purpose and perspective affects its usefulness.
wider: Produce a source evaluation report for a Year 6 inquiry that documents findings for each source and explains how source quality influenced the inquiry conclusions
Evaluate a source set for coverage gaps — identify perspectives, time periods or types of evidence that are not represented, and explain how these gaps affect the conclusions that can be drawn

modes.reason: Integrated source evaluation at Year 6 requires applying all criteria (origin, purpose, fact/opinion, persuasive technique, relevance, context) simultaneously and making a usefulness judgment. Support with a structured evaluation template.

descriptors.title: Develop evidence-based conclusions
descriptors.description: develop evidence-based conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: Students develop evidence-based conclusions (AC9HS5S05). At Y5, they identify valid evidence, distinguish evidence-based conclusions from those based on personal preference or limited sources, and draw conclusions from primary and secondary sources considering differing information. They have practised using source analysis from AC9HS5S04 to feed conclusions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students develop evidence-based conclusions.

nodes.label: Distinguishing evidence from bias and limited sourcing
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify the difference between a conclusion grounded in valid evidence and one shaped by personal bias, preference, or reliance on limited sources.
criteria: Correctly identifies at least one feature that makes a conclusion evidence-based (specific source, verifiable information).
Names at least one way a conclusion can be weakened (bias, personal preference, limited sources).
Does not treat all conclusions as equally valid regardless of evidence quality.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without the ability to distinguish evidence quality, students cannot construct valid conclusions in N2 — they will conflate preference with evidence and the conclusion-building task collapses into opinion writing.

width.minimum: Given two contrasting conclusions on a HASS topic, identify which is better supported by evidence and explain why the weaker conclusion falls short (bias, preference, or limited sourcing).
width.typical: Examine a set of primary and secondary sources and identify which conclusions are well-evidenced and which reflect bias, personal preference, or selective use of sources. Explain the specific weakness in each flawed conclusion.
wider: Analyse historical examples where conclusions based on limited or biased sources led to significant consequences (e.g. early colonial accounts of First Nations peoples).
Compare how different source types (census data, personal narratives, government records) produce different conclusions about the same event — and evaluate which provides stronger evidence.

modes.reason: A worked example comparing a flawed and a sound conclusion — with explicit criteria — is the appropriate scaffold here. The risk is students applying intuitive agreement/disagreement rather than evidentiary criteria.

nodes.label: Drawing conclusions from identified evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students draw conclusions from identified evidence across primary and secondary sources, including sources with differing information.
criteria: Conclusion is explicitly linked to at least two named sources.
Acknowledges at least one source that complicates or qualifies the conclusion.
Conclusion is framed as following from evidence, not as personal opinion.

width.minimum: Draw a conclusion about a HASS topic using at least two identified sources, stating which evidence supports the conclusion.
width.typical: Draw conclusions that synthesise evidence from multiple primary and secondary sources, including sources that offer different or conflicting perspectives. Acknowledge where evidence is stronger or weaker, and explain how conflicting information was weighed.
wider: Use census data alongside personal narrative sources to construct an argument about migration patterns — explaining how quantitative and qualitative evidence complement and sometimes contradict each other.
Draw conclusions about a governance topic (e.g. suffrage reform) using evidence from at least three source types, explicitly addressing the strongest counter-evidence.

modes.reason: Wider students can apply evidence-based conclusion-building to additional inquiry contexts (migration, civic action, environmental decisions) without escalating cognitive demand beyond the descriptor's command term.

nodes.label: Conclusions demonstrating conceptual understanding and question alignment
nodes.checkpoint: Students develop conclusions that demonstrate consideration of inquiry questions, understanding of disciplinary concepts, and identified evidence — forming a coherent, disciplined response to their inquiry.
criteria: Conclusion explicitly references the original inquiry question.
Uses at least one disciplinary concept correctly in the conclusion.
Shows that the conclusion is derived from evidence, not merely consistent with personal views.
Acknowledges at least one complicating factor or alternative perspective.

width.minimum: Produce a conclusion that refers back to the original inquiry question, incorporates at least one disciplinary concept (e.g. federation, migration, democracy, sustainability), and is supported by evidence from at least two sources.
width.typical: Develop a well-structured conclusion that explicitly addresses the inquiry question, demonstrates understanding of relevant disciplinary concepts across the full HASS inquiry (history, geography, civics or economics), and synthesises evidence from primary and secondary sources including conflicting perspectives.
wider: Develop conclusions that address a complex inquiry question requiring integration of evidence from multiple HASS disciplines (e.g. a question about migration with historical, geographical and civic dimensions).

Evaluate the conclusions of a published historical or geographical account against the evidence it uses, identifying where the author's disciplinary understanding strengthens or limits their conclusion.

modes.reason: This node synthesises the prior two — evidence quality judgement and source-based conclusion-drawing — into a full inquiry conclusion. Integration is the appropriate response mode.
Wider students can develop conclusions for additional inquiry topics across HASS disciplines, applying the same disciplined conclusion-building process to new conceptual territory.

descriptors.title: Assess possible effects
descriptors.description: propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to assess the possible effects
descriptors.knowledge: Students propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to assess the possible effects (AC9HS5S06). At Y5, they forecast probable futures, undertake response projects, participate in democratic processes, and make judgements about how effectively challenges have been addressed. They can apply basic criteria to evaluate response options.
descriptors.endpoint: Students propose actions or responses to issues or challenges and use criteria to assess the possible effects.

nodes.label: Identifying and applying criteria to evaluate options
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify relevant criteria for evaluating response options to a HASS issue or challenge, and apply those criteria to assess at least two possible actions.
criteria: Names at least two criteria relevant to the specific issue being investigated.
Applies criteria to at least two distinct response options.
Does not conflate personal preference with criteria-based assessment.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without criteria selection and application skills, students cannot meaningfully assess possible effects in N2 — they will offer unreasoned preference for one option without systematic comparative analysis.

width.minimum: Given an issue and two proposed responses, identify at least two criteria relevant to the issue and use those criteria to compare the options.
width.typical: Identify and justify a set of criteria appropriate to a specific issue (economic, environmental, social, cultural factors), then apply those criteria systematically to compare multiple proposed responses, explaining how each response performs against each criterion.
wider: Investigate how formal evaluation criteria are used in real-world decision-making (e.g. criteria for Australian of the Year, Order of Australia, school captain selection) and compare these with the criteria the class develops for their own issue.
Compare the criteria used by different stakeholders for the same issue and explain why different parties prioritise different criteria.

modes.reason: A decision matrix or structured comparison tool is the appropriate scaffold — students need the criteria visible and consistently applied before synthesis is attempted.

Wider: criteria application can extend to additional issue contexts (environmental, civic, economic) where different criteria sets are appropriate. Each new context requires the same skill in a new domain.

nodes.label: Proposing and planning responses with assessed effects
nodes.checkpoint: Students propose or plan a response to an identified issue or challenge and assess the possible effects of that response using criteria, including consideration of risks and alternative views.
criteria: Proposal is clearly linked to an identified issue or challenge.
At least two criteria are used to assess possible effects.
At least one possible negative effect or risk is identified alongside strategies to address it.
Demonstrates that criteria (not personal preference alone) shaped the assessment.

width.minimum: Propose one response to a real HASS issue and assess its possible effects using at least two criteria, identifying one risk or limitation of the response.
width.typical: Plan a response to a HASS challenge (civic, environmental, economic) with a specification of actions and rationale; assess possible social, cultural, economic and environmental effects using identified criteria; acknowledge alternative views and identify strategies to minimise negative effects.
wider: Plan, execute and evaluate a school-based or community response project (e.g. environmental action, school council proposal, fundraising campaign), assessing its effects against predetermined criteria throughout.

Use the elaboration's negotiation and consensus-building approach: present a proposed response, incorporate critique from peers representing alternative stakeholder views, and revise the proposal accordingly.

modes.reason: Wider students can apply the propose-assess-effects process across multiple issue domains (civic, environmental, economic), with each domain bringing different criteria and effects into focus.

Students who engage with the full project cycle (plan, execute, evaluate against criteria) are building a practitioner repertoire for civic and environmental response — the thinking is only fully legible through enacted work.

descriptors.title: Communicate findings and viewpoints
descriptors.description: present descriptions and explanations, drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, and using relevant terms and conventions
descriptors.knowledge: Students present descriptions and explanations, drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources and using relevant terms and conventions (AC9HS5S07). At Y5, they select and reference ideas from visual and written sources, and use accurate subject-appropriate terminology across HASS disciplines. Their presentations are primarily descriptive and explanatory.
descriptors.endpoint: Students present descriptions and explanations, drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources, and using relevant terms and conventions.

nodes.label: Selecting, referencing and integrating source material
nodes.checkpoint: Students select relevant findings and viewpoints from a range of source types and integrate them into a description or explanation, with appropriate referencing.
criteria: At least two source types are referenced in the presentation.
Sources are integrated into the explanation rather than listed separately at the end.
Does not present source content as personal opinion or without attribution.
nodes.hinge_reason: Without source integration skills, students cannot satisfy the descriptor's 'drawing ideas, findings and viewpoints from sources' requirement in N2 — they will produce personal opinions dressed as explanations.

width.minimum: Select ideas and findings from at least two source types (e.g. a graph and a written source) and integrate them into a coherent description or explanation, referencing each source.
width.typical: Select and reference findings and viewpoints from a variety of source formats — journals, diaries, graphs, tables, timelines, photographs — integrating them into a description or explanation that shows how different sources support the account.
wider: Integrate sources representing conflicting viewpoints and show in the presentation how the tension between sources was handled.
Develop a multimodal presentation that combines written explanation with visual evidence (maps, photographs, data) and explains how each source type contributes differently to the account.

modes.reason: Source integration requires modelling — annotated examples showing how a source sentence becomes part of an explanation are appropriate here before independent production.

nodes.label: Composing informative and persuasive HASS texts
nodes.checkpoint: Students compose informative and/or persuasive descriptions and explanations supported by evidence, using relevant HASS disciplinary terms and conventions, to present conclusions from their inquiry.
criteria: Text is clearly informative or persuasive in purpose and structure.
Uses at least three discipline-appropriate terms accurately.
Conclusions drawn are supported by referenced evidence from sources.
Conventions of the chosen text type are applied consistently.

width.minimum: Compose an informative text presenting conclusions from a HASS inquiry, using discipline-appropriate terms and at least two referenced sources.
width.typical: Compose both informative and persuasive texts that present inquiry conclusions using accurate disciplinary terminology (historical, geographical, civics, economics), appropriate conventions (e.g. argument structure, referencing), and evidence drawn from a range of identified sources including conflicting viewpoints.
wider: Compose a persuasive text that presents a reasoned position on a contested HASS issue, explicitly addressing counter-arguments with evidence.
Produce a multimodal presentation (e.g. documentary-style, oral argument with visual evidence) that applies conventions appropriate to the chosen form while maintaining evidentiary rigour.

modes.reason: Wider students can compose texts across multiple inquiry disciplines (historical argument, geographical explanation, civic position paper), each applying the same communication skill in a different disciplinary register.
Composing persuasive text with counter-argument and multimodal presentation builds a communication repertoire that is only demonstrable through the produced work — not separable from the task.
